In announcing their plans to combine, DoorDash and Instacart said that the acquisition would help its retailer partners, both large and small, better reach customers with innovative technology.

DoorDash said it expects to retain Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products and app. Until the transaction closes, the companies will continue to operate separately.

Founded in 2013, DoorDash initially grew its business as a restaurant delivery provider and expanded into grocery and non-food delivery in recent years.

Founded in 2012, Instacart initially focused on grocery e-commerce before expanding into providing in-store technology like digital shelf labels and smart carts. The company also built out a food as medicine initiative called Instacart Health and added restaurant and non-food retailers as delivery partners.

The deal will give DoorDash access to Instacart’s many grocery partnerships as well as its more than 600,000 delivery couriers, e-commerce capabilities and millions of users. The acquisition also serves up a sizable retail media business — Instacart’s advertising and other revenue totaled $331 million in its third quarter.

Instacart’s ad revenue accounts for roughly 30% of the company’s total revenue, based on its third-quarter results.

Over the last three years, both companies have consistently recorded year-over-year quarterly growth in orders and revenue. DoorDash’s nearly $4.6 billion in Q3 revenue was roughly four times that of Instacart’s.

Year-over-year quarterly revenue growth over the last three years

Both companies have worked on tackling grocery affordability concerns for consumers. Instacart has shared that it is pushing its retailer partners to match their online prices with those in their stores. Meanwhile, DoorDash has rolled out consumer-facing tools to make it easier for shoppers to find savings or understand what their grocery bill will look like.

At Groceryshop in September, top executives at the companies said that addressing the cost concerns that have long plagued grocery e-commerce is becoming a pressing issue for the grocery industry amid ongoing consumer price sensitivity.

DoorDash said the deal would give consumers more choice and savings opportunities in delivery, while delivery couriers get more opportunities to earn money.

The aggregate transaction consideration will be at least 75% cash, according to the announcements, noting that Instacart stockholders will be able to elect cash, DoorDash stock or a combination of both, subject to proration so that DoorDash stock does not exceed 25% of the aggregate consideration. Instacart’s board of directors has unanimously approved the agreement.

Since going public in mid 2023, Instacart’s stock price has risen about 40%.

At approximately $74 billion, DoorDash’s market capitalization is roughly five times that of Instacart, which sits at roughly $14 billion, according to Yahoo! Finance.

text:
NPR: What’s Gone Up Even Faster Than Gas Or Rent? The Cost Of Caregiving

As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average. The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index. (McGowan, 10/28)

Current and former leaders at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on Wednesday advised Medicare beneficiaries to pay close attention to their options this year upon reenrolling in plans, as major changes in recent years have only made the landscape more complex. Speaking at The Hill’s “Bang for Your Buck: Get the Most from Your 2027 Medicare Benefits” event in partnership with the Alliance for Aging Research, CMS Deputy Administrator John Brooks and former CMS Chief Operating Officer Jonathan Blum both noted how provisions in the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), such as the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, had changed how Medicare benefits are handled. Although most observers agree that the No Surprises Act did fix one problem -- nixing unexpected bills for out-of-network care -- lawmakers are still trying to fix other problems caused by the law. The act, passed at the end of 2020, was designed to protect patients who received bills for out-of-network care -- often emergency care -- even though the care was delivered at an in-network facility. text:
By Patrick Wingrove

Oct 29 (Reuters) – Eli Lilly raised its full-year revenue forecast and beat third-quarter earnings expectations on Thursday, propelled by surging demand for injectable weight-loss drugs that could allay investor concerns about price erosion in US government health plans.

The Indianapolis-based drugmaker now expects full-year revenue of $91 billion to $92 billion, underscoring its expanding lead in the multibillion-dollar GLP-1 market over Danish rival Novo Nordisk that has propelled Lilly to a $1.2 trillion market valuation.

Lilly trimmed its adjusted profit outlook, however, to $35.00 to $36.00 per share, as $4.57 per share of acquired research charges from recent deals more than offset a $4.07 improvement in underlying profit guidance at the midpoint. The charges, taken in the third quarter, are primarily related to the acquisitions of AtaiBeckley and Curevo, Lilly said.

Lilly has been investing for growth beyond its GLP-1 drugs through internal research, tuck-in acquisitions and partnerships.

Shares of the company rose nearly 5% to $1,350 before the bell.

Lilly previously forecast revenue of $85.0 billion to $87.0 billion and earnings of $35.50 to $36.50 per share.

Lilly posted third-quarter revenue of $24.4 billion, topping analyst expectations of $22.61 billion, while adjusted profit of $7.48 per share beat estimates of $6.26, according to LSEG data.

Revenue included about $900 million of benefits, primarily $410 million of milestone payments tied to diabetes drug Jardiance, which Lilly said are the last it expects to receive, and favorable adjustments to rebate and discount estimates.

Third-quarter sales of diabetes drug Mounjaro reached $10.72 billion, topping Wall Street expectations of $10.16 billion, according to LSEG data, while its related obesity injection Zepbound brought in $5.35 billion versus estimates of $5.09 billion.

The robust sales will help ease market worries that severe price erosion from the $50-a-month price tag for Medicare recipients would outweigh explosive volume gains. Analysts at Bernstein said data showed that Lilly had captured about 70% of the 700,000 Medicare patients who recently initiated treatment with a GLP-1 medication.

While the new US pilot unlocked coverage for potentially millions who use the government’s Medicare program for people aged 65 and over, the bulk of Lilly’s non-reimbursed volume has historically moved through its $449-a-month cash-pay platform, raising stakes over how the discounts will impact long-term margins.

Lilly’s newer obesity pill Foundayo brought in $184 million, compared with analyst estimates of $216.86 million.

Investors are closely tracking the Foundayo rollout as a key test of whether Lilly can blunt Novo Nordisk’s first-mover edge with its oral Wegovy.

While initial US Foundayo prescriptions have trailed its Danish rival, some investors have downplayed the early lag, expecting the Lilly pill to emerge as a significant growth driver as it launches in more international markets.

Oral Wegovy led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, and Foundayo about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, in separate studies.

Foundayo was launched in the US and Britain earlier this year and could potentially begin selling in other European countries by year-end.

Lilly’s realized prices fell 15% in the third quarter, offsetting part of a 53% rise in volume. US prices fell 7%, a decline Lilly attributed primarily to Zepbound and said was partly offset by adjustments to rebate and discount estimates. Outside the US, prices fell 29%, driven mainly by Mounjaro’s inclusion on China’s national reimbursement drug list.

Even as Lilly’s obesity injections maintain commercial momentum, Wall Street’s attention is shifting toward retatrutide, the company’s next-generation weight-loss candidate slated for regulatory submission next year.

Retatrutide has been shown to drive average weight loss of 24% in midstage trials, topping results from drugs already on the market.

text:
Air Liquide expects its 200MW Normand'Hy electrolyser in northern France to produce its first hydrogen before the end of 2026, with the plant entering a phased commissioning programme.

The facility is designed to produce up to 28,000 tonnes of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen annually, with TotalEnergies' Gonfreville refinery among its principal customers and a quarter of capacity reserved for hydrogen mobility.

Air Liquide expects its 200MW Normand'Hy electrolyser in Normandy to produce its first hydrogen before the end of 2026, marking the start of commissioning at one of Europe's largest PEM electrolysis projects.

The more than €400 million [$445.9 million] plant, located in the Port-Jérôme industrial zone near Le Havre, is designed to produce up to 28,000 tonnes of renewable and low-carbon hydrogen a year for industrial and transport customers.

Air Liquide highlighted Normand'Hy at its October 5 Capital Markets Day. During its October 29 third-quarter earnings call, the company confirmed that the first hydrogen molecules were expected within weeks. Production will begin with one train, followed by the second and a gradual increase in output.

First hydrogen production will be a commissioning milestone and will not mean the full 200MW facility has reached commercial operation at design capacity.

Siemens Energy Supplies 12 PEM Electrolyser Modules

Normand'Hy uses proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis technology supplied through the manufacturing partnership between Air Liquide and Siemens Energy.

The facility incorporates 12 electrolyser modules manufactured through the companies' joint venture, which operates an electrolyser production plant in Berlin.

The new electrolyser will be connected to Air Liquide's existing hydrogen pipeline network serving the Normandy industrial basin.

That network already supplies hydrogen to refining and chemical facilities in the region. Normand'Hy will allow hydrogen produced by electrolysis to enter the established industrial supply system.

TotalEnergies will provide renewable electricity corresponding to the hydrogen supplied to its refinery, equivalent to 100MW of electrolysis capacity.

For the remaining electricity requirements, Air Liquide has outlined plans to secure renewable power purchase agreements, supplemented by low-carbon electricity from the French grid.

Air Liquide expects commissioning to proceed progressively as the two production trains enter operation.

TotalEnergies Refinery Among Main Hydrogen Customers

A substantial share of Normand'Hy's production is intended for industrial customers, particularly TotalEnergies' Gonfreville refining and petrochemical platform.

Under the agreement announced in September 2023, Air Liquide will supply the refinery with renewable and low-carbon hydrogen corresponding to 100MW of electrolysis capacity.

The wider Normandy hydrogen supply arrangement includes approximately 10,000 tonnes of green hydrogen and up to 5,000 tonnes of low-carbon hydrogen annually, according to TotalEnergies' regulatory disclosures.

Those figures cover the broader supply arrangement and should not all be treated as hydrogen produced exclusively by the new electrolyser.

The companies estimate that the arrangement could reduce emissions at the Gonfreville platform by up to 150,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually.

The reduction remains a projection and will depend on actual hydrogen deliveries and the displacement of existing production.

Air Liquide plans to allocate approximately three-quarters of Normand'Hy's production capacity to industrial customers in Normandy.

€50 Million Hydrogen Supply Chain Planned for Transport

The remaining quarter of the electrolyser's capacity is intended to support hydrogen mobility along the Seine corridor, stretching from Le Havre towards Paris.

In November 2024, Air Liquide announced an additional €50 million [$55.7 million] investment in hydrogen packaging and distribution infrastructure to supply refuelling stations.

The company has also signed a renewable hydrogen supply agreement with HysetCo, which operates hydrogen-powered vehicle fleets and refuelling infrastructure in France.

The new distribution facilities are intended to serve hydrogen taxis, buses, commercial vehicles and trucks along the Seine corridor.

Together with the electrolyser, Air Liquide's investment in the Normandy hydrogen production and distribution programme exceeds €450 million [$501.6 million].

French Government Provides €190 Million Support

Air Liquide committed more than €400 million [$445.9 million] to the construction of Normand'Hy.

The project received €190 million [$211.8 million] in French government support under the Important Projects of Common European Interest framework, through France's recovery programme.

At full planned capacity, Air Liquide estimates that Normand'Hy could avoid up to 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually by replacing conventional hydrogen production.

That figure is a projected emissions reduction rather than a measured result from the new plant.

Air Liquide is also developing the 200MW ELYgator electrolyser in Rotterdam, Netherlands, where commissioning is targeted for late 2027.

ELYgator is designed to produce approximately 23,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually, with TotalEnergies among its contracted customers.

For Normand'Hy, Air Liquide has confirmed that initial hydrogen production is approaching, but has not announced a date for the plant to reach its full 200MW operating capacity.

title: STTGDC backs Tokyo data center growth with $588M green loan - Light Reading
description:

It is arranged in compliance with the Green Loan Principles, connecting the loan to established environmental eligibility standards.
STTGDC TYO1, the company's first operational data center in Japan, has already achieved LEED Gold certification.

text:
STTGDC, a Singapore-based data center operator which recently underwent a brand refresh, has secured a green loan facility worth 93 billion Japanese yen (US$588.46 million), which will be used to finance the fit-out and subsequent operations of its first two facilities in its data center campus in the Greater Tokyo area.

Standard Chartered acted as lead coordinator for the financing, alongside Mizuho Bank, OCBC, Société Générale and UOB. Standard Chartered and Société Générale also served as green loan coordinators.

It is arranged in compliance with the Green Loan Principles, connecting the loan to established environmental eligibility standards. These include the data centers attaining an agreed green building certification and achieving a design power usage effectiveness (PUE) ratio of 1.3 or below.

"The green-loan structure aligns our financing strategy with the environmental performance of the assets we develop, reinforcing how sustainability is integrated into our capital allocation and investment decisions," said Nelson Lim, group chief financial officer at STTGDC.

STTGDC TYO1, the company's first operational data center in Japan, has already achieved LEED Gold certification. It is designed to achieve an annualized PUE of less than 1.25. Its closed-loop cooling system is intended to minimize operational water use, with no ongoing water consumption during normal operations.

The facility has obtained ISO 22301, ISO 27001 and ISO/IEC 20000 certifications, and adheres to the guidelines of the Japan Data Centre Council. Since starting operations, it has maintained carbon-neutral operations for Scope 1 and 2 emissions while pursuing the procurement of renewable energy and improvements in energy efficiency.

The STTGDC TYO2 is being developed to support high-density AI and accelerated computing workloads, with provisions for the future deployment of liquid cooling. The project is also targeting TIA-942-C Design Certification and LEED Gold.

Long-term commitment to Japan

STTGDC's Tokyo campus, located within the Goodman Business Park in Inzai City, has been designed to provide a combined IT capacity of 70.8MW in order to support the expanding cloud, AI and other mission-critical digital workloads of hyperscalers, cloud service providers and enterprise customers.

Kiyoshi Maeda, the company's CEO-Japan, pointed out that customers need infrastructure that can grow with their ambitions while delivering the resilience and efficiency required for mission-critical operations.

"The Tokyo campus is central to our long-term commitment to Japan and strengthens our ability to support customers as their cloud, AI and digital infrastructure requirements grow," said Maeda. "Through STTGDC TYO1 and STTGDC TYO2, we are building that capacity in one of Japan's established data center markets and creating a strong platform for our continued growth in the country."

The data center operator, which was previously known as ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STT GDC), underwent a brand refresh as STTGDC in early September following the completion of the acquisition of the company by a consortium led by KKR and Singtel. The deal was valued at 6.6 billion Singapore dollars ($5.15 billion), with KKR holding the majority stake at 75%.

According to STTGDC, it entered this new phase of its corporate journey with strong operating momentum and a substantial development pipeline.

Since the end of 2025, the company's operational capacity has grown by 25%, reaching 780MW. Additionally, contracted capacity has grown by 50%, while annualized earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) have increased by 30%. This reflects the continued demand across its markets.

The data center operator reiterated that responsible growth is an integral part of its business and operations.

STTGDC surpassed its 2028 carbon intensity reduction target three years ahead of schedule by sourcing 83.2% of its electricity consumption across its operations from renewable energy.

text:
Microsoft reduced its forecast for capital expenditure, a rare move in an industry that mostly continues to splurge more on huge AI investments.

The software giant said capex for the 2026 calendar year will be $170 billion from a previous forecast of $175 billion.

Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood gave the forecast on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call on Wednesday.

She said Microsoft was expecting new capacity to arrive from third-parties, but some of these "GPU-as-a-Service contracts" have been delayed until the second half of the fiscal year.

This likely refers to other providers of AI cloud services that use Nvidia GPUs to run their offerings. Microsoft has partnered with some outside providers to meet rampant AI demand.

Hood's comments could refer to a recent spate of AI data center project delays, which have mostly been caused by a lack of electricity, along with local opposition.

The CFO said Microsoft expects capex to accelerate in the second half of its fiscal year, as the delayed capacity kicks in.

Wall Street has become increasingly concerned the huge investments cloud companies are making to expand AI infrastructure. Microsoft last quarter kept its forecast unchanged, notable as many cloud giants have been steadily increasing their AI spending forecasts.

Overall, Microsoft reported $92.3 billion in revenue, up 19%, for the fiscal first-quarter ending Sept. 30. Azure cloud revenue was up 48% to more than $33 billion, surpassing Wall Street expectations.

Microsoft share were up about about 3% in after-hours trading following the earnings call.

Earlier this week, Microsoft offered a buyout to more than a quarter of its workforce. A Microsoft spokesperson told Business Insider on Wednesday that the company expects 5% of eligible employees at most to accept the buyout.

"We expect very few people to select this offer because of the growth opportunities here at Microsoft," Hood wrote in an internal memo viewed by Business Insider. Microsoft's headcount slipped 2% during the fiscal first quarter, the company reported.

US family budgets already burdened by inflation are being gouged by opaque and sometimes deceptive store pricing practices, including surveillance pricing and overcharges by Dollar General and convenience stores.
Several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set different prices based on shoppers habits and online information.

text:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.

Nine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes after investigations and lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and drivers paid different fares based on their personal histories.

The FTC will “scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service”, chair Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.

US family budgets already burdened by inflation are being gouged by opaque and sometimes deceptive store pricing practices, including surveillance pricing and overcharges by Dollar General and convenience stores.

The FTC is tasked with policing “unfair or deceptive acts or practices” in industries except banking and airlines, which means it can not impose any fines or regulations on the airlines named. While the Trump administration has rolled back corporate regulations, the FTC’s consumer protection division has joined with states in some instances to pursue legal action and penalties against some companies.

Companies must “turn over information that will allow the agency to assess whether the pricing for a ticket, ride share, food delivery or other product or service varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data by super-intelligence algorithms”, the FTC said.

Several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels that could be used to set different prices based on shoppers habits and online information.

The probe follows a July 2024 inquiry by the Biden administration into surveillance pricing, which demanded information from McKinsey, JPMorgan Chase and others that offered surveillance pricing products to consumer-facing companies.

“Details like a person’s precise location or browser history can be frequently used to target individual consumers with different prices for the same goods and services,” the FTC found in January of 2025.

Whether the inquiry will result in substantial changes in consumer laws or company practices is unclear.

“What we have seen so far is that they have not been using these studies that produce meaningful reports that ultimately lead to any rule-making changes,” said Rohit Chopra, a former FTC commissioner who is now head of California’s new Business and Consumer Protection Agency.

name: Societe Generale
title: Finery Markets: 100 days of MiCA and the Execution Gap Banks Must Close
description:
According to two reports published by institutional crypto trading infrastructure firm Finery Markets in October 2026, the structural shift playing out underneath the compliance story is about liquidity, not headcount.
EURC, the euro-denominated stablecoin issued by Circle, saw volume on the Finery Markets platform rise 46 times year on year in the first nine months of 2026.
That gap is the commercial proposition underlying the Finery Markets release.
Finery Markets also disclosed two platform updates this month.
The consensus from those conversations, as reported by Finery Markets, was that firms growing fastest are treating routing, settlement and prefunding as infrastructure decisions rather than operational workarounds.
text:
One hundred days after MiCA’s 1 July registration deadline, the headline number, 280 firms on ESMA‘s initial list, down from 2,747 operating under national transitional regimes in 2024, turns out to be the less consequential data point. According to two reports published by institutional crypto trading infrastructure firm Finery Markets in October 2026, the structural shift playing out underneath the compliance story is about liquidity, not headcount.

EURC, the euro-denominated stablecoin issued by Circle, saw volume on the Finery Markets platform rise 46 times year on year in the first nine months of 2026. Yet it still accounts for just 0.12% of total stablecoin flow through the network. Euro stablecoin supply has grown 22.6% this year to approximately $848 million, while dollar-denominated supply has been flat. The figures confirm MiCA opened a race to build native euro liquidity that remains, as the report puts it, a test of volume rather than availability.

The OTC data behind the first report covers 16 million institutional spot trades across nine months. OTC volume grew 57% year on year while the top 20 centralised exchanges collectively lost 47% of comparable activity. Stablecoins now account for 83% of trades on the network. Contributors include Banking Circle, Fipto, The Vault and identity and compliance firm Sumsub.

The execution layer banks have not built

The second report, focused on bank strategy, finds that 89% of banks have an active budget for digital assets, but only 16% have anything in production. Of the largest institutions surveyed, JPMorgan, Citi, BNY, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, Standard Chartered, Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, BBVA and Revolut, nearly every live product runs on third-party rails. Custody, tokenised deposits and exchange-traded product access have been delivered. Trading has not.

That gap is the commercial proposition underlying the Finery Markets release. The firm argues that custody addresses a security question, not a revenue one. The client request that follows custody is the ability to trade held assets without routing them to an exchange the bank does not control. Building that internally requires separate bilateral liquidity relationships, each carrying its own credit agreement, fragmented pricing that complicates best-execution obligations, and a settlement infrastructure build measured in quarters rather than weeks.

Finery Markets’ alternative is a non-custodial connection to firm liquidity across more than 200 crypto and fiat pairs, with automated netting, role-based access controls and a full audit trail. Two deployment models are offered: a white-label master account in which the bank remains the regulated counterparty, and a full white-label network in which clients trade with one another and the bank typically avoids the capital requirements of a broker-dealer licence.

Regulatory context and platform updates

The regulatory read-across is substantial. In the US, the OCC has granted 16 digital asset trust charters in ten months. The GENIUS Act, MiCA, the UK’s evolving digital assets regime and Basel III capital treatment of crypto exposures are all shaping what banks can offer and at what cost. Roughly one fifth of the current MiCA register is now composed of banks, which reflects an appetite but also a compliance overhead that smaller specialist CASPs have been faster to absorb.

Finery Markets also disclosed two platform updates this month. The connectivity hub now allows institutional participants to store exchange API credentials directly within the platform interface, integrating price discovery from venues covering what the firm describes as more than two thirds of global crypto liquidity. The white-label stack has been updated with embedded API documentation, which the company says has reduced client integration timelines by a factor of 18.7 compared with a prior baseline, a figure it attributes to an AI-assisted integration repository. The 18.7 multiplier is not independently benchmarked in the release.

The firm also co-hosted a private luncheon at TOKEN2049 Singapore with Caladan, Utila and Stablecoin Insider, drawing approximately 150 professionals from OTC trading, market making, payments and stablecoin infrastructure. The consensus from those conversations, as reported by Finery Markets, was that firms growing fastest are treating routing, settlement and prefunding as infrastructure decisions rather than operational workarounds.

description:

text:
A late-stage trial of Genmab’s petosemtamab hit its co-primary endpoints at the first interim analysis, the biotech said Wednesday, completing a clean sweep of victories in a high-stakes run of readouts.

The LiGeR-HN1 study tested petosemtamab, a bispecific antibody targeting EGFR and LGR5, in combination with Merck’s Keytruda in nearly 700 patients with PD-L1-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Given as a first-line treatment, the combination significantly improved overall survival (OS) and objective response rate (ORR) compared to single-agent Keytruda, meeting its co-primary endpoints.

The investigational combination reduced the risk of death by 50%, regardless of HPV status.

William Blair analysts in a Wednesday morning note called the result “exceedingly positive,” while their counterparts at Truist Securities hailed the OS finding as “highly compelling and potentially practice-changing.”

Genmab has now delivered positive data on three key candidates in quick succession. At the start of October, the biotech was preparing to share Phase 3 data on its AbbVie-partnered bispecific antibody Epkinly, the antibody-drug conjugate rinatabart sesutecan (Rina-S) and petosemtamab. Weeks later, Genmab has positive data from all three studies.

Genmab’s stock rose 29% to $57.57 in early trading on Wednesday.

“We view the Rina-S and peto OS wins as particularly striking and believe all three franchises can support multibillion-dollar opportunities,” Truist analysts said. “Full data remain important given the first interim analysis, and we look for additional color on OS maturity, absolute ORR, safety and regulatory timing.”

Genmab has yet to disclose the median OS or ORR. Based on Keytruda’s historical performance in the setting, Truist analysts estimate that the petosemtamab combination may have achieved a median OS of about 30 months, broadly in line with the 28.2-month result seen in Phase 2. The analysts forecast that the ORR result could be in the 44% to 58% range.

The earlier-than-expected interim OS hit could accelerate Genmab’s path to market, Truist said. Analysts had initially expected OS results in 2027.

The OS success suggests “a particularly strong treatment effect” and supports potential approval in 2027, Truist said—ahead of the 2028 approval currently modeled by Truist. Bringing petosemtamab to market earlier than expected would give Genmab more time to grow sales of the product before the expiration of patents on Darzalex, its Johnson and Johnson-partnered multiple myeloma drug.

Preparing for the patent loss, Genmab invested in Epkinly, an internally discovered program, and struck deals for petosemtamab and Rina-S. Petosemtamab represented the biggest bet, with Genmab acquiring the drug candidate in its $8 billion takeover of Merus in September 2025.

Bicara Therapeutics’ ficerafusp alfa is a potential competitor to petosemtamab, with the biotech on track to report interim Phase 3 HNSCC data in mid-2027. Shares in Bicara, which is only enrolling HPV-negative patients in its HNSCC trial, were down 48% to $8.94 as of publication.

title: Why Does DoorDash Want Instacart? Inside the Reported $17-Billion Grocery Bet
description:
The strategic question is already clear: what would DoorDash gain by buying a grocery business when it already delivers groceries?
Instacart brings a grocery marketplace, relationships with retailers, advertising capabilities and technology that helps retailers operate their online businesses.
For Uber, a combination could create a stronger rival across restaurant and grocery delivery.
The reported transaction would also illustrate acquisition as a possible outcome after an IPO.

text:
What is happening? Getting dinner delivered brings a customer onto an app. Getting their weekly groceries could keep them coming back.

That helps explain DoorDash’s reported pursuit of Instacart, the US grocery-delivery platform. CNBC reports that an agreement could be announced soon. Earlier reporting put the potential transaction at about $17 billion.

The strategic question is already clear: what would DoorDash gain by buying a grocery business when it already delivers groceries?

Enjoy uninterrupted access to premium content and insights.

WHAT WOULD DOORDASH ACTUALLY BE BUYING?

Instacart brings a grocery marketplace, relationships with retailers, advertising capabilities and technology that helps retailers operate their online businesses.

Its latest available quarterly filing shows the scale. In April–June 2026, Instacart handled 90.3 million orders, up 9% year-on-year. Gross transaction value reached $10.35 billion, up 14%. That measures transactions passing through its platform, rather than revenue retained by the company.

Groceries also present different challenges from restaurant meals.

A supermarket basket may contain dozens of products. Some will be unavailable. Customers may want particular replacements, specific quantities or produce selected carefully. Managing those decisions is part of the service.

Open Magazine Latest Edition is Out Now!

Look Who's Talking Regime Change

22 Oct 2026 - Vol 05 | Issue 43

Buying an established operation could give DoorDash capabilities and customer relationships that would take time and money to reproduce.

DOESN’T DOORDASH ALREADY SELL GROCERIES?

Yes. This would be an expansion of an existing business.

In September 2025, DoorDash and Kroger announced that nearly 2,700 Kroger stores would join its marketplace. The agreement covered fresh food, household essentials and other grocery products, with loyalty discounts integrated into the app.

That existing presence helps explain the opportunity and the potential competition concerns.

DoorDash could seek to introduce its restaurant customers to a stronger grocery offering. Instacart’s customers could become an audience for other services.

Whether either happens profitably would depend on how much the company spends on incentives, integration and fulfilment.

Two customer databases do not automatically become one more valuable business. Customers may already use both services.

WHY WOULD INSTACART CONSIDER SELLING?

The competitive pressure is coming from several directions.

Amazon and Walmart can connect grocery purchases with wider retail offerings. Delivery platforms can bundle groceries with restaurant meals and convenience shopping. Retailers also have reasons to strengthen their own digital channels.

ADVERTISEMENT

Reuters reported that Instacart had explored discussions with both DoorDash and Uber. Its October 23 account described the risk of a specialist being squeezed between retailers’ own services and larger platforms offering several categories.

But considering a sale does not establish that Instacart is failing.

Its second-quarter results reported revenue growth of 14% and net income of $111 million.

A profitable company can still decide that a larger owner offers a better route to competing, investing or rewarding shareholders.

WHAT WOULD IT MEAN FOR UBER, AMAZON AND WALMART?

For Uber, a combination could create a stronger rival across restaurant and grocery delivery. Reuters’ subsequent reporting said Instacart’s discussions with Uber were no longer active.

For Amazon and Walmart, the potential challenge would be a larger intermediary connecting customers to competing retailers.

The responses need not involve another acquisition. Rivals could improve subscriptions, delivery coverage, pricing or retailer partnerships.

The contest also extends beyond the delivery charge. A platform that attracts shoppers can sell advertising to brands seeking visibility near the point of purchase.

ADVERTISEMENT

That makes customer attention, shopping frequency and advertising revenue important parts of the strategic calculation.

These are possible competitive consequences. The reported talks do not establish how any rival will respond.

WOULD CUSTOMERS AND RETAILERS BENEFIT?

They could, if the combination makes ordering more reliable, improves availability or lowers the cost of serving each purchase.

Retailers could gain access to more customers and a broader set of tools.

But concentration can create competing pressures. Retailers may have fewer independent platforms with which to negotiate. Consumers may face fewer distinct offers. Delivery workers could see changes to how orders and incentives are allocated.

Those outcomes depend on the eventual structure and operating decisions.

A larger network could reduce some costs while increasing the owner’s bargaining power. Whether savings reach customers would need to be measured.

WHAT DOES THIS TELL THE STARTUP ECOSYSTEM?

The central lesson concerns defensibility.

Building a popular service in one category can create a valuable company. It can also attract larger competitors that already have customers, delivery networks and subscription relationships.

For founders, the question becomes what remains difficult to copy.

That could be specialised operating expertise, strong retailer relationships, distinctive technology or an ability to earn money without repeatedly subsidising demand.

The reported transaction would also illustrate acquisition as a possible outcome after an IPO. Instacart became a listed company in 2023; public ownership does not prevent a subsequent sale.

For investors, the return would depend on their entry price, dilution and the final consideration. A large headline transaction value cannot establish that every shareholder has enjoyed a successful investment.

ADVERTISEMENT

WHAT IS THE INDIA CONNECTION?

The strategic question is relevant to Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart, Zepto and other delivery businesses: does expansion into more shopping occasions improve customer loyalty and economics?

The American transaction would not answer that question for India. Fulfilment models, order sizes, store networks and customer expectations differ.

DoorDash’s Hyderabad office is a more direct connection. Reporting on its September opening described a centre supporting global operations, initially employing 500 people. That is not evidence that DoorDash has launched a consumer delivery service in India.

ADVERTISEMENT

The useful comparison is how companies combine customers, logistics and repeat purchases, while accounting for local differences.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

First comes confirmation, including the price, payment structure and terms.

Then comes the regulatory question. Because both companies offer grocery delivery, authorities could examine how a combination affects competition. Reported negotiations cannot establish whether approval would follow or what conditions might apply.

text:
The UK’s HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) has awarded Salesforce a £2.4bn (US$3.2bn) contract as it seeks to improve its service operations, replace fragmented legacy systems and expand AI-assisted taxpayer services.

The department has signed a deal with the UK arm of the US-headquartered enterprise software giant to replace numerous fragmented and outdated Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems with a single platform.

“This new modern platform will make it quicker and easier for customers to get the help they need,” an HMRC spokesperson told Global Government Forum’s sister title Global Government Finance. “By bringing customer information together in one place, our staff will be able to resolve queries faster and more consistently, delivering a better service for millions of people.”

“Replacing multiple legacy systems with a single platform will also enable us to better understand and respond to our customers’ needs,” the spokesperson added.

The move comes after a challenging few years for the department’s customer service operations, with the House of Commons public accounts committee (PAC) describing HMRC’s customer service levels as reaching an “all-time low” in 2024. In January 2025 the same parliamentary committee described the department’s “already poor service to taxpayers” as having “become even worse”, accusing HMRC of having “sought to degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels”.

Read more: ‘A blueprint for how the UK government deploys AI at scale’: HMRC signs deal to boost data, analytics and AI firepower

‘Real-time taxpayer insights’

HMRC has previously used Salesforce products and services, but the new deal represents a broader and more significant relationship.

HMRC currently manages customer interactions through systems with limited integration or standardisation, and its new enterprise CRM arrangement with Salesforce will consolidate systems and data sources into a single scalable platform.

As well as case management, customer experience, and AI, additional capabilities to be provided by Salesforce direct or via third parties include identity, verification and authentication; anti-fraud; “non-compliance management”; and Secure Digital Exchange Communications (SDEC) – reference to a digital document and communications platform for interactions between HMRC and citizens.

HMRC will use an AI agent platform named Agentforce to “automate routine administration, triage inbound queries and route complex cases to the right specialists”.

“Operating within tightly governed workflows, these AI capabilities increase operational capacity while ensuring human oversight from trained HMRC staff remains integral to every taxpayer decision,” Salesforce stated.

Salesforce said that, taken together, its technology will enable a “360-degree view of taxpayer interactions to enable faster, first-contact query resolution” and provide a “single, connected view of each customer’s interaction history across every customer contact channel”.

It said that HMRC’s “legacy systems and fragmented channels have made it challenging to deliver seamless and efficient services to taxpayers”, and that the new system will enable citizens and businesses to access “clearer information through their preferred channels and eliminate repetitive contacts”.

Salesforce’s contract runs to September 2036, with a possible extension to September 2041 according to the contract notice.

Read more: UK government agency becomes first in the world to achieve ‘five star’ service desk certification

HMRC’s Capgemini appointment

Capgemini, in collaboration with NiCE and Route 101, has already been appointed to “consolidate HMRC’s legacy infrastructure and existing products into a unified, cloud native platform”.

The Contact Centre as a Service (CCaaS) platform provided by Capgemini and the enterprise CRM system from Salesforce have different roles but aspects of them are expected to work together over time. This integration will be developed and tested as the programmes move through implementation.

In an update to HMRC’s Transformation Roadmap, published this July, JP Marks, the department’s permanent secretary and chief executive, said: “Together, these will help us to join up customer contact across channels and give colleagues the tools they need to provide a faster, more consistent service.”

Phonelines fightback

HMRC has faced criticism over waiting times on its phonelines for years. The new CCaaS platform featured in a section titled ‘Tackling phone lines’ in the ‘Improving day-to-day performance and the overall customer experience’ chapter of the Transformation Roadmap – Update 2026.

“CCaaS will include embedded AI capability, which will be delivered incrementally,” it explained. “This will help HMRC better manage call queues, provide accurate wait times, and offer intelligent digital assistant support. This will allow HMRC to deliver a more responsive and personalised service, both over the phone and through digital channels.”

HMRC will “continue to use technology to support customers calling HMRC helplines, for example through the use of call summarisation, information messages to provide customers with the details they need, and voice biometrics where appropriate,” it added.

title: Human Rights Expertise in the Boardroom: A Governance Gap That Needs Closing
description:
Its central finding is both important and sobering: human rights expertise is largely absent from corporate governance structures, and the decisions that most determine a company’s human rights impact — strategy, resource allocation, risk appetite — are being made without it.
This October I participated in stakeholder advisory board meetings at two companies that have been experimenting, in different ways, with integrating external human rights expertise into their governance processes.
These models are interesting experiments in integrating human rights into corporate governance.
Academic centers at business schools, where research on corporate governance and human rights is conducted, are uniquely well positioned to translate that research into board training.
The NYU Stern Center and the Geneva Center for Business and Human Rights stand ready to do exactly that
text:
On October 29, Robert McCorquodale, member of the UN Working Group on Business and Human Rights, will present a new report on corporate governance to the UN General Assembly in New York. Its central finding is both important and sobering: human rights expertise is largely absent from corporate governance structures, and the decisions that most determine a company’s human rights impact — strategy, resource allocation, risk appetite — are being made without it. The full report is available on the Working Group’s webpage.

This is a gap I encounter directly. This October I participated in stakeholder advisory board meetings at two companies that have been experimenting, in different ways, with integrating external human rights expertise into their governance processes. Michelin has operated a Stakeholder Advisory Committee for over a decade — a model I have recently joined — which provides a structured channel for independent external perspectives to reach the company’s board and senior leadership. Argor-Heraeus, a precious metals refiner, has developed its own sounding board as a platform for constructive engagement on responsible sourcing and human rights performance. In both cases, CEOs, functional sustainability heads, and board members are present. That direct access to decision-makers is what makes these interactions genuinely useful rather than performative. It also creates space for something harder to achieve through public channels: the ability to raise sensitive issues the company is not yet ready to discuss openly, and to help shape how it responds before those issues become crises.

Participation in these bodies is reimbursed for expenses, but not paid as a consulting engagement. More importantly, participation does not constitute endorsement. It is a platform for honest, sometimes critical, exchange — and its value depends entirely on that honesty being preserved.

These models are interesting experiments in integrating human rights into corporate governance. Companies that create space for external human rights expertise at the governance level are better positioned to identify risks earlier and develop more credible responses when things go wrong. The UN Working Group report makes the same argument from a policy perspective: “corporate governance that respects human rights is a core element of the corporate responsibility to respect human rights”, and directors have a duty to ensure it is embedded in how companies are led.

The limitation of these individual company arrangements, however, is that they are not scalable. A handful of external experts participating in advisory boards is a useful experiment, not a systemic solution. What systemic change actually requires is board training on human rights, the full integration of human rights competencies into director selection and evaluation, and governance structures that make human rights expertise a standing feature of board oversight rather than an occasional external input.

External thematic experts can and should continue to support companies on a case-by-case basis. But the goal is to make that external support progressively less necessary. Expertise and accountability must be built into the governance architecture itself.

The report is a timely call to action. Academic centers at business schools, where research on corporate governance and human rights is conducted, are uniquely well positioned to translate that research into board training. The NYU Stern Center and the Geneva Center for Business and Human Rights stand ready to do exactly that

title: BNY Holds $63 Trillion for Clients and Will Now Custody XRP. What If 0.1% of That Went Into XRP?
description:
BNY will also offer custody for XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) holders and for Ripple’s stablecoin, Ripple USD (CRYPTO:RLUSD).
So what would it take for XRP custody to turn into real demand for XRP?
Why XRP Custody Doesn’t Commit Anyone to Buying XRP TopMicrobialStock / Shutterstock.com A custodian holds whatever its clients choose to own.
With XRP custody, BNY holds coins for clients and buys none for its own balance sheet, and nothing in the reporting says any BNY client has committed to holding XRP.
Institutions that wanted XRP custody already had crypto-native custodians such as Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN) and Anchorage to choose from.
text:
Ripple has deepened its partnership with BNY (NYSE:BK), the bank that manages Pershing and Dreyfus. The new agreement now includes custody services and tokenized trade finance, with the trade-finance operations running on Ripple’s blockchain. BNY will also offer custody for XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) holders and for Ripple’s stablecoin, Ripple USD (CRYPTO:RLUSD).

Ripple and BNY are looking into using the XRP Ledger to finance approved invoices, with C2FO bringing trade finance to the ledger. Neither Ripple nor BNY has revealed which clients will receive XRP custody or when the service will begin, and BNY did not mention XRP at all on its October 15, 2026 earnings call.

XRP traded at $1.32 on October 27, 2026, up 2.3% over 24 hours, though it remains down 13% over the past month and 28.3% since December 31, 2025. BNY shares traded near $148, up less than 1% in the session.

BNY’s Q3 2026 results showed $63.4 trillion in assets under custody and administration as of September 30, 2026. XRP holders keep asking what would happen if 0.1% of that figure went into XRP. So what would it take for XRP custody to turn into real demand for XRP?

What BNY’s Ripple Deal Covers and How BNY Makes Its Money

Tamisclao / Shutterstock.com

When a bank provides custody, it holds assets for clients, keeps the ownership records, and oversees settlement. The client still owns the assets and pays the bank a fee. Assets under custody and administration add up everything BNY holds or services in this capacity, separate from BNY’s $2.2 trillion in assets under management, where BNY’s own fund managers decide how to invest.

BNY has been RLUSD’s primary custodian since July 9, 2025, holding the cash and U.S. Treasuries that back each token, and it also provides transaction banking services for the stablecoin. The new reports say BNY holds the tokens and the dollars behind RLUSD.

In Q3 2026, BNY reported $5.68 billion in revenue, with fees up 12% year over year to $4.08 billion. Net interest income, what the bank earns on loans and securities after paying depositors, rose 15% to $1.42 billion. Adjusted earnings per share totaled $2.37, driven by Asset Servicing’s $2.13 billion and Pershing’s $813 million.

BNY’s digital-asset work so far centers on dollars, not tokens like XRP. It holds stablecoin reserves and services tokenized money market funds for clients such as BlackRock (NYSE:BLK | BLK Price Prediction), but has disclosed no digital-asset revenue or custody balance, and XRP appears nowhere in its 2026 guidance for nearly 500 basis points of positive operating leverage.

Why XRP Custody Doesn’t Commit Anyone to Buying XRP

TopMicrobialStock / Shutterstock.com

A custodian holds whatever its clients choose to own. With XRP custody, BNY holds coins for clients and buys none for its own balance sheet, and nothing in the reporting says any BNY client has committed to holding XRP. Most of the $63.4 trillion is stocks, bonds, and fund shares that pensions, insurers, and asset managers already own.

The trade-finance reports also don’t say which asset settles those invoices, and they don’t name XRP. RLUSD is the Ripple product BNY already supports with reserve custody, so a dollar stablecoin looks like the likelier way to pay invoices. If invoices settle in RLUSD, XRP’s role probably shrinks to the tiny network fee every XRP Ledger transaction burns.

BNY’s chief executive, Robin Vince, runs Ripple’s counterparty in this deal, so his comments are BNY’s sales pitch. On the October 2026 call, he said BNY’s strategy is to “innovate the capabilities and act as a partner to our clients as we help them bridge to the digital world,” naming no coin.

Institutions that wanted XRP custody already had crypto-native custodians such as Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN) and Anchorage to choose from. Ripple’s bank deals also continue to favor the stablecoin. Standard Chartered launched institutional custody for RLUSD on Ripple’s blockchain through its Dubai branch on October 12, 2026. Big custody rivals like State Street (NYSE:STT) are chasing the same clients, so the BNY deal reads like a bank keeping pace with its product list.

What the 0.1% Thought Experiment Shows

SergeiShimanovich / Shutterstock.com

0.1% of $63.4 trillion is $63.4 billion, equal to 75.7% of XRP’s entire market value of $83.8 billion. That sounds huge, but BNY has made no such forecast. Clients would have to sell other holdings and buy XRP themselves, and BNY would just hold the coins.

New money also lifts market value unevenly. Only a fraction of XRP’s supply trades on any given day, so buying can push the price up more than its size when sellers are scarce, while the same buying moves the price less once long-term holders start selling into that demand. Market value is price multiplied by circulating supply, so it can swing far more than the cash coming in.

Does BNY’s XRP Custody Help XRP’s Price?

Based on the evidence so far, the answer is no. BNY gets a product to sell to clients who hold XRP or want to, a closer tie to Ripple, and more fee business around RLUSD. XRP gets an easier on-ramp for institutions whose compliance teams only approve big-bank custodians, but it still needs buyers to drive the price up.

XRP trades below its 50-day and 20-day averages, at $1.40 and $1.34, though it holds above its 200-day average of $1.28, and trades 63.8% below its all-time high of $3.65 from July 17, 2025. BNY’s next earnings report is the clearest test. A disclosed custody balance or client mandate would show demand arriving, while a report that mentions nothing about XRP leaves the deal as a service for people who already own the coin.

A 0.1% allocation from BNY's $63 trillion would equal $63 billion, roughly 76% of XRP's entire market cap, but BNY made no such commitment.

Trade finance invoices are more likely to settle in RLUSD than XRP, shrinking XRP's role to tiny network fees burned per transaction.

Ripple has deepened its partnership with BNY (NYSE:BK), the bank that manages Pershing and Dreyfus. The new agreement now includes custody services and tokenized trade finance, with the trade-finance operations running on Ripple's blockchain. BNY will also offer custody for XRP (CRYPTO:XRP) holders and for Ripple's stablecoin, Ripple USD (CRYPTO:RLUSD).

Ripple and BNY are looking into using the XRP Ledger to finance approved invoices, with C2FO bringing trade finance to the ledger. Neither Ripple nor BNY has revealed which clients will receive XRP custody or when the service will begin, and BNY did not mention XRP at all on its October 15, 2026 earnings call.

XRP traded at $1.32 on October 27, 2026, up 2.3% over 24 hours, though it remains down 13% over the past month and 28.3% since December 31, 2025. BNY shares traded near $148, up less than 1% in the session.

BNY's Q3 2026 results showed $63.4 trillion in assets under custody and administration as of September 30, 2026. XRP holders keep asking what would happen if 0.1% of that figure went into XRP. So what would it take for XRP custody to turn into real demand for XRP?

When a bank provides custody, it holds assets for clients, keeps the ownership records, and oversees settlement. The client still owns the assets and pays the bank a fee. Assets under custody and administration add up everything BNY holds or services in this capacity, separate from BNY's $2.2 trillion in assets under management, where BNY's own fund managers decide how to invest.

BNY has been RLUSD's primary custodian since July 9, 2025, holding the cash and U.S. Treasuries that back each token, and it also provides transaction banking services for the stablecoin. The new reports say BNY holds the tokens and the dollars behind RLUSD.

In Q3 2026, BNY reported $5.68 billion in revenue, with fees up 12% year over year to $4.08 billion. Net interest income, what the bank earns on loans and securities after paying depositors, rose 15% to $1.42 billion. Adjusted earnings per share totaled $2.37, driven by Asset Servicing's $2.13 billion and Pershing's $813 million.

BNY's digital-asset work so far centers on dollars, not tokens like XRP. It holds stablecoin reserves and services tokenized money market funds for clients such as BlackRock (NYSE:BLK), but has disclosed no digital-asset revenue or custody balance, and XRP appears nowhere in its 2026 guidance for nearly 500 basis points of positive operating leverage.

Why XRP Custody Doesn't Commit Anyone to Buying XRP

A custodian holds whatever its clients choose to own. With XRP custody, BNY holds coins for clients and buys none for its own balance sheet, and nothing in the reporting says any BNY client has committed to holding XRP. Most of the $63.4 trillion is stocks, bonds, and fund shares that pensions, insurers, and asset managers already own.

The trade-finance reports also don't say which asset settles those invoices, and they don't name XRP. RLUSD is the Ripple product BNY already supports with reserve custody, so a dollar stablecoin looks like the likelier way to pay invoices. If invoices settle in RLUSD, XRP's role probably shrinks to the tiny network fee every XRP Ledger transaction burns.

BNY's chief executive, Robin Vince, runs Ripple's counterparty in this deal, so his comments are BNY's sales pitch. On the October 2026 call, he said BNY's strategy is to "innovate the capabilities and act as a partner to our clients as we help them bridge to the digital world," naming no coin.

Institutions that wanted XRP custody already had crypto-native custodians such as Coinbase (NASDAQ:COIN) and Anchorage to choose from. Ripple's bank deals also continue to favor the stablecoin. Standard Chartered launched institutional custody for RLUSD on Ripple's blockchain through its Dubai branch on October 12, 2026. Big custody rivals like State Street (NYSE:STT) are chasing the same clients, so the BNY deal reads like a bank keeping pace with its product list.

What the 0.1% Thought Experiment Shows

0.1% of $63.4 trillion is $63.4 billion, equal to 75.7% of XRP's entire market value of $83.8 billion. That sounds huge, but BNY has made no such forecast. Clients would have to sell other holdings and buy XRP themselves, and BNY would just hold the coins.

New money also lifts market value unevenly. Only a fraction of XRP's supply trades on any given day, so buying can push the price up more than its size when sellers are scarce, while the same buying moves the price less once long-term holders start selling into that demand. Market value is price multiplied by circulating supply, so it can swing far more than the cash coming in.

Does BNY's XRP Custody Help XRP's Price?

Based on the evidence so far, the answer is no. BNY gets a product to sell to clients who hold XRP or want to, a closer tie to Ripple, and more fee business around RLUSD. XRP gets an easier on-ramp for institutions whose compliance teams only approve big-bank custodians, but it still needs buyers to drive the price up.

XRP trades below its 50-day and 20-day averages, at $1.40 and $1.34, though it holds above its 200-day average of $1.28, and trades 63.8% below its all-time high of $3.65 from July 17, 2025. BNY's next earnings report is the clearest test. A disclosed custody balance or client mandate would show demand arriving, while a report that mentions nothing about XRP leaves the deal as a service for people who already own the coin.

text:
USA | DoorDash is reportedly close to acquiring Instacart in a deal potentially worth US$17 billion, bringing together two major players in online grocery delivery.

Reuters has reported that the companies are in advanced negotiations, while CNBC has since reported that an announcement could come as early as Thursday morning, US time. Neither company has formally confirmed an agreement.

The proposed acquisition would combine DoorDash's restaurant, grocery, and retail delivery network with Instacart's established supermarket partnerships, fulfilment services, and retail technology operations.

Instacart works with major supermarket operators, providing online ordering and delivery services alongside advertising technology that allows brands to promote products to shoppers. DoorDash has expanded beyond restaurant delivery into grocery, convenience, and general retail.

A merger would significantly strengthen DoorDash's position in online grocery, where delivery platforms are competing for retailer partnerships and customer orders.

For supermarket operators, the proposed deal could change their relationships with third-party delivery providers. Retailers using both platforms may find themselves negotiating with one company over services previously supplied by competing businesses.

The acquisition could also expand DoorDash's involvement in retail media, adding Instacart's advertising business to its existing delivery and marketplace operations.

In November 2025, Kroger expanded its relationships with Instacart, DoorDash, and Uber Eats as part of its online grocery strategy. Instacart was named its primary fulfilment partner for orders through Kroger's digital channels, while DoorDash provided another route to customers through its marketplace.

DoorDash already operates in New Zealand, including through its partnership with Costco. There has been no indication of how a potential acquisition might affect local services.

The reported negotiations come as delivery companies seek further growth in grocery and retail while facing increasing competition and pressure on profitability.

Any agreement would remain subject to final terms and potential regulatory scrutiny, particularly given the overlap between the two companies' grocery delivery operations.

The Federal Trade Commission is demanding information from Walmart, Uber and seven other companies on whether and how they use consumers’ personal data such as location, browsing history and income to set individual prices, wages and job offers, a senior FTC official said Wednesday.

The FTC is flexing its consumer protection powers ahead of the congressional elections next week, as voters consistently rank the cost of living as the most important issue.

Target, along with app services Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart, and airlines Delta, United, JetBlue, are also receiving demands, the official said.

The FTC will use the information to eventually publish a study to help inform regulators and lawmakers about personalized pricing and wage setting practices.

The advance of algorithmic pricing technology, including tools that incorporate AI, has fueled concern that companies are able to set prices for shoppers on an individual basis in order to extract the maximum price each shopper would be willing to pay.

Personalized pricing strategies are difficult to observe from the outside, because they serve different prices to different people.

The FTC study aims to fill in that knowledge gap, demanding comprehensive information about the tools, strategies, and data companies use as well as how they affect prices, wages and job offers.

Efforts by state lawmakers to ban personalized pricing, along with the use of algorithms to individually tailor wages, have taken off in recent years.

The National Retail Federation has criticized the laws and defended retailers’ use of data-driven discounts as a means of incentivizing loyalty.

FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson has said personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws where consumers do not expect it and that companies should expect enforcement.

After the FTC called for public comment, hundreds of commenters urged the FTC to ban the practice outright.

The FTC has said it does not have the authority to issue a blanket prohibition against the practice.

JetBlue said it doesn’t use personal information or web browsing history to set individual pricing.

Fares are determined by demand and seat availability, and all customers have access to the same fares on jetblue.com and our mobile app.

text:
Microsoft generated $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing payments, in the quarter ended September 30, the company said in a regulatory filing on Wednesday. That represents nearly 11% of Microsoft’s total quarterly revenue of $92.3 billion, highlighting the enormous financial ties that remain between the two companies even as they increasingly compete for the same customers.

(Microsoft’s financial year begins in July, making the quarter ended September 30, 2026 the first quarter of its fiscal 2027.)

For the full 2026 fiscal year, revenue from OpenAI hit $24.1 billion. At its latest quarterly pace, Microsoft would pull in $40 billion annually from OpenAI-related arrangements.

Microsoft also reported $7.2 billion in outstanding receivables from OpenAI at the end of September, up from $6 billion at the end of June. That money represents amounts OpenAI owes for previous transactions, not additional revenue.

It’s not clear how much of Microsoft’s revenue from OpenAI came from revenue-sharing payments or Azure cloud computing services. TechCrunch has reached out for more information. In November 2025, TechCrunch reported, citing leaked documents, that Microsoft had received $865.8 million in net revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI during the first nine months of that year.

OpenAI reportedly shares 20% of its revenue with Microsoft as part of a previous deal in which the software giant invested more than $13 billion in the AI startup. (Neither the AI lab nor Microsoft have publicly confirmed this percentage.) As part of an April 2026 agreement, OpenAI is on the hook to continue sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030, subject to a cap, even as OpenAI is allowed to work with competing cloud providers.

The companies began loosening the ties of their once-exclusive partnership in October 2025, when Microsoft relinquished its hold on OpenAI to give the startup more freedom to partner with other cloud providers. In exchange, OpenAI committed to buying an additional $250 billion in Azure services as part of an October 2025 agreement.

Microsoft’s ownership stake in OpenAI has also declined slightly from about 25% in June to 24% in September. That continues a gradual decline from roughly 27% following the October 2025 recapitalization. Microsoft did not specify what caused the dilution.

text:
Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) reports fiscal first-quarter results after the market close on Wednesday, with investors looking for evidence that its heavy investment in artificial intelligence is translating into growth as the company prepares to disclose Azure revenue in dollars for the first time.

Wall Street expects revenue of about $90.6 billion to $90.7 billion for the three months ended September 30, up 16.6% from $77.67 billion a year earlier. Earnings per share are forecast at $4.71 to $4.72, compared with $4.13 in the prior-year quarter.

The revenue consensus sits near the upper end of Microsoft's guidance range of $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, setting a high bar for the results.

A key change this quarter is Microsoft's move from three reporting segments to two, Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. The revised structure is intended to give investors a clearer view of its cloud and AI businesses, although it will require adjustments to year-over-year comparisons.

Azure revenue in dollars

For the first time, Microsoft will disclose Azure's quarterly revenue in dollar terms rather than reporting only its percentage growth rate. The change should give investors a clearer measure of the cloud platform's scale as demand for AI computing drives investment in data centers.

Agents and Infra will combine Azure, Microsoft 365 cloud services, enterprise productivity and server licensing, support services, and frontier and industry solutions. Based on recast fiscal 2026 figures, it accounts for about 81% of revenue and 88% of operating income.

Microsoft expects the segment to generate between $75.15 billion and $75.75 billion in first-quarter revenue. Devices and Consumer, which includes Windows, Xbox, search and advertising, is forecast to contribute $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion.

AI spending under scrutiny

Capital expenditure is likely to be another focus, with Wall Street expecting spending, including leases, to exceed $45.9 billion in the quarter, up sharply from $19.3 billion a year earlier.

The investment reflects Microsoft's efforts to expand the computing capacity needed to support Azure and its AI products. However, investors are increasingly focused on how quickly that spending will generate returns.

Microsoft's remaining performance obligations stand at about $678 billion, providing visibility into future contracted revenue. Enterprise adoption is also growing, with Volkswagen equipping more than 330,000 employees with Microsoft Copilot.

Still, uncertainty over AI monetization and development challenges at key partners, including OpenAI and Anthropic, could weigh on expectations for future growth.

Microsoft has also introduced a voluntary buyout program open to around 60,000 employees across four countries, aiming to improve cost efficiency as infrastructure spending rises.

Analysts remain broadly bullish, with some recent price targets reaching about $665. Investors will nevertheless be looking for guidance on Azure demand, capital expenditure and AI returns to determine whether growth can justify the scale of Microsoft's investment.

text:
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission said Wednesday it is ordering Delta Air Lines, Walmart and other companies to provide detailed information on how they use consumers’ data when they’re setting prices.

The commission said it is also studying how ride-sharing and delivery companies like Uber use their independent drivers’ personal data when setting compensation rates.

“We intend to scrutinize the opaque methodology that some companies in these industries may be using to determine how much consumers pay or how much gig workers are paid for the same product or service,” FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson said in a statement.

Orders were also issued to United, JetBlue, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart and Target, the FTC said.

Each company must share information that will allow the commission to assess whether pricing for tickets, rides, food delivery or other products and services varies from one person to the next based on factors such as participation in loyalty programs or analysis of personal data, the agency said.

The FTC said it is also examining whether companies compensate workers based on personal data like their phone usage or their history of accepting rides or deliveries. If the companies fail to turn over data, the FTC said it could compel compliance in federal court.

Delta said in response that it has “zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing” and fully complies with pricing and advertising laws.

“There is no fare product Delta has ever used, is testing or plans to use that targets customers with individualized offers based on personal data,” the company said in a statement.

JetBlue said it doesn’t use personal information or web-browsing history to set individual prices.

“Fares are determined by demand and seat availability, and all customers have access to the same fares,” the company said.

The Associated Press reached out to Walmart, Target, DoorDash and others for comment. Walmart’s CEO said in a statement last month that the retailer doesn’t use personal information like income, shopping history or a customer’s willingness to pay to set prices, and it won’t be doing so in the future either.

The FTC’s actions reflect customers’ increasing concerns about pricing technology and the use of artificial intelligence to collect vast amounts of data. Legislators in at least 30 states have considered pricing-related bills this year, including measures addressing algorithmic and personalized pricing, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

In August, the FTC announced a proposed policy that would require businesses to “clearly and conspicuously disclose” if they are engaging in personalized pricing and share the types of data they’re using to set those prices. The agency has extended the comment period on that policy until Nov. 21.

In a preliminary report filed in January 2025, the FTC found that grocers, clothing companies and others were using third-party companies to help them individualize online prices based on shoppers’ locations, browsing histories and other factors, including how long they left items in their virtual shopping carts.

But Ferguson, who assumed the chairmanship of the FTC when President Donald Trump took office, has said that report was rushed and should have asked the companies directly for data instead of focusing on third-party intermediaries.

___

Durbin reported from Detroit. AP Business Writer Rio Yamat contributed from Las Vegas.

Today, a brief rundown of news involving Eli Lilly and Novartis, as well as updates from Astellas Pharma, Pfizer and Bolt Biotherapeutics that you may have missed.

Patrik Jonsson will retire from Eli Lilly at the end of 2026, completing a 36-year run at the Indianapolis-based drugmaker. Jonsson started at Lilly as a sales representative in Sweden in 1990 and rose through the ranks to eventually lead the company’s global pharmaceutical business, “Lilly International.” Once he steps down, Lilly’s U.S. and international divisions will combine into an entity called “Lilly Global Markets” and be headed by Ilya Yuffa, a Lilly executive vice president and head of global customer capabilities. The new structure will “accelerate decision-making, increase scalability” and help broaden access to medicines globally, Lilly said. — Ben Fidler

Novartis will take a $1.9 billion impairment charge after seeing an experimental drug it acquired in a $12 billion buyout of Avidity Biosciences fail a late-stage trial in August. The Swiss drugmaker revealed the write-off in its latest quarterly earnings report Tuesday, which included sales figures that topped Wall Street’s expectations and news that the company hiked its 2026 financial forecasts. Novartis is facing multiple key patent expirations in the near future and is looking to key drugs in its late-stage pipeline, like Avidity’s del-desiran, to spur future growth. Though that drug fell short in a study in a rare muscle-wasting disease, the company hasn’t given up on its approval chances. An open-label extension to that trial is ongoing, and executives told analysts Tuesday that they assume Novartis will need to run an additional Phase 3 study. — Delilah Alvarado

Astellas Pharma has secured from Australian biotech Audax Biosciences an option to license an experimental cancer immunotherapy nearing human testing. Called DAX-044, the therapy is an “antibody-cytokine fusion” designed to deliver the immune protein IL-12 into cancer cells. In a statement, Astellas said DAX-044 has “best-in-class” potential. The deal involves $285 million in up front and future option payments, and could include another $1.05 billion in additional consideration if certain milestones are met. Phase 1 testing should begin in 2027, Astellas said. — Ben Fidler

The Food and Drug Administration has expanded use of a two-drug regimen involving Pfizer’s cancer medicine Talzenna and the hormone therapy Xtandi. The combination was first approved in 2023 for certain patients with metastatic prostate cancer who’d stopped responding to hormone treatments. The new clearance makes treatment available earlier, when the benefits might be greater. The approval was based on study results showing the regimen cut the risk of cancer progression or death by more than half when compared to Xtandi and a placebo. — Delilah Alvarado
