title: NVIDIA Is Buying a Piece of Meta: What the $3 Billion Stake Means - Yahoo Finance
description:
The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying a piece of Meta itself.
Nvidia said Tuesday that it will invest $3 billion in a stock offering from Meta Platforms.
Meta Platforms upsized the common stock part of this offering to 25 billion up from 22.5 billion originally and priced at $625 a share.
Nvidia's money goes into Meta, Meta turns around and spends more on Nvidia infrastructure.
Nvidia owns a piece of Meta.
text:
The company that sells Meta its AI chips is now buying a piece of Meta itself.

Nvidia said Tuesday that it will invest $3 billion in a stock offering from Meta Platforms.

So, what is that check exactly? Well, it's an equity investment. Nvidia is buying shares, which make Jensen Wong's chip giant a shareholder in one of its biggest customers.

Here's how it came together.

Meta announced the offering Monday as reported by Axios. Nvidia's stake is part of an expanded AI partnership between the two companies. And the timing tells you a lot about where the AI race stands right now.

Because Meta needs cash and lots of it. Meta Platforms upsized the common stock part of this offering to 25 billion up from 22.5 billion originally and priced at $625 a share.

That's only the start though. According to the Wall Street Journal, Meta plans to raise as much as $95 billion through a series of share sales to cover AI infrastructure spending.

The question is, why does Meta need so much money? Well, the company has guided to 2026 capital expenditures, which is the money it's putting into data s and servers of 135 to 145 billion.

In the third quarter alone, CAPEX hit 34.91 billion. Free cash flow, which is the money left over after those investments, came in negative at 2.12 billion.

That's from a company that just posted 64.6 billion in quarterly revenue. On the earnings call, Meta CFO at the time, Susan Lee said Meta wanted access to a diverse pool of funding sources.

Now, we know what she meant. So what does Nvidia get beyond the shares? The partnership expands work on Meta's Muse family of models and agents with the goal of improving inference and training performance.

Now, inference, if you're wondering what that is, it just means running a model to answer real requests. Meta plans to scale up its usage of Nvidia hardware for its next generation of AI agents, including Vera Rubin and Vera CPUs, plus Nvidia's Spectrum X Ethernet networking and Bluefield 4.

As Jensen Wong put it, AI agents represent a new computing paradigm, software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf. Mark Zuckerberg kept it even simpler. Muse is how we bring personal superintelligence to everyone.

And good for Meta shareholders, Muse is catching on. Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up Muse personal agents in about a month and a half. The catch, he admitted it's a very compute intensive service.

Which is why it hasn't launched globally yet. Wang explained the math from Nvidia's side back in August. An AI agent needs probably 15 to 100 times the compute of a human doing the same task.

Every Muse user meta adds is more demand for Nvidia Silicon. That's the loop investors need to understand. Nvidia's money goes into Meta, Meta turns around and spends more on Nvidia infrastructure. For Nvidia's shareholders, that locks in a customer already tied to a multi-year, multi-generational deals covering millions of Blackwell and Ruben GPUs.

Nvidia has already invested nearly $50 billion in frontier AI labs and Wong has heard the criticism. In his words, we know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently. If Meta's AI products deliver, both companies will win. If they stall, Nvidia holds a stake in a customer that may slow its spending, and that's a double hit.

For Meta shareholders, the trade-off is dilution. New shares mean each existing share owns a slightly smaller piece of the company. In return, Meta gets a deep-pocketed anchor investor and the hardware pipeline to scale Muse.

So far, the market's reaction to this news is muted. In pre-market trading on Tuesday, Meta trades at 628, down just 0.41% and just above that offering price. and Nvidia is at 217.90 in pre-market, up about 0.9%.

So what should you watch? Meta says its AI businesses could start adding additional revenue in 2027 through subscriptions, commerce fees, advertising, and enterprise deals. Zuckerberg also expects to improve Muse's cost efficiency by more than 10x across the next year. Those two numbers will decide whether this spending turns into profit.

Nvidia owns a piece of Meta. It's up to Muse to prove that piece is worth the price. Thanks for tuning in. This has been 24/7 Wall Street for all your top news on finance's biggest stories. Make sure to check in with 24/7 Wall Street. Thank you.

title: Nvidia, AMD to buy $4B in Meta shares as part of expanded chip partnerships
authors: Maria Deutscher, DEVONY HOF, SLOANE KALI FAYE, RYAN STEVENS
description:
Meta Platforms Inc. today announced that Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. plan to buy $4 billion worth of its shares.
That suggests the networking chip giant will buy $1 billion in shares.
Notably, Meta plans to broaden its use of the chipmaker’s Rubin graphics processing units and Vera central processing units.
Meta also plans to buy more Nvidia networking gear.
Additionally, Meta plans to explore “collaboration opportunities” related to Nvidia’s recently introduced OpenShell Reference Architecture.
text:
Meta Platforms Inc. today announced that Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. plan to buy $4 billion worth of its shares.

The chipmakers will purchase the equity as part of an up to $95 billion stock sale that the Facebook parent intends to kick off in the near future. The fundraising initiative will also include the participation of Broadcom Inc. Meta didn’t specify how much the company is investing, but it stated on Monday that Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom together plan to invest $5 billion. That suggests the networking chip giant will buy $1 billion in shares.

Nvidia is investing $3 billion as part of a newly expanded partnership that also includes other components. Notably, Meta plans to broaden its use of the chipmaker’s Rubin graphics processing units and Vera central processing units. Companies often deploy the two chips together in Nvidia-designed DGX Vera Rubin NVL72 appliances. Each system includes 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs.

Meta also plans to buy more Nvidia networking gear. It will expand its use of the Spectrum-X Ethernet product family, which includes SuperNICs and switches. SuperNICs are chips that connect servers to a data center’s network, while switches coordinate how traffic flows through that network.

GPU clusters’ traffic patterns tend to change rapidly. As a result, connectivity bottlenecks sometimes emerge faster than the network can respond to them. Nvidia says that its Spectrum-X Ethernet product series addresses the challenge by checking GPU traffic for anomalies at sub-microsecond time intervals. A microsecond corresponds to one millionth of a second.

Another focus of Meta’s planned network investment is Nvidia’s BlueField-4 chip family. The accelerators in the series are designed to speed common networking, storage and cybersecurity tasks.

Nvidia will help Meta improve the performance and cost efficiency of its Muse large language model family. The effort will extend to the Facebook parent’s eponymous consumer AI agent.

Additionally, Meta plans to explore “collaboration opportunities” related to Nvidia’s recently introduced OpenShell Reference Architecture. It’s a collection of technical resources that makes it easier to run the chipmaker’s OpenShell toolkit. The toolkit runs AI agents in isolated sandboxes designed to mitigate cybersecurity risks.

“Nvidia and Meta are expanding our partnership to optimize the computing infrastructure end to end for capable, efficient and secure AI agents, so Muse can empower billions of people to achieve more and pursue greater ambitions,” said Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang.

AMD, which will invest $1 billion in Meta, today revealed that the Facebook parent has adopted its Helios rack design. Helios contains 72 GPUs much like the DGX Vera Rubin NVL72. It’s based on AMD’s latest Instinct MI450 graphics card architecture, Epyc CPUs and Pensando data processing units, which are the chipmaker’s answer to the BlueField-4.

It says Meta has deployed an “initial” set of Helios racks in its data centers and is currently testing them. The social media giant plans to deploy additional systems in the near future.

Further down the line, Meta will adopt a custom AI accelerator based on AMD’s Instinct graphics card architecture. The chipmaker, for its part, will use the technical data collected through the partnership to improve its future chip and rack designs.

“Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta’s most ambitious superintelligence models and services,” said AMD CEO Lisa Su.

Key highlights:

INDIANAPOLIS, Oct. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY) today announced that Patrik Jonsson, executive vice president and president, Lilly International, has decided to retire at the end of 2026 after a 36-year career at Lilly.

Jonsson joined the company in 1990 as a sales representative in Sweden. He went on to lead Lilly in Sweden, Scandinavia, Italy and Japan, then served as president of Lilly Bio-Medicines and Lilly Immunology, as well as president of Lilly USA and Lilly's cardiometabolic health business, before leading Lilly International.

"For more than three decades, Patrik has dedicated his career to improving lives by bringing our medicines to people around the world," said David A. Ricks, Lilly chair and CEO. "He has held multiple executive roles in the company spanning drug development and customer operations, including head of immunology, cardiometabolic health and Lilly USA. Today he applies his deep expertise in global launches across Lilly International. Patrik is a patient-focused, engaging team leader who has mentored countless colleagues. On behalf of our Board, leadership team and thousands of employees he has worked alongside, I thank Patrik for his service to our company."

Effective Jan. 1, 2027, Lilly's U.S. and international businesses will come together as Lilly Global Markets, led by Ilya Yuffa, who will become executive vice president and president, Lilly Global Markets.

Bringing these organizations together will accelerate decision-making, increase scalability and provide a unified capability to improve human health through expanded access to medicines around the world.

Yuffa joined Lilly in 1996 as a financial analyst and has held leadership roles in finance, business development, sales and general management, including president and general manager of Lilly's Italy Hub, which covered more than 25 countries, president of Lilly Bio-Medicines, president of Lilly International and currently executive vice president and president, Lilly USA and Global Customer Capabilities.

Ricks continued, "To build on our momentum, now is the right time to consolidate our geographies for greater impact. Ilya has run both our international and U.S. businesses, and his range of experience and commitment to excellence make him uniquely qualified to lead our customer-facing operations worldwide. He is joined by a proven team with the expertise and focus to help us reach even more people with our medicines."

The following executives will lead the company's six geographic hubs and report to Yuffa:

Laura Steele, currently group vice president, U.S. Cardiometabolic Health, will be promoted to president, Lilly USA. In 23 years at Lilly, Steele has held leadership roles in marketing, value and access, and commercial operations inside and outside the U.S., including Lilly's U.S. neuroscience business.

Elias Khalil, currently president and general manager of Lilly's Italy Hub, will be promoted to group vice president and president, Lilly Europe and Canada. In 18 years at Lilly, Khalil has held leadership roles across the Gulf region, Saudi Arabia and the U.S. neuroscience business.

Nabil Daoud will continue in his role as group vice president and president, Lilly InterContinental.

Karla Alcazar, Huzur Devletsah and Winselow Tucker will continue in their roles as president and general manager of Lilly Japan, Lilly China and Lilly India, respectively.

title: Anthropic IPO Filing Reveals Looming Threat to Nvidia's Pricing Power - Business Insider
description:
Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance.
Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply.

text:
Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance.

The AI lab says it manages compute "as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners" — with software that can direct its work to different chips depending on where they're most productive, according to Anthropic's S-1 filing, which came out Monday as the company prepares to go public.

Anthropic says it uses hardware from four chip families: Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

That flexibility, which Anthropic said "took years and significant investment to build," could make major AI companies less dependent on Nvidia over time and give them more negotiating leverage, analysts said.

"The real exposure could be Nvidia's pricing power," said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, "because a customer that can shift work across four platforms negotiates very differently than one that can't."

Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply.

Breaking Nvidia's grip isn't easy

Although Anthropic's chip mix isn't new, the company is now pitching it as a core advantage to investors, Moorhead said.

The threat has its limits. Switching between chips is still difficult — especially when it comes to training AI models as opposed to running them, Moorhead said — and only the biggest AI companies have the resources to do it.

Anthropic also continues to spend billions on Nvidia compute, Moorhead said.

Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said that while other major companies like OpenAI likely take a multichip approach, it may not be worth the effort and investment for smaller players.

Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said Anthropic's strategy doesn't represent a major near-term threat. Having more chip options doesn't erase Nvidia's advantages in performance, networking, and software, he said.

There's a broader risk for Nvidia if AI compute becomes more of a commodity.

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has warned that if supply overtakes demand, it could drive down rental prices.

"GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run," he told Bloomberg last week. "The moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

title: The platform approach to becoming Frontier - The Official Microsoft Blog
description:
Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000.
By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.
To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot.
Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market.
Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale.
text:
Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There is no path where this notion of infinite cognitive compute replaces human purpose. Frontier Transformation is an opportunity for a wholesale reinvention of how you think about your unique ideas coming to life and how your organization can thrive in your industry.

Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. We are taking a platform approach toward enabling the same: Copilot as the place to call home for interacting with AI to empower human ambition; the Microsoft IQ platform to compound and amplify your intelligence from within while protecting your unique differentiation; and Agent 365 to enable Trust and Observability at every layer of the stack so that you can govern, manage, secure and get business value and return out of the capabilities you deliver.

Our latest earnings are another important marker on that journey. Behind the numbers are thousands of customers, partners, developers and employees putting AI to work in meaningful ways. We have so many inspiring stories from our customers that highlight these outcomes, and below are some of our favorites.

Empowering human ambition with Copilot

Volkswagen has scaled Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees as it expands the role of AI in decision-making and knowledge-based processes across the enterprise. Building on Copilot Chat adoption that reached more than 300,000 monthly active users, employees are now using Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced scenarios, bringing greater organizational context to decision-making and knowledge-based work. Volkswagen is also working with Microsoft to further scale its Intelligent Data Foundation on Microsoft Fabric to make data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. With this investment, Volkswagen is demonstrating how companies have evolved from using Copilot as a productivity tool to an operating system to empower human ambition.

Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000. Copilot usage has surpassed 90%, and the company is using the tool to connect employees with specialized agents and business systems. AI agents are already automating roughly 75% of initial responses and triage for a service desk that receives nearly 300,000 inquiries annually, while new agents are supporting work across sales, systems engineering, procurement, finance and accounting. As customer zero, Fujitsu is using Copilot as the front door to a multi-agent work environment and using insights from its own AI adoption to better serve its customers.

KOHLER is using GitHub Copilot to transform software development, with one organization improving code releases by 25% and reducing error defects by 75%. These engineering breakthroughs are part of a broader effort to embed AI processes across the company, spanning IT, finance, marketing, supply chain and operations. Microsoft Copilot has reached 98% adoption, saving an average of 2 to 5 hours per month as employees are making informed decisions and getting answers faster in the flow of their work. Employees across the company have also created more than 3,000 agents to date, with hundreds active daily.

At Krafton, Microsoft Security Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR are helping the security team respond to a growing volume and complexity of threats. The global gaming company automated key parts of security operations, from alerting and investigation to reporting, combining Microsoft Security solutions with its own systems and data to quickly gather context that helps distinguish real threats from false positives. This approach is having immediate results: security alert recognition time has fallen by approximately 95% to less than one minute, investigation work that previously took tens of minutes now takes about three minutes and roughly 95% of report creation has been automated. By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.

To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot. NASA employees are using Copilot to sift through massive amounts of academic literature and streamline daily tasks, and specialized assistants are helping researchers navigate complex Earth science data through natural language, extending access to information that once required significant technical expertise. Hydrology Copilot, for example, can analyze variables like precipitation and soil moisture to help communities better understand water conditions, prepare for droughts and anticipate flood risks, while automatically performing calculations and analyses.

To transform frontline work, Williams, a US natural gas company, is using Microsoft Copilot to help employees spend less time searching documents and completing manual processes, and more time on critical field operations. Copilot helps teams generate plans, interpret procedures, assess regulatory requirements, troubleshoot issues and complete safety reporting, while employees can create agents tailored to their own workflows. Demonstrating that the person closest to a problem is often the best one to solve it, one operations technician built an anomaly detector using Copilot that compares equipment data against baseline statistics and alerts teams to potential issues before they become costly or dangerous. Since deploying Copilot, AI adoption at Williams has grown from single digits to more than 90%, helping employees accelerate operations, improve reporting and compliance and identify equipment issues earlier.

Bristol Myers Squibb has rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 25,000 employees, reaching 96% adoption, and is now putting AI agents to work across everyday use cases such as document review and project management in support of the company’s mission to bring more medicines to more patients faster. One agent, called RABIT, analyzes meeting transcripts, surfaces action items and delivers insights directly within employees’ workflows.

Facing rising patient demand and financial pressures, Brown University Health is using Dragon Copilot to give clinicians more time to focus on patients. The health system adopted Dragon Copilot, and an early pilot across 420 clinicians found users spent less time on after-hours documentation and reported lower cognitive burden. Building on that experience, Brown University Health deployed Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio across departments, which led to the creation of more than 24 AI agents to support clinical workflows, hospital policies, patient access and operations. These AI solutions are not only supporting clinicians in the flow of their work but also helping to improve the patient experience and access to care.

Microsoft IQ compounds and protects your intelligence

BNY has made AI part of how its employees work through Eliza, its in-house AI platform built with Microsoft Azure, Microsoft Foundry, Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot – with plans to add Work IQ. More than 300 solutions now run on Eliza, ranging from inquiry management to client onboarding, and 100% of employees have been trained on the platform. Across the bank, that scale is translating into meaningful results: client transaction inquiries are being resolved 80% faster and AI-assisted client onboarding is 20% faster on average. Through the Microsoft CEO Co-Innovation program, BNY also worked with Microsoft to develop an AI research capability with Foundry that investigates complex data issues, analyzes context across multiple sources, identifies likely root causes and recommends next steps, bringing AI-assisted reasoning into processes that have traditionally relied on human investigation alone.

Docusign is helping 1.9 million customers across 180 countries turn agreement data into actionable business insights. The company built an Intelligent Agreement Management platform on Microsoft Azure and used Microsoft Foundry to shift from general-purpose models to a system of task-specific models that better understand context. This change allows Docusign to process more than a million agreement documents daily with up to eightfold greater throughput and 90% lower AI processing costs. Foundry also supports a model lifecycle designed for continuous improvement, where processes are fine-tuned before deployment and monitored in production, while also providing the governance and traceability needed to meet enterprise requirements for compliance, visibility and control. Now agreement content is structured data that compounds from within, so organizations can use it to make decisions and automate workflows, knowing their IP is protected.

To help marketers create more effective content, Kantar turned decades of proprietary advertising intelligence into action with Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry. Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market. The new approach can process and score large volumes of videos 20x faster while reducing platform operating costs by 4x, helping customers move from insight to action in minutes rather than hours. By bringing its unique intelligence into a continuous loop of observation and improvement, Kantar is creating new ways to help marketers turn insight into better creative and business outcomes.

Kinaxis, a Canadian supply chain software company, runs Maestro, its AI-driven supply chain orchestration platform, on Microsoft Azure. Maestro helps businesses make better decisions faster amid constant disruption. It brings together traditionally disparate business data like sales orders, inventory and production capacity with external signals like weather, market shifts and breaking news to give planners a near real-time view of their supply chains. With this unified data foundation, planners and analysts can use predictive AI and optimization models to anticipate demand shifts, evaluate constraints and recommend action, while generative AI agents act as assistants to ask questions, explore scenarios and automate parts of the planning process. With this intelligence in one platform, businesses can understand how disruptions ripple across their interconnected operations, weigh trade-offs and adjust plans as conditions change.

Moody’s is making more than a century of credit and risk intelligence directly accessible through Microsoft Copilot, giving customers trusted, protected context for complex decisions. Through a federated connector built using Model Context Protocol, customers can access live, decision-grade Moody’s intelligence through Researcher in Copilot and within Word, Excel and Teams, without copying or exporting the underlying data. A single question can synthesize information across credit ratings, company financials, ownership information and physical risk models, helping customers reach insights in minutes instead of spending hours or days on research and analysis. This brings trusted, connected intelligence directly into workflows where customers make complex decisions.

To turn conversations into actionable intelligence at global scale, Plaud, an AI hardware and software company, is using Microsoft Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models and Azure Speech in Foundry Tools to power transcription, summarization and AI inference across long-form audio and multilingual scenarios. Serving more than 2 million users worldwide, Plaud increased transcription accuracy and processing speed by 35% and improved inference performance by 30%, helping professionals turn spoken content into structured outputs and insights. Even as its user base doubled, the company used Foundry’s elastic scaling and flexible deployment models to reduce overall compute costs by 35%, while strengthening its ability to meet security, privacy and compliance requirements across global markets.

Rockwell Automation built a Maintenance Copilot using Microsoft Foundry to put decades of manufacturing expertise in the hands of employees. The AI assistant brings together expert knowledge from veteran engineers, manufacturing data and machine manuals, allowing technicians to quickly identify likely causes of equipment issues, see how colleagues have solved similar problems and access step-by-step troubleshooting guidance. At its Singapore factory, the approach has helped reduce machine downtime by 33% and cut servicing and spare-part costs by about 25%. Rockwell estimates it has also reduced the time it takes new workers to learn to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three months.

With 1.5 billion passengers riding its elevators and escalators every day, TK Elevator knows that every minute of downtime affects how people move through airports, hospitals and offices. Building on a decade of connected-equipment data on Microsoft Azure, the company created AI agents with Microsoft Foundry that brief service technicians before they enter a building, telling them which elevator, which floor, what the issue is and which tools to bring. After each job, a voice agent records the technician’s account of the work in their own words, with no typing, and adds that expertise to a shared record. With 25,000 technicians caring for 1.4 million units worldwide, TK Elevator is turning each technician’s know-how into compounded intelligence every colleague can draw on.

Telstra partnered with Microsoft Frontier Company to deploy an AI-powered Migration Payment Agent that helps simplify one of the most complex aspects of customer migration: reconciling billing and payments across legacy and new platforms. The agent uses intelligence across these systems to proactively identify inconsistencies, recommend corrective actions and create enriched cases for human review, combining AI-driven insights with human-in-the-loop validation to maintain operational trust and governance. Already supporting more than 272,000 service migrations and delivering recommendations at 95%+ accuracy in production, the solution demonstrates how Telstra is applying agentic AI at enterprise scale to transform complex operations, improve customer outcomes and build reusable AI capabilities while compounding and protecting Telstra’s operational intelligence.

Agent 365 observes AI solutions across the stack

To advance its transformation into an AI-powered organization, Manulife is adopting Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite, expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 30,000 employees and leveraging Microsoft Agent 365 to govern, manage and secure AI agents at enterprise scale. With Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry supporting its global enterprise AI platform, Manulife is building a foundation for teams to develop and deploy AI and agentic solutions while maintaining standards for quality, security and cost efficiency. AI is already delivering impact across the business, from generative AI solutions supporting more than 110 million customer calls annually to developers increasing productivity by 30% with assisted and autonomous AI capabilities. With agentic solutions and AI-powered workflows already in production, Manulife is creating the foundation to scale AI responsibly across its global operations and accelerate its next phase of enterprise transformation.

Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale. As a Microsoft customer zero organization for Agent 365, Insight Enterprises is quick to adopt new capabilities internally and pass those learnings on to clients. With Microsoft engineering, it tested how Microsoft and third-party agents could be observed, managed, governed and secured through a unified control plane. To date, Insight Enterprises has discovered 9,734 agents with visibility into which are active, what data they can access and how to monitor their activity over time. The experience has helped Insight Enterprises build practical AI governance expertise it can bring to customers, including organizations in highly regulated industries.

KPMG is adopting Microsoft Agent 365 to manage and secure AI agents across its global organization, providing centralized observability and control as it scales agentic AI. Agent 365 will also strengthen KPMG Workbench, its multi-agent platform built on Microsoft Foundry that coordinates agents across client service delivery platforms. At the same time, KPMG is expanding Microsoft Copilot to more than 276,000 professionals worldwide, helping embed AI more deeply across audit, tax and advisory services. Together, these capabilities are giving KPMG the confidence and security to move agents from experimentation into enterprise-wide deployment, while helping clients do the same.

Operating in one of the most highly regulated industries, where protecting sensitive customer information is essential, Truist Financial Corporation is using Agent 365 to manage, govern and observe more than 13,000 AI declarative agents across its organization. Truist manages its agent ecosystem with discipline: every agent has an accountable owner and agents are automatically disabled after 45 days of inactivity. That rigor is driving strong retention and adoption, with more than 8,000 agents active each month. Building on this trusted foundation, Truist has advanced its broader AI strategy through their investment of more than 50,000 Microsoft 365 E7: The Frontier Suite seats.

—

Every quarter gives us an opportunity to step back and look at the progress we are making with our customers and partners around the world. What continues to strike me is not simply the pace of change, but the ambition we see from organizations using technology to achieve aspirations that simply weren’t possible before. We look forward to working alongside you on the path to becoming Frontier, and we hope to see many of you at Microsoft Ignite this year in November to share the latest innovations that will enable you to reach that destination.

Judson Althoff is the chief executive officer of the commercial business at Microsoft. He is responsible for the product strategy, sales, services, support, marketing, operations and revenue growth of the company’s commercial business, which operates in more than 120 regional and national subsidiaries globally.

text:
All three major US stock indexes were up in late-morning trading Tuesday, as oil prices fell and investors look ahead to the Federal Reserve's next announcement on interest rates at the conclusion of officials' two-day meeting on Wednesday.

In company news, Ares Capital (ARCC) will acquire MidCap Financial Investment (MFIC) in a stock-and-cash deal with a total enterprise value of around $2.6 billion, the companies said Tuesday. Under the deal terms, MidCap shareholders are expected to receive total consideration of $10.88 per fully diluted share, representing a premium of 30.1% to its closing share price on Monday. The acquisition is expected to close in H1 of 2027.

Separately, Ares Capital reported Q3 core earnings Tuesday of $0.46 per share, down from $0.50 a year earlier and below the FactSet consensus analyst estimate of $0.47. Total Q3 investment income was $763 million, down from $782 million a year ago. Ares Capital shares were up 0.2% around midday, while MidCap shares were up 23.7%.

S&P Global (SPGI) has initiated a strategic review of alternatives, including a potential separation, for Capital IQ and associated data businesses, which constitute the majority of Kensho Data & Platforms within Market Intelligence, the company said Tuesday.

Separately, S&P Global reported Q3 adjusted EPS Tuesday of $4.58 per share, up from $4.20 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus of $4.43. Revenue was $3.68 billion, up from $3.44 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $3.64 billion. For full-year 2026, the company expects adjusted EPS of $17.70 to $17.95, up from its prior outlook of $17.50 to $17.75 and compared with the FactSet consensus of $17.84. S&P Global shares were up 0.3%.

Meta Platforms (META) said Tuesday it priced 40 million Class A common shares at $625 each, raising the stock offering to $25 billion from $22.5 billion, with both offerings set to close Thursday.

Separately, Meta and Nvidia (NVDA) are expanding their partnership to develop the social media giant's Muse family of AI models, and Nvidia is also planning to invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering, Nvidia said Tuesday. Lastly, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Meta also said they are advancing their strategic partnership to power Meta's superintelligence infrastructure. Meta shares were down 0.8%, while Nvidia and AMD shares were up 0.8% and 4.7%, respectively.

Boeing (BA) reported a Q3 core loss Tuesday of $0.34 per share, narrowing from a loss of $7.47 a year earlier and compared with the FactSet consensus of a loss of $0.25. Revenue was $24.19 billion, up from $23.27 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $23.95 billion. Boeing shares were down 9.9%.

Coca-Cola (KO) reported fiscal Q3 comparable diluted EPS Tuesday of $0.91, up from $0.82 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus of $0.88. Net operating revenue was $13.38 billion, up from $12.46 billion a year ago and above the FactSet consensus of $12.92 billion. For full-year 2026, the company expects comparable EPS growth of at least 11%, up from its previous guidance of 9% to 10% growth. Coca-Cola also expects organic revenue growth of at least 5%. Coca-Cola shares were down 0.4%.

Novartis (NVS) reported Q3 core diluted EPS Tuesday of $2.46, up from $2.25 a year earlier and above the FactSet consensus of $2.27. Net sales were $14.52 billion, up from $13.91 billion a year ago but below the FactSet consensus of $14.53 billion. For full-year 2026, the company expects core operating income growth of low-single digits, up from its previous guidance of a low-single-digit decline. Novartis shares were up 0.9%.

Qualcomm (QCOM) and Anduril Industries are collaborating on a laptop designed and assembled in the US under a new product line called BlueChip, which seeks to rebuild American computer manufacturing, the companies said Tuesday. Qualcomm shares were up 1.0%.

title: Nvidia backs AI inference optimisation startup Simplismart - Global Corporate Venturing
description:

text:
Simplismart, an AI infrastructure startup, has raised $14m in a series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with participation from Nvidia, Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The company develops software designed to make AI inference — the process of running trained models to generate outputs — more efficient, helping enterprises reduce costs while enabling cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into services they can sell.

As companies move AI from experimentation into everyday business applications, the cost of running models is becoming a pressing concern. Every question answered, document processed or video generated consumes computing resources, and the expense can mount quickly as usage scales.

Businesses building AI products increasingly need to balance delivering fast enough responses with keeping inference costs down. Access to powerful models is becoming less of a differentiator as open-weight alternatives proliferate. The critical factor is cost.

“Nvidia’s investment reflects where AI is heading: from training models to running them profitably,” said Amritanshu Jain, co-founder and chief executive of Simplismart (pictured above, left).

“The industry has spent years pushing the limits of what AI models can do. With frontier-class open models now readily available, access alone is no longer enough to set a business apart. The advantage comes from how you run them: what each interaction costs, how quickly the application responds, and whether it stays reliable as demand grows.”

Simplismart aims to optimise that trade-off. Its software sits between AI models and the GPUs that run them, configuring how workloads are served and managing their deployment, scaling and operation. Rather than simply providing access to a model through a fixed endpoint, the platform allows customers to tune infrastructure around the performance and cost requirements of each application.

“We’ve spent four years building the software between the model and the GPU, bringing workload optimization, deployment, and ongoing operations into one platform. Enterprises use it to run AI applications; cloud providers use it to turn GPU fleets into services they can sell. We’ve built the infrastructure that makes model capability commercially usable.”

Simplismart said its annualised revenue run rate grew 14-fold over the past six months, with customers including HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema.

“We don’t own compute; we build the software that makes it productive. Thus, our work complements the ecosystem Nvidia has built. At this stage, as we expand into cloud providers and sovereign AI, that alignment matters more than the capital,” said Jain.

Finding the right price-performance balance

Inference costs depend on more than the headline price per token. The choice of model, GPU, inference framework, quantisation method, caching strategy and other technical settings can all affect how much computing is needed to generate a response. Each choice involves trade-offs between latency, throughput, output quality and cost.

Simplismart’s inference engine allows customers to configure these components around the needs of individual applications. Its objective is to identify a combination that meets a customer’s service requirements at the lowest viable cost, rather than forcing the application to use a standard configuration.

The company cites one customer that needed response times of roughly 200 milliseconds at a cost of about 9 cents per million tokens. Simplismart said its optimisation process identified several alternatives, including one costing 5 cents per million tokens with 350-millisecond latency and another costing 12 cents with 100-millisecond latency. The configuration ultimately deployed cost 7 cents per million tokens and delivered a response in 180 milliseconds, according to the company.

Each business will optimise differently. A business running a consumer-facing application may need near-instant responses, while an enterprise processing documents in batches can often tolerate longer waits in exchange for lower costs.

Helping cloud providers monetise GPUs

The economics of inference also matter to the companies supplying the computing power. GPUs are expensive assets, but demand fluctuates by workload, geography and time of day. Cloud providers may have capacity sitting idle while customers elsewhere struggle to secure the resources they need.

Simplismart’s software lets infrastructure operators turn their GPU fleets into managed AI services, sold directly to their own customers. At Indian cloud provider Yotta, for example, Simplismart’s platform supports the serverless inference layer of Shakti Studio, allowing customers to run AI models without managing the underlying inference infrastructure themselves.

The model gives cloud providers a way to compete on more than access to hardware: they can offer managed services that simplify deployment and help customers control costs.

“Inferencing is emerging as one of the biggest game changers in AI economics,” said Dayakar Puskoor, managing partner at Dallas Venture Capital.

“Simplismart is rapidly emerging as a global player helping enterprises run AI workloads more efficiently, while enabling cloud providers to turn GPU capacity into scalable services. We are backing this fast-growing company because of its proven technical prowess in addressing a critical need in the AI infrastructure ecosystem globally, as well as the strong execution capabilities of its founding team.”

From optimisation to capacity markets

Simplismart’s longer-term ambition is to match fluctuating AI demand with available GPU capacity across providers and regions.

The mismatch is structural. Consumer applications may experience sharp peaks in demand, while batch-processing workloads can run overnight. Yet infrastructure providers often make longer-term commitments to GPU capacity, whereas customers want the flexibility to pay for what they use. Better coordination could help reduce idle capacity and improve the economics for both sides.

Simplismart is developing a scheduling layer intended to match workloads with available resources, taking account of timing, latency, geography and compliance requirements. As more customers and cloud providers join the platform, the company expects to gain a clearer picture of demand patterns and available supply.

You can't spell AI without Nvidia

Concerns about the company's legal challenges and heavy spending on AI have weighed on Meta, which has shed 16% over the past year. However, at 21 times earnings, the stock has much of the downside potential priced in.

text:
Institutional custody now extends to two more crypto assets, while a proposed route into invoice financing remains exploratory. The Bank of New York Mellon Corporation NYSEBNY, a New York financial services group, said on Oct. 27 that its digital custody platform now supports XRP and RLUSD.

The expansion deepens its relationship with Ripple, the blockchain payments and custody provider founded in 2012. BNY also intends to support more tokenized assets issued on the XRP Ledger and work with Ripple to let bank clients mint and redeem RLUSD directly.

BNY shares traded at US$147.31, up 0.09 per cent, at 9:47 a.m. EDT on Tuesday on the NYSE, according to NYSEBNY.

Tuesday's announcement gives no custody fees, client commitments or expected revenue from the expansion. The companies describe their proposed supply chain finance work as exploratory and subject to client requirements, separating the available custody service from the business they hope to build around it.

Token Custody Extends The Reserve Relationship

Ripple selected BNY as the primary custodian of RLUSD reserves on July 9, 2025. That agreement covered the assets backing the stablecoin and included Ripple's use of BNY transaction banking services.

Tuesday's expansion adds custody of the tokens themselves. Eligible institutional clients can safekeep, hold and transfer XRP and RLUSD through BNY's platform, which the bank says operates within its broader governance, controls and resiliency framework.

Ripple put RLUSD's market capitalization at approximately US$2.5 billion in the Oct. 27 announcement. That is the size of the stablecoin, rather than an amount BNY says it holds on its digital custody platform.

BNY reported US$63.4 trillion in assets under custody or administration as of Sept. 30. The release does not break out digital asset custody within that total, so the bank's overall scale provides no measure of the new service's existing client balances.

"With BNY, we're connecting the necessary components of financial infrastructure on the XRP Ledger so institutions can move from holding digital assets to using them within capital markets and trade finance seamlessly," Ripple president Monica Long said in the release.

The Oct. 27 statement places direct RLUSD minting and redemption among intended initiatives. It gives no start date for that capability or for expanded support of tokenized investment products issued on the ledger.

Invoice Financing Remains An Initiative

C2FO, a working capital platform that connects businesses with financing against approved invoices, is the proposed supply chain finance collaborator. In a separate Oct. 27 announcement with Ripple, it described plans to bring financing and settlement supporting its Instant Pay service onto the XRP Ledger.

That release says participating capital providers would fund instant payments, with RLUSD used for settlement. Suppliers would continue accessing early payment through C2FO, while the invoices' agreed terms and due dates would stay unchanged.

The companies say the arrangement could replace settlement delays of several days with receipt of funds in seconds. That is their description of the intended service; the Oct. 27 release directs interested businesses to a waitlist and provides no measured deployment results.

The two announcements also describe different stages of work. C2FO and Ripple outline the payment initiative, while BNY and Ripple say they are exploring a supply chain finance initiative with C2FO to expand investor access to trade finance assets.

BNY Is Adding Other Digital Asset Relationships

Galaxy Digital Inc. NASDAQGLXY, which operates digital asset trading, investment management and data centre businesses, reported a multiyear agreement with BNY in its Oct. 27 results. It includes support for staking on BNY's digital custody platform, with Galaxy also acting as a platform design partner.

Galaxy held US$812 million in stablecoins at Sept. 30, according to those results. The holdings form part of the liquidity discussed in Mugglehead's coverage of its third-quarter earnings; they do not establish that Galaxy holds RLUSD or uses the new Ripple custody service.

Read more: Galaxy Digital reports US$323M profit as Helios contribution grows

The proposed use of stablecoins for institutional settlement also faces a competing model. In a June 24, 2025 assessment, the Bank for International Settlements argued that stablecoins fall short on acceptance at par, timely discharge of obligations and safeguards against financial crime.

Hyun Song Shin, then the BIS's economic adviser and head of its Monetary and Economic Department, advocated integrating tokenized bank deposits and central bank settlement money on one programmable platform. That assessment predates this agreement and addresses stablecoins broadly, rather than BNY's custody controls or RLUSD specifically.

title: Airlines are trading nearly 23% higher ticket prices for emptier planes as jet fuel prices spike | Fortune
description:
Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group have angled their businesses to generate more passenger revenue through higher individual prices as jet fuel prices climb—U.S.
Jet fuel prices forcing their hand The central pressure on airlines is the cost of fuel, one of the industry’s largest operating expenses.
The International Air Transport Association’s jet fuel price monitor tracked global jet fuel prices at about $99 per barrel in February before prices more than doubled to $209 in April.
“All airline bottom lines are suffering from the rapid 70% rise in jet fuel prices,” Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General, said in a press release.
The carrier reported record Q3 revenue of $16.3 billion, but higher fuel expenses continued to weigh on its bottom line.
text:
Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group have angled their businesses to generate more passenger revenue through higher individual prices as jet fuel prices climb—U.S. airfares have climbed 22.4% year over year.

The five major airlines generated nearly $8.8 billion more in passenger revenue in Q3 2026 than in Q3 2025—an 18% increase, according to Reuters. But passenger traffic grew less than 1%.

“If fuel stays elevated, we have to continue to push yield up so that we can make a bit of money,” Devon May, American Airlines chief financial officer, told Reuters.

Jet fuel prices forcing their hand

The central pressure on airlines is the cost of fuel, one of the industry’s largest operating expenses. Gulf Coast spot jet fuel prices rose from $2.43 per gallon before the war began in February to $4.63 in October—an increase of roughly 91%, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

The increase has been driven mainly by disruptions to oil supplies and refining capacity associated with the conflict. The International Air Transport Association’s jet fuel price monitor tracked global jet fuel prices at about $99 per barrel in February before prices more than doubled to $209 in April.

Fuel’s importance to airline economics makes that swing extremely costly—and potentially dangerous for airlines. The IATA projects that fuel will account for nearly one-third of airline operating expenses in 2026, compared to about one-quarter in 2025.

“All airline bottom lines are suffering from the rapid 70% rise in jet fuel prices,” Willie Walsh, IATA’s Director General, said in a press release. “Some of the additional cost is being recuperated by adjusting prices and improving efficiency, but it will not be sufficient to maintain profitability at the previous year’s level. Smaller carriers that started the year with weak balance sheets are certainly struggling.”

The cost increases also expose the timing problem. Airlines typically sell tickets months ahead of departure, meaning they can’t raise the price of seats that passengers have already purchased. That leaves carriers to recover expenses through ticket fares on the few that haven’t already been sold.

Higher fares, more revenue, fewer passengers—but no profit?

Higher fares are lifting revenue even when passenger growth remains weak, but fuel costs are absorbing much of that additional income.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index for September, airline fares were 22.4% higher than a year earlier. The inflation rate was only 3.7%, meaning the airfare increases were substantially outpacing the overall rise in consumer prices.

American Airlines is a clear example of that in action. The carrier reported record Q3 revenue of $16.3 billion, but higher fuel expenses continued to weigh on its bottom line. Chief commercial officer Nathaniel Pieper said the airline deliberately accepted lower load factors—or seat occupancy—in exchange for higher revenue per passenger.

“We were deliberate in how we managed revenue during the quarter,” Pieper said in the Q3 2026 earnings call. “We prioritized yield over load factor, proactively securing meaningfully higher yields in exchange for slightly lower loads.”

United Airlines adopted a similar approach. Its leisure load factor—which measures the share of available seats occupied—declined 1.3 percentage points in Q3. Chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella said in the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call that higher prices produced some sensitivity among travelers, but the airline considers the tradeoff worthwhile—saying it’s a “trade we would make every day.”

Southwest also reported strong fare growth—its average passenger fare rose 21.6% in the first nine months of the year, and by the third quarter, that rose to 26.9%.

“Customers are responding to the enhanced Southwest offering, and it shows in our results,” Bob Jordan, president and CEO of Southwest Airlines,said in a press release. “Demand remained strong as we lapped last year’s bag fee and other commercial initiatives, reinforcing our belief that the earnings power we’ve built is durable, even with significantly higher fuel costs.”

And the revenue gains didn’t eliminate the financial strain of rising costs for the airlines. Delta Air Lines cut its annual earnings forecast as it expects “to generate a pre-tax profit of roughly $4.5 billion, absorbing a $6 billion increase in fuel costs.”

Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest Airlines and Alaska Air Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune.

Investors have focused heavily on technology giants in recent years as these companies are driving the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. They are the ones spending on the infrastructure build-out, or developing and providing the products and services needed to advance the AI story.

And as a result, this week, with big tech set to report earnings, should be a big one for investors. Microsoft (MSFT -0.24%) and Alphabet (GOOG +0.84%) (GOOGL +1.19%) kick things off with quarterly updates on Oct. 28 after the closing bell, and Amazon's (AMZN +1.61%) report is scheduled for Oct. 29 after the close of trading.

These reports should be important for the entire market, considering that AI has set the tone for the overall direction of the S&P 500. Tech giants are heavily weighted in the index and therefore guide its ups and downs. But investors in one particular company should be keenly interested in this week’s reports: I'm talking about Nvidia (NVDA +0.90%) investors. In fact, they should watch one crucial number. Let's zoom in for a close look.

Nvidia's role in AI

It's important to first consider Nvidia's role in the AI boom. This technology company makes graphics processing units (GPUs), chips that were originally known for their use in the video gaming market. And the gaming customer was once Nvidia's biggest. Then, about a decade ago, Nvidia recognized the AI opportunity and focused the design of GPUs to suit the needs of this industry.

Fast forward to the start of the AI stock market boom, about three years ago, and it was clear that Nvidia had won its AI bet. The company's earnings have been soaring in the double and triple digits, quarter after quarter, to record levels. This is as customers knock at the door, eager to get in on Nvidia's GPUs. The company faces rivals in the space, but so far, it has remained ahead thanks to the speed of its GPUs and its vast selection of related offerings.

title: Microsoft Is Paying Workers to Leave So It Can Pay for AI - 24/7 Wall St.
description:
The offer comes as AI spending rises fast.
Microsoft spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, up 79.62%, while free cash flow fell 6.46%.
The link to AI comes from the spending figures and the teams invited to leave, and that evidence is strong enough to take seriously.
What Microsoft Offered Employees The company’s post, “Introducing a Voluntary Exit Offer,” was signed by Amy Coleman as executive vice president and chief people officer.
Going from a targeted retirement offer to layoffs to a broad exit offer looks like a structural reset.
text:
On Monday, October 26, 2026, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees. That is roughly 27% of the 223,000 people it employed full-time as of June 30.

The stock rose 1.54% to $532.60 and was little changed after hours at $532.45, leaving the company worth about $3.95 trillion.

The offer comes as AI spending rises fast. Microsoft spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026, up 79.62%, while free cash flow fell 6.46%.

Microsoft’s announcement never mentions AI or cost cutting. The link to AI comes from the spending figures and the teams invited to leave, and that evidence is strong enough to take seriously.

What Microsoft Offered Employees

The company’s post, “Introducing a Voluntary Exit Offer,” was signed by Amy Coleman as executive vice president and chief people officer. It describes a time-limited offer for employees at level 70 and below on participating teams in the U.S., Canada, India, and the U.K.

Participation “varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs,” and the company added, “The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us… We’ll learn from it.”

Uptake, total cost and exact severance terms were not disclosed, but terms are reportedly similar to standard severance, and eligible staff reportedly have until early December to accept, with departures on December 31.

Who Is Protected and Who Is Exposed

Participating parts reportedly include Xbox, Windows, Copilot and Finance. Data center, sales, and marketing staff are largely left out, which means the teams that build and sell AI capacity are protected.

This is also the third workforce move of the year. An April retirement program covered 8,750 U.S. workers and drew acceptance above 30%, and in July Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs, or 2.1% of staff, mostly in Xbox.

Going from a targeted retirement offer to layoffs to a broad exit offer looks like a structural reset. A one-time trim would not follow that sequence.

Spending Math Behind the Timing

Industry data center investment is likely to top $700 billion this year. In July, CFO Amy Hood put Microsoft’s calendar-2026 capex at about $175 billion. The earlier figure was $190 billion, and it came down only because longer asset lives moved some leases out of capex.

Capex hit about $41 billion in the June quarter, and the forecast for the September quarter was more than $50 billion. Depreciation, the annual expense charged as that equipment wears out, weighs on margins for years. Payroll is the largest cost management can change quickly.

Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) rates the stock Overweight with a $725 target. It estimated that if one-third of eligible workers accept, operating margin would gain about 2 percentage points a year. The one-third figure is an assumption, though April’s uptake makes it plausible.

What Investors Are Pricing In Before Earnings

Fiscal first-quarter results are expected after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Analysts expect EPS of $4.7199 on revenue of about $90.75 billion. The key questions are clear. Investors want to know whether management can quantify the offer’s charges or savings, whether capex guidance rises again, and whether cloud growth can stay ahead of depreciation.

Why Microsoft’s Margin Case Hinges on This Exit Offer

Azure grew 43% last quarter, commercial backlog reached $678 billion, and demand still tops capacity. A lower payroll in slower units makes that expansion cheaper to carry.

The main risks are clear. The best people may be the ones who leave, morale in Xbox and Windows could suffer, and the savings are small next to quarterly capex.

The stock trades below its $553.72 52-week high. The margin case was wrong. That would be the outcome if the October 28 report increases capex without quantifying the offer’s savings, and shares have not recaptured that high by December 31.

HOUSTON, Oct. 27, 2026 — The Walmart Healthcare Research Institute (WHRI) and Care Access, a health and research company, today announced plans to open three additional Clinical Trial Centers in Livonia, Michigan; Las Vegas, Nevada; and San Antonio, Texas in the first half of 2027. Houston, TX – Walmart Houston on Highway 6 S

Tyler, TX – Walmart Tyler on State Highway 64 W

Dalton, GA – Walmart Dalton on Shugart Rd

Brandon, FL - Walmart Brandon on Causeway Blvd

Today, Walmart and Care Access celebrated this progress with a grand opening event at the Houston location, located at 3506 Highway 6 S. With the addition of new locations planned for next year, the partnership continues to grow its reach, bringing clinical research opportunities closer to more communities across the country.

For many people, traditional clinical research can mean finding a study site far from home or navigating unfamiliar processes. By bringing research information and services to locations within Walmart stores, the partnership aims to reduce some of those barriers and make opportunities easier to discover and explore.

The growing network of Clinical Trial Centers by Walmart and Care Access will support Phase 2, 3 and 4 clinical trials and help expand awareness of clinical research opportunities by bringing research information and services, and health screenings, into familiar community settings. Study offerings and eligibility vary by location.

“Opening these locations is an important step in advancing our mission to make clinical research accessible to all,” said Ahmad Namvargolian, CEO and co-founder of Care Access. “For more than a decade, Care Access has developed the infrastructure, technology and community relationships needed to bring clinical research directly to participants. Our collaboration with Walmart allows us to go one step further: helping clinical research become part of everyday life—visible, approachable and integrated into the places and routines people already know and are comfortable with.”

At each of the Clinical Trial Centers, Care Access teams will provide a range of health and research-related services, including:

Opportunities to participate in clinical trials conducted at the centers, including studies in cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer’s disease, GLP-1 therapies and more, depending on local study availability.

Health screenings that assess important risk factors, including advanced biomarker blood testing, such as Lp(a) and other measures, as available.

Tailored health education resources and one-on-one consultations to help individuals understand available clinical research opportunities and decide whether participation may be right for them.

Participation in clinical research is voluntary, and individuals are welcome to visit a location to learn more about available health screenings and research opportunities.

Care Access leads clinical operations at the Clinical Trial Centers, drawing on the experience and capabilities developed from its network of over 200 clinical research sites around the world and its global Future of Medicineopens in a new tab community health screening program. WHRI supports research awareness and accessibility by connecting that expertise with Walmart’s community presence and reach.

“Expanding access to clinical research starts with making opportunities available in more communities,” said Emily Aaronson, MD, MPH, chief medical officer at Walmart. “These additional locations build on the foundation we've established with Care Access and bring us closer to a future where more people, regardless of where they live, can learn about and participate in research that could improve health for themselves and for generations to come.”

Walmart’s commitment to expanding access to clinical research goes beyond opening new trial sites. Through nationwide outreach and recruitment efforts, the WHRI is also helping connect people to clinical trials already underway in their communities, bringing more opportunities to participate in medical innovation within reach of more Americans.

“Expanding access to clinical research has long been a priority for Lilly because the future of medicine depends on participation from people with a wide range of backgrounds, experiences and health needs," said Michael Franklin, vice president, Community-Based Research & Innovation, Eli Lilly and Company. "For years, we've been developing community-based approaches that bring screening and research opportunities closer to where people live. With studies enrolling through these centers, we're encouraged by the opportunity to engage people who may not otherwise participate, improve representation and generate evidence that reflects the patients and communities we hope to serve."

To learn more about the Clinical Trial Centers, screening availability and research opportunities, visit careaccess.com/walmartopens in a new tab.

When someone is interested in joining a study, we help identify potentially appropriate clinical trials and connect them with the investigators and research sites conducting them.

For sponsors, CROs and research sites, Care Access provides a vital connection to the communities whose participation makes clinical research possible. Our community presence and engagement capabilities help studies enroll more efficiently and expand the industry’s capacity to conduct research. We also support study delivery through more than 200 research sites worldwide, hundreds of traveling clinicians, a fleet of over 150 mobile health clinics and purpose-built technology and workforce solutions including Peter the Protocol Readeropens in a new tab,Study Team by Care Accessopens in a new tab, centralized virtual clinical staffopens in a new tab andon-site staffing supportopens in a new tab.

text:
Oracle on Tuesday announced an expanded collaboration with OpenAI that brings the artificial intelligence lab’s ChatGPT and Codex into the software maker’s applications to make databases more actionable.

Mahesh Thiagarajan, Oracle’s president of Cloud Infrastructure, told CNBC at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that using ChatGPT “allows anybody to build an application, deploy it, manage it.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is set to join Oracle co-CEO Clay Magouyrk on stage for an Oracle AI World keynote on Tuesday at 12:40 p.m. ET.

For OpenAI, the announcement represents another example of the frontier lab’s push into the enterprise market, just one day after its key competitor, Anthropic , filed its S-1 as it heads toward an initial public offering.

Oracle’s database plays a crucial role in underpinning businesses across healthcare and finance in logging and securing data.

CNBC

Thiagarajan said his team observed OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model get trained at Oracle’s Stargate data center campus in Abilene, Texas, and could see the real-time benefits.

“More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use,” said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI, in the press release.

Oracle also said Tuesday that it is making different hardware accessible on its cloud infrastructure, including Google ’s tensor processing unit AI chips and OpenAI’s Jalapeño chip.

“Now customers can actually have infinite possibilities in terms of how they can drive AI,” Thiagarajan said.

It is the first time Google’s custom chips will run on another hyperscaler’s cloud, and illustrates how the companies are increasingly looking for opportunities to get their hardware in the hands of the frontier labs.

Thiagarajan added that the scarcity of chips remains an ongoing issue and that customers like OpenAI can benefit from having different accelerators to choose from. When asked whether this marks a pivot away from Nvidia GPUs, Thiagarajan said no, adding that Nvidia chips are “the best, most fungible,” and that the AI market remains incredibly large.

OpenAI’s Jalapeno chip and Cerebras will also run on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The Cerebras deal is material, but the AI chipmaker won’t be disclosing the scale because it’s in a quiet period, a Cerebras spokesperson said.

Cerebras stock climbed about 8% following the news. Oracle shares were up nearly 5% on Tuesday.

The announcement comes seven months after market-leading cloud Amazon Web Services announced plans to bring Cerebras hardware into its data centers, a major point of validation.

Thiagarajan also addressed Oracle’s multibillion New Mexico data center dubbed Project Jupiter and the ongoing pushback it’s receiving from the local community. He said Jupiter represents just one of the 30-40 different data center projects in development, per quarter, for the company.

“We’re actually not too worried about what we’re doing because I think we’re building global infrastructure,” he said.

A hearing to address air quality permitting is scheduled for Dec. 7 in Sunland Park, where the controversial data center has already broken ground. The political pushback tied to the project prompted Oracle to deliver a force majeure notice to its backer Blue Owl Capital last month. Right now, Oracle maintains that the project is on schedule.

Investors are now counting down to Oracle’s investor day, where investors will want to see if the company can back its fiscal year 2030 revenue targets and if the margin profile of its cloud deals has changed due to the rising cost of capital.

Bank of America analysts wrote to clients that updates on Oracle’s major data center projects are among the topics they expect clarity on at the meeting.

Oracle shares are down more than 30% this year due in part to concerns about how the company plans to finance its ambitious digital infrastructure pipeline.

—CNBC’s Jordan Novet contributed to this article

text:
If DoorDash and Instacart come together, what gets better for the operator?

Photo: Claude

October 27, 2026

Three weeks ago, when Uber agreed to buy ezCater, the question operators kept asking was a simple one. California Tortilla's Mike Dolinger put it best when hetalked with Fast Casual: "Simply put: What gets better for the operator as a result of this partnership?"

Now DoorDash may be about to make that question a lot bigger.

DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire Instacart in a deal that could value the grocery delivery company at roughly $17 billion, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday, citing people familiar with the discussions. An agreement could come as early as this week, though there's no guarantee the talks produce one. Investors sent the two stocks in opposite directions Monday, with Instacart up about 8% and DoorDash down roughly 6%, according to Fox Business.

DoorDash nor Instacart returned Fast Casual's request for comment, and nothing is signed. What follows is speculation, but it's worth thinking through now, before the ink dries.

The ezCater deal set the table

Uber announced Oct. 6 that it would acquireezCater for $2.3 billion in cash, a deal expected to close in the coming months pending regulatory approvals. ezCater serves more than 140,000 restaurants and generated more than $2.5 billion in annual gross bookings.

When Fast Casual asked operators what that meant for them, the answers ranged from hopeful to uneasy. Jason's Deli's Gracie Prasanson hoped it would push more catering customers back to first-party ordering. Cowboy Chicken's Brittany Mercer noted that Uber had raised her brand's commission rate to 28% in the second quarter and wasn't sure what the acquisition would mean on top of that.

That's the backdrop for a possible DoorDash-Instacart combination: the biggest platforms buying their way into each other's lanes.

What the spending data shows

Michael Gunther, senior vice president of research and market intelligence at Consumer Edge, said the talks reflect a market that has shifted under everyone's feet.

"DoorDash's potential acquisition of Instacart comes as the competitive landscape for delivery has changed considerably over the past several years," Gunther said in an emailed statement. "Consumer Edge U.S. credit and debit card data shows DoorDash's share of spending across major delivery platforms, including restaurant and grocery delivery, increased from approximately 44% in Q2 2021 to nearly 59% in Q3 2026, while Instacart's shares declined from approximately 26% to 18%."

Uber Eats also gained share over that period, increasing from approximately 16% to 18%, although its share has been relatively stable over the past year while DoorDash has continued gaining ground.

These trends partly reflect the expansion of DoorDash and Uber Eats into grocery, convenience and other retail categories, increasingly competing in areas historically associated with Instacart, and highlight how the boundaries between restaurant, grocery and broader retail delivery have become increasingly blurred," he said.

What I'm watching as an operator would

Leverage: Fewer, bigger platforms usually means less room to negotiate. If Mercer's 28% commission is any signal, operators who already feel squeezed won't gain bargaining power from consolidation.

Who you're competing with:Gunther's point about blurred boundaries is the one restaurant operators should sit with. If the same app that delivers your burrito bowl also delivers grocery store prepared meals and convenience store snacks, your competition for tonight's dinner order isn't just with the fast casual down the street.

Who owns the customer: Uber now has a catering marketplace. DoorDash could soon own the grocery leader. Both are racing to be the one app a customer opens for everything. The more that happens, the more valuable a brand's own app, loyalty program and direct catering channel become.

None of this means walking away from third-party delivery. The reach is real, and many brands depend on it. But the ezCater conversation already showed that reach alone isn't the win. The win is reach that comes with margins you can live with and a relationship with the guest you actually keep.

If DoorDash and Instacart come together, Dolinger's question gets louder: What gets better for the operator?
