text:
Oracle AI World, LAS VEGAS—Oct 27, 2026

Oracle today announced a major new collaboration with OpenAI to redefine how the world’s businesses run in the age of AI. By bringing together OpenAI models, ChatGPT, and Codex with Oracle’s applications, data, and cloud infrastructure, both companies are putting AI directly to work across the systems and operations used by customers that power the world’s economy. An expanded suite of products brings that approach to life, by helping people work across systems with AI, enabling them to build and deploy applications, finding and fixing security vulnerabilities, and giving entrepreneurs an integrated foundation to build and run companies.

“OpenAI is transforming how enterprises solve business problems, from chat, to coding, to analytics, to autonomous agents,” said Clay Magouyrk, CEO, Oracle. “With this new product suite, we are uniting their transformative AI capabilities with Oracle applications, data, and cloud infrastructure—technology that businesses around the world rely on to run their most critical operations.”

“More businesses are choosing OpenAI as we make it easier to put AI to work through the tools and systems they already use,” said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder, OpenAI. “Our expanded partnership with Oracle helps bring that opportunity to more companies, putting frontier AI into everyday operations so teams can build software faster, strengthen security and take on more complex knowledge work.”

Oracle and OpenAI are putting AI to work across enterprise operations, application development, cybersecurity, and business creation:

Run Your Business Through ChatGPT

OpenAI and Oracle share an ambition to set the standard for the agent-ready enterprise. Both companies are partnering across the full innovation cycle to transform Oracle’s applications for agents and bring them into a unified experience in ChatGPT.

Oracle AI Workspace provides a single user experience that brings OpenAI frontier models together with Oracle applications, enterprise data, and cloud services. Through the plugins in ChatGPT on Oracle AI Workspace, employees can access information, complete approved business workflows, and take action alongside Oracle systems. It is designed to connect Oracle Fusion Applications, Oracle NetSuite, Oracle AI Database, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and other enterprise tools, and data sources.

The Oracle AI Workspace will make the breadth of Oracle’s capabilities agent-ready and accessible to ChatGPT users. People can describe business goals and these plugins in ChatGPT will bring together the right Oracle tools and information to help them accomplish it. With ChatGPT, Oracle AI Workspace puts AI directly into the flow of enterprise work while maintaining the governance, approvals, and controls required for enterprise operations.

Strengthen Security with Frontier AI

Oracle and OpenAI are working to make advanced security testing easier for organizations to put into practice. Oracle AI Security Mesh, a managed service that uses OpenAI cyber models, helps customers find and fix vulnerabilities in their applications and infrastructure across OCI, other clouds, and on-premises environments before attackers can exploit them.

The service combines OpenAI frontier cyber models with Oracle’s testing tools, independent validation, testing infrastructure, and operational safeguards managed by Oracle, so customers don’t need to build and operate their own agentic defensive/offensive systems. DoorDash has expanded beyond restaurant orders into groceries and other retail products, and said it had more than 200,000 grocery and retail stores on its marketplace.

Instacart operates a marketplace covering more than 2,200 grocery brands and 100,000 stores, giving DoorDash access to a substantial network of retail partners.

The potential deal comes as delivery platforms seek growth beyond restaurant orders and face pressure from rising labour costs, tighter regulation of delivery workers and competition from retailers building their own online services.

Instacart generated $3.75 billion in revenue last year, compared with DoorDash's $13.72 billion.

The companies have not announced a completed transaction, and the reported negotiations remain uncertain.

The grocery industry is ever-changing, and many concepts and formats that once seemed so promising eventually end up six feet under in the grocery graveyard.

This year’s cemetery is particularly haunted by store formats that didn’t measure up and were abandoned by grocers.

In the spirit of Halloween, here’s a list of store concepts and partnerships that are now nothing more than ghosts.

RIP to Hy-Vee’s discount format

The Midwest grocer is ditching its dollar format by rebranding all of its Dollar Fresh Market stores into its namesake banner, CEO Jeremy Gosch said in September during a Groceryshop keynote address.

It’s been a slow death for the discount format. At the start of this year, Hy-Vee announced it was rebranding four of its 22 Dollar Fresh stores — a change that indicated the unique format was having trouble scaring up sales. Hy-Vee brought Dollar Fresh to life in 2018 in an attempt to take on dollar retailers.

The Grim Reaper came for Amazon’s physical store concept

Amazon kicked off this year by announcing it would close all of its physical Amazon Fresh and Amazon Go stores after years of trying to inject new life into the chains.

Amazon’s decision came about five years after the company entered the conventional supermarket space with the opening of the first Amazon Fresh store. The company said in its closing announcement that it would convert an unspecified number of locations into Whole Foods Market stores.

Schnucks buries another small-format store

Schnuck Markets closed its 18,000-square-foot Schnucks Fresh location in Jasper, Indiana, back in May. The grocer’s CEO, Todd Schnuck, said the location “simply has not generated the business it needs to stay open.”

Schnucks still runs a Fresh store in Oak Grove Village, Missouri, that opened in 2023. A company spokesperson said in May that it doesn’t plan to open any other locations under that banner.

This decision to shutter the Jasper location came about two years after Schnucks announced it would close down its natural and organic banner Eatwell Market.

Fareway’s experimental meat store never made it out of the lab

The Fareway Meat Market in Luverne, Minnesota, spanned just 2,300 square feet and housed a full-service butcher counter. The store was an experiment to see if Fareway’s meat market concept could shrink down to the size of a convenience store — but unfortunately, that small size hindered its success, the company said.

The experimental location, which opened in 2022, closed its doors in mid-January

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Grocery Dive free daily newsletter

Will Amazon’s grocery partners haunt the company?

Earlier this month, Amazon confirmed to Grocery Dive that it is closing an unspecified number of grocery partner storefronts on Amazon.com. The move effectively ended a program through which Amazon helped power e-commerce for other grocers.

The company said transitioning away from individual storefronts would simplify the e-commerce shopping experience, adding that it will guide shoppers to the best available grocery options offered on its marketplace as individual storefronts close.

This move will also allow Amazon to give more attention to its own rapidly growing grocery e-commerce business.

Instacart’s smart carts won’t be rising from the dead

Like Dr. Frankenstein, Instacart put a charge in the smart cart trend when it acquired Caper AI back in 2021. Several years later, though, smart carts have struggled to catch on with retailers, and now Instacart is abandoning the business. Instacart announced Monday it will stop offering its Caper Cart smart carts to grocers as part of the next phase of its in-store strategy.

text:
To thinkPorschewould wipe the slate clean of combustion engines in favor of electric motors is a thought so chilling it keeps us up at night. The knee-jerk reaction of most purists wasn’t one of excitement, as the skepticism was warranted given Porsche’s efforts to save combustion engines for future use.

What the firm conjured up as its first all-electric sedan, however, was one of the fizziest and most engaging EVs that dams any thoughts cast to spite its propulsion system. What was a $106,500 electric sport sedan just a few years ago is now a $50,000 bargain thanks to the used EV anomaly that spares no badge. Are Taycans worth the hype at half-price? Have we got news for you...

How a $107,000 Porsche Became A $50,000 Bargain – And Why It Still Drives Like One

A quick drive behind the wheel of any large or medium-sized electric vehicle will provide its driver with a lesson in all three of Sir Isaac Newton’s laws. EVs are better described as "dense" more than "heavy". The latter is used often when describing electric cars, but it conjures thoughts of something the size of a Toyota Camry handling like a Chevy Tahoe.

That’s not always the case. It’s much easier to pinpoint where the weight of a vehicle is hiding when it has an electric powertrain, since they all have a battery beneath the floorboards and, in some cases, act as a structural support for the vehicle if built on a dedicated EV platform. But if any company were to take a crack at fixing the way an electric car behaves on both road and track, it would be Porsche.

Electric vehicles offer horsepower in bulk and the curb weight to match, which sounds like the blueprints for something horrible if you’re not prepared. Modern performance-oriented EVs aren't controlled with the same spaghetti-thin reins other powerful EVs might use to keep a car at bay. But Porsche – with its ability to make the wrong things work flawlessly – turns the tables on how EVs should handle, and the Taycan is living proof of its hard work.

What We’d Buy: 2020–2024 Taycan 4S

The 4S sits smack in the middle of the Taycan range without suffering from middle-child syndrome. It’s got enough power to defend itself and doesn’t post a premium for five little letters spelling out “Turbo” across the trunk. New, 2020 Turbo models were $150,900. Now, they’re between $60,000–80,000. Its 670 horsepower and 626 pound-feet of torque are better felt than read aloud, especially now that new models produce 874 hp and carry a $184,600 base MSRP.

The base 2026 Taycan offers slightly better value at $105,800, with its single-motor RWD system producing 402 hp. Base models from 2021-2024 produced just 321 hp from the same drivetrain layout and cost nearly the same as the potent 4S. For the same money, the 4S offers AWD and extra power thanks to the same value retention statistics as every other Taycan.

$50,000-70,000 gets you the best concoction of useable power and balanced performance from an electric sedan that just happens to be a Porsche. Oh, it also comes in the shape of a wagon, if you’re into the idea of an electric Porsche station wagon – which we very much are.

Not since it decided to build the Panamera in a long-roofed version did Porsche make a station wagon. Granted, Audireceived a little advice from one engineering consulting firm to build the original RS2 Avant. If it weren’t for that, Porsche’s decision to make its own wagon would’ve been met with the same pushback as the Taycan.

The Panamera proved valuable to saving the brand, just as the original Cayenne did. To keep the run of sports cars going until the bitter end, it needed a product to fund such dreams in modern times. That meant going electric, but that didn’t mean it had to stop being a Porsche.

The bonus of being a station wagon is that it’s both usable and immensely cool. The 2023 Cross Turismo 4S is one of the best station wagons available for the price. It just happens to be electric. 60 mph comes faster than you think at 3.9 seconds.All 482 hp is used on each intoxicating jab of the accelerator, activating the primal part of the brain that wants to keep touching the fire or poke the bear.

Poke it too long, and it’ll quickly turn its occupants green. It’s mysteriously light, noticeably more docile than the Tesla Model S or even the equivalent Panamera, and braking doesn’t bring about fears of outrunning its tires (especially when those six-piston calipers are the size of a brick phone).

Before you start browsing listings, there are a few ownership costs that don't show up on the window sticker — and one of them could shift your calculus entirely.

Hidden Costs of Taycan Ownership

The 4S might be the bargain buy, but used Porsche ownership comes with costs that don't show up in the listing price — here's what to budget for. Besides the premium the Porsche crest calls for, the Taycan is still the better of the two options when discussing the similarAudi RS e-tron GT, which uses the same underpinnings to offer a similar experience tuned by the four rings.

​​​​​​​Like any EV, the cost to add a charging station to your home will be a substantial fee for first-time EV owners. Wiring a 240-volt outlet (if needed) can drive the price up by a few thousand dollars, but houses with sockets already in the garage keep costs between $800–2,000.

Registration and document fees vary by state, with some charging extra for PHEVs and EVs to supplement lost revenue from tax levied on gasoline. Insuring an EV is a complicated venture as well, even if you bought it at a discount on the used market. Powertrain components that might need to be replaced are a little more expensive than gasoline cars, which can be reflected with higher premiums.

Specific to the Taycan, however, there are fewer issues than you might expect. It earned 4.4 out of 5 stars in reliability ratings submitted by owners to Kelley Blue Book. The largest cut of the cost of ownership, depreciation, has already taken effect, which is how we’re able to shop for them on a budget. Without it factored in, repairs, insurance, and maintenance all ring up to a few thousand dollars a year.

Porsche’s factory warranty coverage for high-voltage batteries is eight-years/100,000 miles, and its certified pre-owned bumper-to-bumper warranty starts after the vehicle’s original four-year/50,000-mile warranty ends. An additional one-year warranty can be purchased for Porsche CPO cars as well at the time of purchase.

Why EV Depreciation Is A Buyer's Market – And Why It Won't Last Forever

The depreciation of EVs is an alchemy straightforward enough that it makes sense to everyone, yet no one understands why it happens. It's a multi-pronged school of thought that pulls together consumer input, technological advancements, and the overall market to depict a clear enough picture of why they take massive hits. The gap between residual values of combustion engine cars and EVs is closing, but the ones that have already fallen through can be picked up for quite the steal.

The biggest culprits, which set a precedent for all others to follow, were short-range, small electric vehicles whose batteries degraded so much they couldn’t achieve their original mileage estimates. Range was cut significantly in excessively hot or cold climates and was comparatively worse than gasoline counterparts, if it had any. Tesla came along to flip the script with the 2012 Model S, which offered near-alien levels of range for the time, and it continued to innovate and push forward with the idea of EVs for everyday use.

Flash-forward to the end of the 2010s, when the Model S and Model X crossover were the golden examples of what electric mobility would be, with others following the charge. It, however, would not be saved from the depreciation that all EVs suffer because of battery degradation, range depletion, and quality issues. The new EVs of the time, however, were boasting bigger and stronger batteries, with more power available and increased range.

This continues today, with battery technology increasing exponentially each year, and the marathon races proving more important than the quarter-mile sprints. Even if the battery technology is strong one year, the fact that the next round will be even more robust still dings the value of shiny-new cars with barely any miles on them.

The reason we don’t see this in ICE-powered vehicles is because that technology hasn’t changed as drastically as EVs have in the last 15 years. Once the innovation curve starts to even out, we will certainly see similar depreciation rates. Until then, luxury vehicles with electric powertrains that normally cost twice as much on the used market can be had for a bargain simply because they run on electrons and not premium unleaded.

text:
As the AI boom strains computing capacity, Nvidia has backed Indian startup Simplismart in a $14 million funding round, betting on software that helps companies run AI models more efficiently and, in some cases, with fewer GPUs.

Nvidia participated in the all-primary Series B round alongside Accel, Shastra VC, and Micromax, with Dallas Venture Capital leading the investment. The deal values the four-year-old startup at about $100 million, including the new funding.

Companies are nowadays spending heavily on GPUs to power AI applications, but running those models reliably and economically at scale remains a challenge. Different workloads demand distinct trade-offs between speed, cost, and performance. Deploying and operating AI models to meet business requirements often also requires complex adjustments. Simplismart says its software automates much of that work, tailoring how models run on existing computing infrastructure instead of requiring customers to manage those configurations themselves.

“Nobody actually needs the fastest or the cheapest inference,” Amritanshu Jain (pictured above, left), co-founder and CEO of Simplismart, said in an interview. He added that companies instead need to run AI models at speeds and costs that make sense for their specific applications.

Simplismart’s software sits between AI models and the computing infrastructure they run on and adjusts how models are deployed and managed to meet customers’ requirements. It says it can optimize factors such as how quickly a model responds, how many requests it handles, and how much computing power it consumes, helping companies get more out of their existing GPU stack.

The Bengaluru-based startup offers companies a way to deploy and run AI models through its own platform or within their existing cloud and on-premises infrastructure. It also provides tools to fine-tune models, automatically scale computing resources as demand changes, and monitor performance. Additionally, Simplismart allows cloud providers build and operate their own AI inference services on GPU infrastructure using its software.

Simplismart says it helped AI video-generation platform InVideo cut its GPU serving costs by 56% using its software. The startup also works with AI video companies HeyGen and Higgsfield, as well as enterprise AI startup Ema, among others. Moreover, Indian cloud provider Yotta uses Simplismart’s technology to power the serverless AI inference service within its Shakti Studio platform.

Simplismart’s annualized revenue run rate has grown 14-fold over the past six months to an eight-figure sum, Jain told TechCrunch. The figure is based on recent customer usage rather than contracted recurring revenue and excludes revenue passed through to infrastructure providers, the company said. He did not disclose the exact figure.

More than half of Simplismart’s revenue comes from the U.S., despite the startup having more customers in India, Jain said.

Alongside its investment, Nvidia has been working with Simplismart on technical integrations, including around its Dynamo inference software, Jain told TechCrunch. The collaboration involves Simplismart’s engineers and Nvidia’s solutions architects, while Nvidia has also helped introduce the startup to potential customers and partners, Jain stated.

Interestingly, the investment presents an apparent paradox as Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI chips, is backing software that can help companies run some workloads with fewer GPUs. Jain, however, argued that making AI inference more efficient could ultimately benefit Nvidia by making its hardware more attractive to customers and encouraging wider adoption of AI applications.

Simplismart is serving customers in an increasingly crowded market for AI inference software, competing with offerings from Nvidia itself, as well as major cloud providers and hyperscalers including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. A growing number of startups are also developing tools to make AI models faster and cheaper to run as there is growing demand in this segment, driven by rising demand for AI applications and the need to make better use of expensive GPU resources.

“Where we tend to win is where people have to be more stringent on their SLAs [service-level agreements] and TCO [total cost of ownership],” Jain said, referring to demanding performance requirements and tight cost constraints. Unlike rivals that offer preset options for faster or cheaper inference, Simplismart aims to find a balance tailored to each customer’s needs, he said.

Founded in 2022 by former Oracle engineer Jain and former Google engineer Devansh Ghatak (pictured above, right), Simplismart grew out of the pair’s experience building and deploying machine-learning systems. The two met while studying at BITS Pilani, and the startup now employs 58 people, Jain said.

Simplismart plans to use the new funding to expand its presence in the U.S., grow its team, and invest further in developing its inference software. Jain told TechCrunch that the U.S. remains a key market for the startup as it looks to build on its existing customer base there.

text:
Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices have said they will invest a total of $4 billion in Meta after the social media and artificial intelligence giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it would invest $3 billion in Meta’s equity offering, with AMD announcing it would invest $1 billion.

Meta’s Monday announcement said Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.

Nvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant’s AI agent that launched last month.

“AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf,” said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.

“This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents.”

“We’re excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people,” said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

AMD said that its Helios racks were running at Meta and its EPYC processors were powering Meta’s Muse.

“Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta’s most ambitious superintelligence models and services,” AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a statement.

AMD was up 3% on Tuesday, while Nvidia stayed flat. Meta was down 1%.

Nvidia and AMD have been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom.

Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI and participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

AMD in July said it would make an equity investment of up to $5 billion in Anthropic. The company has been involved in 25 funding rounds in 2026, up from just two in 2022.

"Our ambition is to unlock the full potential of these categories, creating collections that feel as considered and desirable as the apparel. At Renfro, we take brand stewardship seriously. We understand the responsibility that comes with a brand of this stature, and we see tremendous opportunity to pair DKNY's equity with our category expertise, consumer insight, and retail relationships to build something exceptional."

Building on DKNY's Momentum

The partnership comes at a significant moment for DKNY. A key brand in G-III Apparel Group's owned portfolio, DKNY continues to build momentum as it looks to expand further across categories, channels, and geographies.

"Renfro brings deep expertise in the category, strong retail relationships, and a proven track record of stewarding globally recognized brands," said Jeff Goldfarb, Executive Vice President of G-III. "We believe they are the right partner to bring a fresh perspective to the category while remaining true to the fashion, quality, and New York attitude that define DKNY."

The first collection developed under the partnership will debut for Fall 2027 at select department stores, specialty retailers, e-commerce accounts, and other authorized channels across the licensed territory.

A Strategic Addition to Renfro's Fashion Portfolio

The addition of DKNY further enhances Renfro's portfolio of globally recognized brands, complementing its existing fashion offerings with a distinct contemporary perspective. The partnership creates opportunities to broaden consumer reach, deepen retail partnerships, and drive incremental growth, reinforcing Renfro's commitment to building long-term value across its diverse portfolio.

description:
DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire grocery delivery platform Instacart in a deal that could value the company at approximately $17 billion, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal and Reuters.
The third-party aggregator previously acquired U.K.-based Deliveroo for approximately $3.9 billion and Finland-based Wolt for $8.1 billion.
Uber, meanwhile, announced an agreement this year to acquire Germany-based Delivery Hero in a deal valued at $14.8 billion.

Grubhub changed hands in early 2025, when Wonder completed its acquisition of the delivery company.
text:
This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider.

DoorDash is in advanced talks to acquire grocery delivery platform Instacart in a deal that could value the company at approximately $17 billion, according to reports from The Wall Street Journal and Reuters.

The Journal first reported the discussions Monday, citing people familiar with the matter. A deal could be finalized as soon as this week, though the sources cautioned that an agreement is not guaranteed.

A source familiar with the matter told Reuters that a deal could come as early as Wednesday. Instacart also previously had active discussions with Uber.

The potential acquisition would bring together DoorDash's delivery network and customer base with Instacart's grocery marketplace and retailer relationships. Instacart had a market value of approximately $13 billion at the close of trading Friday, Reuters reported. Its shares rose roughly 8 percent during regular trading Monday, while DoorDash shares fell approximately 6 percent.

The discussions follow a shift in consumer spending across major restaurant and grocery delivery platforms. According to U.S. credit and debit card data from Consumer Edge, DoorDash's share rose from approximately 44 percent in the second quarter of 2021 to nearly 59 percent in the third quarter of 2026. Instacart's share fell from approximately 26 percent to 18 percent during that period.

Michael Gunther, senior vice president of research and market intelligence at Consumer Edge, said the trends partly reflects DoorDash expanding into grocery, convenience, and other retail categories that have historically been associated with Instacart.

"The boundaries between restaurant, grocery and broader retail delivery have become increasingly blurred," Gunther said.

DoorDash has opened up its wallet in recent years.

The third-party aggregator previously acquired U.K.-based Deliveroo for approximately $3.9 billion and Finland-based Wolt for $8.1 billion. It also acquired restaurant technology company SevenRooms in 2025.

Uber, meanwhile, announced an agreement this year to acquire Germany-based Delivery Hero in a deal valued at $14.8 billion. Uber also purchased Postmates in a $2.65 billion deal announced in 2020.

Grubhub changed hands in early 2025, when Wonder completed its acquisition of the delivery company. The transaction included $150 million in cash and the assumption of $500 million in debt.

text:
S&P Global delivered adjusted diluted EPS of $4.58 in Q3 2026, beating expectations, with revenue also ahead of estimates. Reported revenue fell on a continuing-operations basis following the July 1 spin-off of the Mobility division into Mobility Global.

Indices revenue grew 20% in the quarter, led by asset-linked fees as global equity markets and ETF inflows expanded. Demand for passive-investment benchmarks tied to S&P indices remains a durable growth engine.

S&P Global opened a formal review of Capital IQ and the related Kensho data assets. CEO Martina Cheung framed it as portfolio stewardship, saying the businesses involved have significant opportunities ahead as technology changes how customers access, analyze, and use information, and that the review reflects a priority to invest where the company is strongest. The company gave no specific timeframe, and full-year guidance assumes Market Intelligence continues in its current structure.

Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted diluted EPS guidance to a range of $17.70 to $17.95, and also lifted the revenue growth and adjusted operating margin expansion outlooks. The company now expects to repurchase more than $7 billion of stock for the full year.

A higher adjusted effective tax rate of 23.1% created a modest drag on earnings, while ratings transaction revenue grew at a slower pace than other segments and currency weighed on organic revenue. Cash and equivalents give the company meaningful financial flexibility as the Capital IQ review plays out.

name: Barclays
title: Sweden's SEB pauses buybacks as Barclays plans further capital returns ahead of Basel 3.1
description:
Changes in capital requirements are shaping banks’ capacity to lend and return money to shareholders.
Bank of the Philippine Islands’ quarterly provisions fell as problem-loan metrics weakened, while India’s IndusInd Bank reported lower fresh slippages alongside substantial write-offs.
Barclays expected Basel 3.1 implementation in January 2027 to reduce its CET1 ratio by 30–55 basis points through higher risk-weighted assets.
EU agrees lower capital requirements for qualifying securitisations The Council and European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on 21 October to revise the EU securitisation framework.
The changes included lower capital requirements for qualifying transactions, a new “resilient” category and reduced administrative burdens.
text:
Changes in capital requirements are shaping banks’ capacity to lend and return money to shareholders. Major Swedish lender SEB paused buybacks as supervisory model adjustments and loan growth put pressure on its capital buffer. Barclays announced another repurchase as lower requirements were expected to cushion the initial impact of Basel 3.1, while EU lawmakers agreed capital relief for qualifying securitisations.

Credit quality and valuation losses presented a more mixed picture. Bank of the Philippine Islands’ quarterly provisions fell as problem-loan metrics weakened, while India’s IndusInd Bank reported lower fresh slippages alongside substantial write-offs. At US lender Huntington Bancshares, interest-rate-related valuation losses weighed on equity measures even as its regulatory capital ratio improved.

Read more on the week’s key developments:

1. SEB pauses buybacks as model adjustments constrain capital headroom

Sweden’s SEB announced on 22 October that it would pause share buybacks, citing continued loan growth and the capital impact of the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority’s review of its internal credit-risk models. The bank reported a common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 17.1% and a capital buffer of 250 basis points at September-end.

The supervisor required SEB to increase risk-weighted exposures to address deficiencies in its regulatory models, reducing its capital buffer by an estimated 120 basis points based on its June-end position. The temporary adjustment will take effect by 31 December 2026 and remain until revised models receive regulatory approval. SEB expects to begin submitting model applications by the third quarter of 2027 at the latest. Pausing buybacks preserves capital as the bank accommodates the adjustment alongside continued lending growth.

2. Barclays announces another buyback as lower requirements cushion Basel 3.1 impact

Barclays announced a further GBP 500.0 million ($668.4 million) share buyback on 22 October, following completed repurchases totalling GBP 1.5 billion and an ongoing GBP 1.0 billion programme announced with its second-quarter results. Its CET1 ratio stood at 14.2% at September-end and would have been 14.0% after incorporating the new repurchase, at the upper end of its 13–14% target range.

Barclays expected Basel 3.1 implementation in January 2027 to reduce its CET1 ratio by 30–55 basis points through higher risk-weighted assets. However, a 59-basis-point reduction in its Pillar 2A CET1 requirement would lower the threshold for automatic distribution restrictions from 12.2% to 11.6%. This would preserve its headroom for shareholder distributions despite the initial Basel 3.1 impact.

3. EU agrees lower capital requirements for qualifying securitisations

The Council and European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on 21 October to revise the EU securitisation framework. The changes included lower capital requirements for qualifying transactions, a new “resilient” category and reduced administrative burdens. Legal finalisation and formal adoption remained outstanding.

Under the existing internal ratings-based and standardised securitisation approaches, senior simple, transparent and standardised (STS) positions carried a 10% risk-weight floor. Banking industry association AFME reported that the agreement would introduce ultimate floors of 5% for resilient STS securitisations and 7% for non-resilient STS securitisations, while acknowledging that it had not seen the final legal text. Lower floors can reduce capital requirements where they determine the applicable risk weight. Shaun Baddeley, AFME’s managing director of securitisation, said the reported treatment of non-STS transactions under the standardised approach remained overly conservative.

4. RBI sets April 2027 implementation for operational-risk capital and leverage changes

The Reserve Bank of India issued directions on 23 October setting 1 April 2027 as the commencement date for its operational-risk capital framework and revised leverage requirements. The leverage framework specified base minimum ratios of 4% for domestic systemically important banks and 3.5% for other banks, with additional provisions for global systemically important banks. The operational-risk amendments completed financial-statement mappings and clarified calculation inputs.

The outgoing Basic Indicator Approach linked operational-risk capital to average gross income over three years, using a 15% charge. The replacement combines a broader business indicator with a bank’s historical operational losses for larger institutions holding at least five years of qualifying loss data. Past losses can therefore influence capital requirements after their initial effect on earnings, differentiating banks with similar business volumes but different loss histories. RBI can impose a loss multiplier above one where the prescribed data criteria are not met.

5. Huntington’s capital ratios diverge as interest-rate losses deepen

Huntington Bancshares reported on 22 October that its regulatory CET1 ratio increased from 10.0% in June to 10.1% in September, while its tangible common equity-to-tangible assets ratio declined from 7.1% to 6.9%. The bank attributed the latter decline principally to valuation movements associated with higher market interest rates and growth in tangible assets. It also repurchased $100.0 million of shares during the quarter.

Accumulated other comprehensive losses widened by $761.0 million during the quarter. Huntington’s adjusted CET1 measure, which included accumulated other comprehensive income or losses but excluded cash-flow hedges, fell from 9.0% to 8.9%. This was a supplementary measure rather than a regulatory requirement.

6. BPI’s quarterly provisions fall as problem-loan metrics weaken

Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) reported on 21 October that nine-month provisions reached PHP 19.9 billion ($312.7 million), up 69.2% year on year. Its non-performing loan (NPL) ratio rose quarter on quarter to 2.50%, while NPL coverage stood at 89.6%. Third-quarter provisioning nevertheless declined 16.5% from the preceding quarter.

In June, BPI had reported an NPL ratio of 2.42% and coverage of 92.98%, attributing higher first-half provisions to deteriorating macroeconomic conditions and expectations. By September, the NPL ratio was eight basis points higher and coverage approximately 3.4 percentage points lower. The quarterly earnings charge had therefore eased while the reported problem-loan measures weakened.

7. IndusInd lowers provisions as new problem loans decline, with write-offs also reducing reported stress

IndusInd Bank disclosed on 23 October that consolidated provisions and contingencies fell 54% year on year to INR 12.2 billion ($128.8 million) in the September quarter. Its gross NPL ratio declined from 3.25% in June to 2.73%, while annualised credit costs fell from 1.74% to 1.40%. Chief financial officer Viral Damania attributed the lower provisions to reduced net additions to non-performing loans.

The improvement reflected both lower fresh stress and the removal of existing bad loans. Write-offs of INR 16.7 billion ($176.0 million) exceeded new non-performing loan additions of INR 14.6 billion ($153.8 million). Separately, the annualised gross slippage rate, measuring loans newly becoming non-performing, fell from 2.1% to 1.8%.

8. First Citizens expands fund lending as aggregate reserve coverage falls

First Citizens reported on 23 October that loans and leases reached $157.2 billion, up 4.1% quarter on quarter, with commercial growth concentrated in Fund Banking. Its allowance-to-loans ratio declined to 0.91% from 0.98%. The quarter included a $48.0 million reserve release, although the bank still recorded a positive $50.0 million provision for loan and lease losses.

The bank attributed part of the reserve movement to growth in capital-call lines, which had lower historical losses than its other portfolios. These facilities bridge the interval between fund investments and calls on limited partners. Their repayment mechanism differs from asset-based fund lending supported by portfolio investments. These differences matter when assessing banks’ exposure to private-credit funds. Growth in a lower-loss product can therefore reduce aggregate reserve coverage.

9. UK proposes reducing senior approvals and removing annual staff certification

The Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority proposed changes to the Senior Managers and Certification Regime on 22 October. Regulatory pre-approval would be replaced by notification for selected roles, including chairs of risk and audit committees. The proposals would also remove the Certification Regime for approximately 139,000 employees below senior-manager level. Chief executives, chief financial officers and board chairs would retain pre-approval requirements.

The PRA proposed ending prescribed fitness-and-propriety assessments on appointment and annually for staff leaving that regime, alongside the requirement to obtain regulatory references. Its consultation acknowledged that firms might consequently receive less detailed information about recruits, but judged the existing burden disproportionate. Broader competence and conduct obligations would remain.

10. ECB sets BPER’s 2027 CET1 requirement at 9.60%

BPER Banca announced on 21 October that the European Central Bank’s supervisory review required it to maintain a consolidated CET1 ratio of 9.60% and total capital ratio of 14.15% from 1 January 2027. The bank cited a pro-forma CET1 ratio of 14.95% at June-end, including eligible retained interim profits. That comparison indicated 535 basis points above the announced CET1 requirement, although it compared June capital with a requirement taking effect in January.

Compared with BPER’s October 2025 decision, the CET1 requirement was 20 basis points higher, but the CET1 component of its bank-specific Pillar 2 requirement remained unchanged at 1.35%. The difference came from combined buffers increasing from 3.55% to 3.75%.

text:
Barclays said artificial intelligence is already reshaping its workforce, with the British bank planning to cut about 5,000 full-time jobs, roughly 5% of its staff.

A large portion of those reductions is expected to fall on support roles, including developers, demonstrating how directly Barclays is connecting some layoffs to early AI-related efficiency gains.

Here's what to know

Support functions are set to absorb about three-fifths of the planned cuts, Barclays said during its third-quarter earnings report, with developers among the affected roles, Banking Dive reported.

After trimming about 1,000 jobs, the bank appears on pace to remove roughly 4,000 additional positions by the end of December.

The workforce update arrived alongside weaker performance in one part of Barclays' business: third-quarter revenue from fixed-income and currency trading fell 19% from a year earlier. Even so, Barclays explicitly said AI-driven productivity was part of the rationale for the planned cuts.

"The changes that we're making in the third and fourth quarters of this year are sizable," Barclays CFO Anna Cross said. "They relate both to the simplification of the organization and to some of the impacts that we're starting to see from AI."

More background

Other major banks have also pointed to AI when discussing workforce changes, so Barclays is not alone in using that rationale.

In May, Standard Chartered said it would eliminate more than 7,800 roles in "corporate functions" by 2030, including jobs across human resources, risk management, and regulatory compliance.

That puts Barclays within a wider industry shift toward automating work once handled by large support teams.

Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the bank intends to "employ AI at scale."

AI systems can help optimize complex systems such as clean energy management. At the same time, the technology can also require significant electricity and water for data-center cooling, which can put additional pressure on the energy grid, contribute to rising costs, and drain crucial resources.

What's being done?

Venkatakrishnan indicated that while Barclays wants to use AI broadly, the technology is not the sole force behind its strategy or staffing decisions.

Standard Chartered also shifted its messaging around AI. Speaking at Standard Chartered's May investor day, CEO Bill Winters said, "It's not cost cutting; it's replacing, in some cases, lower-value human capital with the financial capital and the investment capital we're putting in. We don't have job losses, but we do have job role reductions in favor of the machines, and that will accelerate as we go forward into AI."

The remark drew criticism for appearing to rank workers by worth. Winters apologized in a memo, writing, "Where roles do fall away, it reflects changes in the work, not the value of our people."

AI-linked job cuts have become a sensitive issue even for companies moving aggressively to expand the technology.

"AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake," Venkatakrishnan said.

NVIDIA and Meta will expand their partnership on Muse and the Muse family of models, reflecting popular demand for AI agents.

NVIDIA and Meta today announced they will partner to expand their work on Muse and the Muse family of models to improve inference and training performance, reflecting popular demand for useful AI agents.

Meta’s Muse models and agents, which leverage NVIDIA’s infrastructure, have delivered frontier-level benchmark performance and surging consumer downloads since launch. text:
Amid K-beauty's growing influence in the global cosmetics market, L'Oreal, the world's largest beauty company, mentioned the competitiveness of K-beauty and Korean ODM companies. In particular, as strategic cooperation based on the deep relationship between the two companies has begun in earnest, expectations for Cosmax's solid performance growth are rising.

At L'Oréal's recent third-quarter earnings conference call, L'Oréal CEO Nicolas Hieronimus called K-beauty "The boom is real," noting that Korean brands are showing steep growth of about 30% on average.

It is noteworthy that L'Oreal cited close cooperation with Korean ODM manufacturers as a key success factor, not only with Korean brands. CEO Eronimus emphasized that K-beauty is an important business opportunity to utilize the outstanding technology of Korean manufacturers as well as Korean brands. As a prime success story, we introduced Yves Saint Laurent (YSL) cushion products that have been very successful in the U.S. market.

In the midst of this, L'Oreal's own growth is still solid. L'Oreal's Q3 revenue was up 12% year-over-year. The solid growth of global beauty giants is expected to lead K-beauty ODM companies to secure stable sales of large customers.

Cosmax's relationship with L'Oreal dates back 20 years. Since Cosmax supplied eyeshadow to L'Oreal's makeup brand "Maybelline" at the time, the cooperative relationship between the two companies has steadily evolved.

In fact, after signing an MOU for joint research on skin microbiome raw materials and developing eco-friendly formulations in 2023, it has completely improved its constitution by moving away from a simple subcontract production structure and putting its heads together from the early stages of R&D.

In September, the newly signed agreement further embodied the depth and field of cooperation. Through joint R&D strengthening, L'Oreal's advanced beauty science and technology and global consumer insights will be combined with Cosmax's outstanding product development capabilities. It is also actively seeking to discover new cosmetic ingredients and highly functional active ingredients.

text:
Walmart is expanding its Better Care Services platform in a new partnership with General Medicine, a digital healthcare services marketplace.

The expanded platform brings together services from General Medicine and more than 10 third-party providers with options for urgent care, pediatric care, mental health, nutrition and weight management.

"Healthcare needs a store," said TJ Parker, chief executive of General Medicine, in a news release. "We're building the care catalog that makes options easier to understand, compare and buy."

General Medicine did not respond Monday to a request for comment. The company provides the technology behind the platform and manages customer accounts and health information separately from Walmart's retail business.

"Expanding Better Care Services brings more care options into one place, helping customers explore what's available, compare choices and take the next step in a way that works for them," said Ralph Clare, executive vice president of Health & Wellness for Walmart U.S., in the release.

Walmart did not respond Monday to a request for comment.

The platform allows shoppers to browse services and see estimates for out-of-pocket costs tied to their insurance plans. Cash prices are also included when providers list them. Users can sort health service options by cost, availability and location before booking appointments.

Walmart opened up the Better Care Services platform in January as a one-stop online health hub to connect customers to third-party telehealth providers and prescription services. In April, the retailer added to its weight management support services for customers who are on or who are considering GLP-1 therapies.

The expansion fits into the Bentonville-based company's healthcare affordability strategy that started more than 20 years ago with a $4 charge for generic prescriptions from its thousands of pharmacies and vision centers.

Walmart shares rose 40 cents or less than 1%, to close Monday at $120.29, The shares have traded between $135.16 and $98.88 over the past 52 weeks.

Microsoft said on Monday (Oct 26) it is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, or more than a quarter of its global workforce, as the technology giant looks to contain costs and help fund its massive AI investments.

Staffers across the Windows maker would be eligible for the offers, including those working in AI experiences, Copilot, finance, human resources, Xbox and Windows + Devices, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, requesting anonymity as the matter was private. text:
In a note to employees on Monday, chief people officer Amy Coleman introduced the new program, noting that eligible employees include senior leaders, up to vice presidents.

“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” Coleman wrote to employees in a memo that Microsoft published on its blog. Microsoft has been cutting headcount to trim costs while investing billions to build out AI data centers. In April, the company offered a similar voluntary buyout program to long-tenured employees, its first time making such an arrangement. At the time, Coleman noted that Microsoft was aiming to move faster and simplify its operations.

Employees who take the latest buyout will get severance payments based on tenure at the company. The specific terms will vary according to labor laws in different countries but will be consistent with standard separation packages, a Microsoft spokesperson told Fortune. In the U.S. that means a minimum of eight weeks’ pay, with continued stock vesting, health care, and career services. To be eligible, employees in the U.S., the U.K., Canada, and India must accept by the first week of December, with those participating leaving on Dec. 31.

description:
Helping retailers deliver a great experience both online and in-store is one of our most important jobs.
Retailers and brands today are balancing a number of competing priorities, and we’re seeing them prioritize investments in solutions that can modernize stores at scale.
As we look ahead and work closely with retail and brand partners, the next phase of our in-store strategy will be focused on intelligence and software.
Most recently, we announced new in-store software solutions that give grocers and CPG brands a live view of stores, so shelves stay stocked, and customers can find what they need.

text:
Helping retailers deliver a great experience both online and in-store is one of our most important jobs. That means building tools that connect those experiences and enabling all of our partners to grow and better serve customers, however they choose to shop. Today, we offer a robust suite of in-store solutions, including:

FoodStorm – order management technology for prepared foods

Carrot Tags – electronic shelf label software that increases found rates

In-Store Mode – digital shopping companion for the Instacart App and retailers’ apps

Store View scanning technology – AI and Arpalus-powered computer vision that analyzes videos captured by ~600,000 Instacart shoppers, giving partners a real-time view of the shelf

Inventory Intelligence – software that provides stores with real-time shelf visibility, merchandising optimization, and demand forecasting

Store Excellence Portal – software that gives CPG brands a daily store-level view of what’s on the shelf

As we plan the next phase of our in-store strategy, we’ve made the strategic decision to wind down our Caper Cart business and focus our time and resources on areas where we believe we can scale and deliver the greatest impact for our retail and brand partners, in addition to their customers.

Over the past several months, we’ve been evaluating Caper’s progress and the investment required to scale the business. Retailers and brands today are balancing a number of competing priorities, and we’re seeing them prioritize investments in solutions that can modernize stores at scale. While Caper is a great product, the business reality is that retailer adoption has not scaled quickly enough to justify our continued investment.

To be clear, in-store remains an integral part of the operating system we’re building for grocery: a single system that seamlessly powers both online and physical stores, giving retailers and brands the information and control they need to run their business.

As we look ahead and work closely with retail and brand partners, the next phase of our in-store strategy will be focused on intelligence and software. We believe our strengths in software, data, and AI give us a greater opportunity to help retailers and brands understand what’s actually happening on store shelves and take action on that information.

Whether it’s helping a retailer anticipate what customers need or keeping shelves stocked with the products they love, we believe these in-store technologies can scale and deliver the greatest impact for partners and their customers. This is our integrated platform at work: we take intelligence generated at an enormous scale across our platform and put it directly into our partners’ hands.

Most recently, we announced new in-store software solutions that give grocers and CPG brands a live view of stores, so shelves stay stocked, and customers can find what they need.

We’re so proud of what the Caper team built: a truly innovative smart cart that customers genuinely love. The experience taught us a lot about building technology for the complexities of physical stores, and we’ll carry those lessons forward. The opportunity in physical grocery is enormous, and we’re just getting started.

text:
Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees — over a quarter of its workforce — as the software giant works to cut costs and revamp its staff for the AI era.

Employees in the US, Canada, the UK, and India on Monday received a memo saying the voluntary exit offers “are a few of the ways we’re trying to meet different business needs while continuing to create opportunities for our own people to grow and contribute.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees at the time the memo went out.

Microsoft’s Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance divisions are getting the offers, according to Bloomberg, which first reported the news. Workers have until Dec. 31 to make a decision, a Microsoft spokesperson said, adding that US employees will get at least eight weeks’ pay if they take a buyout.

“My promise is to continue to provide clarity, listen and learn and keep improving,” Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman wrote in Monday’s missive.

The company has been going all in on AI infrastructure. This past summer, it reported an 18% revenue increase, with its cloud products responsible for a big chunk of the growth.

The company, which is behind Azure and Github, is also funneling cash to its data center network.

“The best thing that can happen to Microsoft is what’s happening right now,” Microsoft’s Jared Spataro said of the company’s AI efforts at a Citigroup conference in September.

The company reported $130 billion in new data center leases earlier this year, according to Bloomberg.

name: OpenAI
title: Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of AI's existential risk to humanity
authors: Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press, Bernard Condon
description:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion.
At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."
Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.

READ MORE: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled

The filing comes weeks after CEO Dario Amodei argued in an essay for slowing the development of the most advanced AI models. An IPO could provide Anthropic with enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price, but even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world's most valuable companies and potentially boost the wealth of Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela, by billions of dollars.

The 335-page document showed Anthropic's revenue is growing rapidly, but like many other tech companies going public, it has yet to turn a profit. The company behind the chatbot Claude reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, though its losses after taking out certain items were a fraction of that. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion.

Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world's most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.

As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the current record set by one of Elon Musk's companies, SpaceX, earlier this year.

In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol "ANT."

Risks aplenty, but a big payoff to the founders

In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.

Formed in 2021 by ex-OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company, and the two leaders, Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, are widely seen as bitter rivals.

But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX's AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs in resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.

The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI's plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse in the coming months. Investors have become increasingly jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic's seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. Collectively they own nearly 500 million shares, though it's unclear from the offering document how much that will represent of the company after the IPO.

Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic's president, are worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.

Reflecting AI's dangers, the document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic has also appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn't put financial interests ahead of public safety.

READ MORE: AI discovered a software vulnerability that could impact 70% of websites worldwide. The rush is on to patch it

Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of "risk factors," a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading.

Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of "malicious actors" using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and, given the numerous hacking incidents from rogue AI agents recently, the possibility Anthropic's AI models could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

Calls for an AI slowdown

The IPO comes as reports emerge about AI's ability to solve problems beyond human capacity for good, but also to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks while humans lose control.

In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.

He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.

"I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong," Amodei wrote.

Clashes with the U.S. government

Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the "good guys," focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs and with few guardrails.

Some of this sentiment stems from the company's dispute with the U.S. government, which broke out in February when President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk.

Anthropic sued the Pentagon over the supply chain risk designation in March for what it called an "unlawful campaign of retaliation" over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified an unusually public dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI made its own deal to work with the Pentagon hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.

A California judge ruled in Anthropic's favor in the first case and a Washington D.C. judge sided with the government in the second. Both sides are appealing the decisions.

Condon reported from New York.

Take, for instance, Eli Lilly, the Indianapolis maker of the tirzepatide drugs Mounjaro and Zepbound, which has more than doubled its R&D spending in recent years, increasing it from about $6.0 billion in 2020 to $13.3 billion in 2025, with continued growth into 2026.

Anthropic is approaching Lilly’s spending, according to the S-1 registration statement it filed with the SEC on Oct. 26. Over the 12 months to June 30, the AI company, founded in 2021, spent about as much: Anthropic, the San Francisco developer of the Claude models, recorded $14.2 billion of R&D against Lilly’s $14.6 billion.

Alphabet and Meta each spent well over $50 billion on R&D in 2025.

Revenue vs. R&D, 2025

Sources: Anthropic S-1; OpenAI figures from leaked audited accounts reported by Fortune and verified by the Financial Times; Lilly and Merck 10-K filings; AstraZeneca full-year 2025 results.

In the Anthropic S-1, the R&D figure appears only in a note to the financial statements. During 2025 Anthropic reorganized its income statement around types of cost, such as compute and personnel, and moved research and development into Note 8, which keeps the older breakdown by function. That note shows R&D of $422 million in 2023, $2.28 billion in 2024 and $6.34 billion in 2025. In the first half of 2026, R&D hit $9.74 billion, 5.3 times the $1.85 billion of a year earlier. Anthropic defines the category as mainly compute for “model development, research, and internal usage workloads,” plus staff, software and overhead.

The six-month total tops the ongoing R&D of every large U.S. drugmaker over the same period. Merck spent about $8.5 billion, excluding a $13.8 billion charge for acquired research projects; Lilly spent $7.3 billion, excluding $3.4 billion of acquired in-process R&D; and Johnson & Johnson spent $7.2 billion. Including acquired in-process R&D, Lilly’s first-half total reached $10.7 billion.

Tech companies overtook drugmakers at the top of corporate R&D rankings a decade ago. Pfizer or Roche led the European Commission’s Industrial R&D Investment Scoreboard in 2004 and every year from 2006 to 2010, and three to five drugmakers sat in its global top 10 each year through 2014. Since 2019 the top 10 has held one: Roche through 2022, then Johnson & Johnson, ninth in 2024. In their latest fiscal years, Alphabet ($61.1 billion) and Meta ($57.4 billion) each spent more than three times the largest drug-industry R&D budgets. Microsoft ($35.6 billion) and Apple ($34.6 billion) spent more than twice as much.

Drugmakers still spend more of each sales dollar than most tech companies. R&D equaled 24.3% of Merck’s 2025 revenue, 24.2% of AstraZeneca’s and 20.5% of Lilly’s, against 15.2% at Alphabet, 10.7% at Microsoft and 8.3% at Apple; Meta, at 28.5%, ran above all of them. The AI labs run far higher. Anthropic’s R&D equaled 138% of its revenue in 2025 and 60% in the first half of 2026, as first-half sales rose 14-fold to $16.3 billion.

OpenAI, the ChatGPT developer, spent $19.2 billion on R&D in 2025, 147% of its revenue, according to leaked audited accounts the Financial Times verified in June. That exceeds any drugmaker’s 2025 R&D spending, including Lilly’s $16.3 billion with acquired research projects counted. OpenAI and Lilly both appear on R&D World’s list of the 100 most innovative companies of 2026.

Compute, software and overhead account for at least two-thirds of Anthropic’s first-half R&D spending, by R&D World’s calculation. Anthropic had about 5,300 employees at Sept. 30, a majority of them in research, engineering and product development. description:
Why I Keep Hitting the Buy Button Every AI cluster needs a network fabric, and Arista sells the open Ethernet option.
Q2 revenue reached $3.0357B, up 37.69%, the company’s first $3 billion quarter.
Non-GAAP operating margin rose to 49.9% from 48.8%.
Purchase commitments almost tripled to about $9.7 billion under multiyear vendor agreements, and operating margin rose even as gross margin fell.

text:
After its last earnings report, I added to my Arista Networks (NYSE:ANET | ANET Price Prediction) position, and I bought again this month when the stock fell 15.28% in four weeks. I keep adding because every quarter gives me a new reason to.

Why I Keep Hitting the Buy Button

Every AI cluster needs a network fabric, and Arista sells the open Ethernet option. It builds on merchant silicon from Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and adds EOS, its own operating system, on top. Ethernet keeps taking ground from proprietary interconnects. Arista’s Etherlink AI fabrics now have more than 100 cumulative customers, up from 4 to 5 in 2024. CEO Jayshree Ullal remembered the move from InfiniBand to Ethernet and said “that transition took two to three years.” I want to own the company that keeps winning that move.

Three Receipts Behind My Conviction

Growth is speeding up. Q2 revenue reached $3.0357B, up 37.69%, the company’s first $3 billion quarter. The 2026 outlook was raised to about $12.6 billion, or 40% growth. Its Analyst Day goal was $10.5 billion.

Margins are expanding while sales grow. Non-GAAP operating margin rose to 49.9% from 48.8%. EPS of $1.02 beat the $0.8856 consensus. That makes six consecutive earnings beats.

Its balance sheet funds itself. Cash and marketable securities came to about $13.3 billion. Deferred revenue climbed to roughly $6.9 billion, and Q2 capex was only $29.7 million.

Why My Money Skips Nvidia and Cisco

NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) trades at a lower P/E, about 42, and its networking revenue grew 138%. I pass anyway. Its supply obligations reached $279.00 billion, guarantees for partners go as high as $108.5 billion, and days sales outstanding rose to 60 days from 45. I’d rather own the open fabric that also links AMD chips and Google TPUs.

Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) pays a $0.42 quarterly dividend, and Arista pays none. Even so, Cisco’s FY2026 revenue grew 11.77%, its operating margin guidance is 35.5%–36.5%, and its cash fell 23.8%. For building wealth over decades, I’ll take compounding over a check each quarter.

Risk That Could Break This Position

Arista relies on a few buyers. Microsoft and Meta are its anchor customers, and Ullal expects “1, maybe 2 10% customers” this year. It also relies on a predominant merchant silicon vendor, and gross margin slid to 63.4% from 65.6%. At a P/E near 62, a lost customer would hurt.

My thesis still holds. Purchase commitments almost tripled to about $9.7 billion under multiyear vendor agreements, and operating margin rose even as gross margin fell. With more than 100 AI customers, Arista depends less on any one name every quarter.

What Keeps My Buy Button Active

For Q3, Arista guides to about $3.30B in revenue and EPS of $1.06-$1.08. Ullal sizes the scale-across market at $15 billion to $20 billion by 2030, and 1.6T switches should reach production in 2027. Every new AI data center needs a network, and that keeps sending my money to Arista.

The AI data-center expansion is the whole background here, and the picks-and-shovels names beyond the chipmakers are worth knowing (we covered seven of these suppliers, from power to networking, which you can read here).

description:

The deal means two of Europe's three biggest budget airlines have committed to Starlink.
That leaves Ryanair, the continent's largest airline and the world's third-largest, as the only one of Europe's biggest budget carriers without the service.
That trend has also prompted US budget airlines to offer comfier seats and package deals.
However, easyJet and Wizz may see Starlink as a way to gain an edge over Ryanair.
text:
Elon Musk's Starlink has won its latest customer, a budget airline that could put pressure on one of the WiFi service's biggest critics.

EasyJet announced on Monday that the high-speed WiFi service would be deployed on its airplanes from the first half of next year. The British airline, which carries 100 million passengers a year, hopes to have Starlink installed across its 300-strong fleet by early 2028.

The deal means two of Europe's three biggest budget airlines have committed to Starlink.

Wizz Air, a Hungarian carrier that flies about 70 million passengers a year, signed up in June.

That leaves Ryanair, the continent's largest airline and the world's third-largest, as the only one of Europe's biggest budget carriers without the service.

Its CEO, Michael O'Leary, is well-known for being outspoken and took aim at Starlink earlier this year, leading to a spat with Musk.

"We don't think ‍our ⁠passengers are willing to pay for WiFi for an average ⁠one-hour flight," O'Leary told Reuters in January.

While Starlink is typically offered free to passengers, O'Leary also complained about increased fuel costs due to the aerodynamic drag of a Starlink terminal, installed on the top of airplanes.

Musk responded in an X post, arguing that Ryanair — which carries over 200 million passengers a year — would lose customers to airlines that do have internet access.

Over the next week, the two CEOs called each other idiots while Musk called for O'Leary to be fired and joked about purchasing the airline.

But Ryanair appeared to have the last laugh, using the publicity to launch a "Big 'Idiot' Sale" with 100,000 tickets starting at £16.99, or about $23.

The situation has some parallels with the US's Big Three airlines. While United Airlines has Starlink on almost half of its fleet and American Airlines is starting installations early next year, Delta Air Lines has instead tapped Amazon Leo, beginning in 2028.

This has led Musk to insult Delta's CEO, Ed Bastian, and call for his firing.

But American passengers are wealthier and more interested in premium offerings than their European counterparts. That trend has also prompted US budget airlines to offer comfier seats and package deals.

Adding free amenities for passengers is at odds with the typical no-frills budget-airline business model that relies on extra charges to turn a profit.

However, easyJet and Wizz may see Starlink as a way to gain an edge over Ryanair.

That may not last forever, though. In a January earnings call, O'Leary said, "I think as the WiFi technology improves over the next four or five years, we'll all be offering free WiFi access."
