title: How NVIDIA Minerva Turns Telemetry Chaos Into Peak GPU Yield
description:
This post covers how NVIDIA Minerva, an AI-native AIOps platform designed around AI factory topology and workloads, addresses these operational gaps.
NVIDIA Minerva ingests metrics, logs, and topology from GPUs, Spectrum-X and NVLink switches, SuperNICs, DPUs, storage, NVIDIA NCCL, schedulers, and AI workloads.
Convergence with DSX OS NVIDIA Minerva is being developed in alignment convergence with NVIDIA DSX OS.
NVIDIA Minerva capabilities beginning with the data collector will become open-source parts of DSX OS.
NVIDIA Minerva bridges that gap by unifying telemetry across GPUs, networking, storage, and workloads provides the end-to-end observability to detect subtle degradations that static thresholds miss.
text:
AI Factories are some of the most technologically complex operational environments ever created. Hundreds of thousands of GPUs, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out, scale-across and scale-in fabrics, NVIDIA NVLink scale-up fabrics, distributed schedulers, and multi-week training runs operate in continuous lockstep.These layers function as one production system even when different teams own their telemetry. In synchronous distributed training, a job advances at the pace of its slowest rank. One degraded GPU, interface, storage device, or switch path can waste useful time across many healthy resources.

The failures that hurt yield are often subtle: A GPU runs a few degrees hotter than its peers. An NVMe device loses performance only under sustained load. A switch generates a pause-frame storm that looks like dozens of unrelated symptoms. None of these signals necessarily crosses a static threshold. Together, they create stragglers, extended step times, and delayed checkpoints.

Diagnosis becomes harder because the evidence is split across teams. Network operators see interface counters and fabric events. Compute operators see node and GPU health. ML teams see changing step times, failed jobs, or unstable inference latency. Each view is accurate, but the relationships between them remain hidden. Triage becomes a chain of dashboard searches and cross-team handoffs, which can turn a contained fault into hours or days of lost production time before the affected node or fabric path is identified.

This post covers how NVIDIA Minerva, an AI-native AIOps platform designed around AI factory topology and workloads, addresses these operational gaps.

NVIDIA Minerva collects telemetry across the stack, maps infrastructure to active jobs in a dynamic knowledge graph, applies purpose-built machine learning, and correlates dependent symptoms into high-fidelity incidents. An AI agent-powered assistant and MCP server connected to external agentic tools give operators a conversational path through the same live evidence. The goal is practical: preserve effective GPU hours and keep model training moving.

Why conventional monitoring breaks at AI factory scale

Rule-based monitoring assumes that a known metric crossing a known boundary indicates a known condition. That model works for clear failures. It struggles with so-called “gray failures,” where a component stays available, and the relevant issue may appear only under load or in comparison with peers. Absolute thresholds can miss the shift. Aggressive thresholds often add warnings during normal workload changes, leaving the on-call engineer to decide which deviation matters.

Scale adds alert amplification. One physical fault can produce interface errors, RX (receive) pause frames, congestion indicators, GPU utilization changes, and slower job progress. These observations describe the same dependency chain, but separate dashboards or alerts present them as unrelated events. The on-call engineer receives a volume of alerts and needs to manually correlate the alerts, determine the signal from the noise, analyze the root cause and the jobs exposed to it.

For operations, the workload is the unit that matters. Teams need to know which job is affected, which resources it occupies, where those resources sit in the physical and logical topology, and how current behavior differs from a healthy baseline. That context must remain current as jobs start and stop and as nodes are drained, replaced, or returned to service. Without it, a healthy component dashboard can coexist with poor job throughput and offer no explanation.

Building a live model of infrastructure and jobs

Solving these challenges requires end-to-end visibility across the AI Factory. NVIDIA Minerva ingests metrics, logs, and topology from GPUs, Spectrum-X and NVLink switches, SuperNICs, DPUs, storage, NVIDIA NCCL, schedulers, and AI workloads. Auto-discovery supplies the relationships that raw telemetry lacks. The resulting knowledge graph maps infrastructure, scheduler, and workload elements, then updates those relationships as the environment changes. It can span multiple data centers and support navigation from a factory-wide view to an individual interface.

The topology graph is the key to changing the investigation path. Starting with an anomalous interface, an operator can identify its node, the fabric path it serves, current job placement, and nearby components in the same failure domain. Starting with a job ID, an ML engineer can trace the workload through GPU, host, NIC, switch, and log evidence. Network and compute teams can start from an infrastructure event and see the affected jobs, or conversely see an affected job and investigate the cause using NVIDIA Minerva. Everyone works from the same current causal map instead of reconciling separate inventories.

Detecting gray failures with purpose-built machine learning

NVIDIA Minerva processes billions of metric and log data points per hour with supervised and unsupervised models developed for AI factory infrastructure and workloads. Supervised detection identifies known critical error patterns and can associate recognized conditions with specific remediation guidance. Unsupervised models cover behavior with no predefined signature. They learn normal patterns for a hardware or logical component and compare it with the relevant peers.

Peer comparison matters because a measurement can look acceptable in isolation and still be anomalous in context. Sustained errors on a network interface may look normal in isolation but compared to other interfaces, they stand out as anomalous. A GPU temperature may remain within specification while running substantially hotter than sibling GPUs under the same load. Multivariate models can combine temperature, power, clocks, utilization, and workload state to detect that degradation before the component fails outright.

Logs receive similar treatment. NLP-based anomaly detection surfaces previously unseen patterns, while supervised matching identifies known critical errors. A detection can feed scheduler workflows so an affected node is drained before another job lands on it or at a safe point between checkpoints.

Collapsing event storms into actionable incidents

Topology-aware correlation connects detection to operator action. The correlation engine’s algorithms leverage the knowledge graph to determine which events share a dependency path. Downstream symptoms are then grouped as one incident instead of competing for attention.

The result is less alert noise and more context. NVIDIA Minerva can collapse redundant events and related metric series into a single signal with affected topology and workloads attached. NVIDIA testing shows significant reductions in notified events and tickets for supported scenarios. Operators still need to determine the root-cause using other capabilities provided by NVIDIA Minerva, but they begin with a much smaller search space. Once NVIDIA Minerva creates a high-confidence incident, teams can consume it through the platform UI or existing workflows.

Agentic debugging

Correlated evidence still requires interpretation. NVIDIA Minerva includes a native AI agent called Sherlock which is grounded in live telemetry and the knowledge graph, so an operator can ask why a specific job slowed during a particular interval, which components changed state, or whether other nodes share the same failure domain. Sherlock enables network ops, compute ops and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams to query the system for root-cause-analysis in human language.

Sherlock can present supporting evidence and recommend remediation without requiring every operator to know the exact metric, dashboard, or query language. This gives less experienced operators a route to domain knowledge that has traditionally required escalation to a specialist. Its value in an operations workflow depends on the evidence that Sherlock provides. A recommendation leads back to the telemetry and topology that support it.

NVIDIA Minerva’s MCP server lets external agentic tools query the same operational context. Teams can incorporate live AI factory evidence into their own workflows. Mitigation can remain human approved or selected actions can be automated according to local policy and the risk of the action.

Use cases from NVIDIA AI factories

Detecting a single link degradation in a 400K interface AI factory

In a large AI data center running many multi-node training jobs at once, an SRE noticed one job’s step time slowly getting worse. There was no hard failure, no alert and no obvious culprit. Tracking it down by hand would have meant hours of triage across GPUs, NVLink switches, SuperNICs and the network fabric while the job kept burning GPU hours at reduced throughput.

Instead, NVIDIA Minerva’s Full Stack AIOps Debugging took in telemetry from every layer of the workload topology. Anomaly detection found the one NVLink connection out of roughly 400,000 interfaces that was quietly losing bandwidth. It then linked that NVLink switch to the training jobs whose traffic crossed it. Now that the SRE could see in one UI view the failing link, the affected jobs and where both sat in the datacenter hierarchy, they drained and rescheduled the affected nodes, isolated the link for repair, and brought the jobs back to full speed. The team caught the problem before it spread across the cluster, diagnosed it in minutes instead of hours, and kept the fleet’s goodput and token production up.

SuperNIC Proactive Maintenance

A GPU node logged one kernel line: a hardware error reported by the platform’s firmware (APEI, error source 5). It was a PCIe-level fault on the node’s SuperNIC path. The error was rare enough that no static rule or threshold would have caught it, and it came with no job failure or customer complaint.

NVIDIA Minerva’s real-time rare log anomaly detection marked the message as a rare, never-before-seen event. The platform posted an alert to the cluster operations team’s Slack channel. Alongside the alert, NVIDIA Minerva explained what the error meant and laid out step-by-step remediation, starting with the error context and the system logs to check. The on-call engineer confirmed the fault and removed the node from the allocation pool before any customer workload landed on it. This saved hundreds of GPU hours a failing node would have cost in crashed and restarted jobs.

Straggler job due to NVMe power fault

The ops team was trying to explain why several training jobs were running slower than expected. The slowdown pointed to straggler nodes, but not to a cause.

NVIDIA Minerva’s full-stack job RCA dashboard traced the problem to one host whose logs showed an NVMe device failing. The drive hadn’t been able to wake from a low-power state. The node lost access to its storage, which set off a series of I/O write errors that dragged down every job running on it. With the root cause confirmed, the team drained the node and sent the faulty hardware back for RMA. The fix saved an estimated 5,530 hours of job runtime.

Pause-frame storm

A switch issue produced RX pause frames, GPU utilization spikes, and thousands of metric series. The incident surfaced as many as 81 noisy events. Alerts came in from many devices, but none of them explained the slowdown. The cause was a page fault error that had forced a network switch to restart. The restart set off congestion that spread across the fabric, with RX pause frames propagating between switches, repeated link downs, and spikes in GPU temperature and utilization anomalies.

NVIDIA Minerva’s topology-aware correlation linked 81 separate events and anomalies to the affected job and sent them to the team as a single incident. Handling it as one incident instead of 81 cut time to repair and saved about 54 hours of total cluster uptime.

Turning operational gains into useful compute

NVIDIA’s internal testing shows an increase in mean time between interrupts (MTBI) through proactive maintenance, coupled with a decrease in mean time to repair (MTTR) through automated root-cause analysis, and a significant reduction in alert noise. These translate into an increase in effective GPU hours by minimizing downtime.

Convergence with DSX OS

NVIDIA Minerva is being developed in alignment convergence with NVIDIA DSX OS. It reuses and plans on integrating selected DSX OS health and resilience components such as NVIDIA Attribution. NVIDIA Minerva capabilities beginning with the data collector will become open-source parts of DSX OS. This provides a modular telemetry foundation aligned with NVIDIA reference architectures while keeping observability, analytics, and automation composable.

Bridging the gap

As AI factories grow in scale and complexity, the gap between traditional monitoring and operational reality widens. NVIDIA Minerva bridges that gap by unifying telemetry across GPUs, networking, storage, and workloads provides the end-to-end observability to detect subtle degradations that static thresholds miss.

By collapsing noisy event storms into single actionable incidents and enabling agentic debugging through conversational AI, NVIDIA Minerva transforms triage from hours of cross-team handoffs into minutes of guided investigation.

text:
L’Oréal East Africa has emerged as Kenya’s top resource-efficient manufacturer after cutting resource consumption and environmental impacts while increasing production at its Nairobi factory, underscoring the business case for cleaner industrial production.

The beauty products manufacturer won the Overall Resource Efficiency Award at the 2026 Industry Resource Efficient and Cleaner Production (RECP) Awards, alongside category honours in energy management, solid waste management, greenhouse gas emissions and environmental compliance.

The recognition highlights how manufacturers can improve operational efficiency, lower production costs and reduce their environmental footprint through investments in cleaner technologies, recycling and better management of energy and water.

The awards, organised by the Kenya National Cleaner Production Centre (KNCPC), come as Kenya seeks to strengthen its manufacturing sector, improve industrial competitiveness and promote sustainable production practices.

Kerstin Bird, president of L’Oréal’s Sub-Saharan Africa zone, said resource efficiency was increasingly central to the company’s manufacturing strategy.

“We believe that business growth and environmental responsibility must go hand in hand. At this facility, we are demonstrating how focused action on resource efficiency can support production while reducing water consumption and greenhouse gas emissions,” Bird said.

The company’s Mombasa Road factory completed its transition to renewable energy in 2024, combining a biomass boiler, a biodiesel generator, solar photovoltaic systems and electricity from the national grid.

Other measures include installing variable frequency drives, energy-efficient LED lighting with motion sensors, heat-loss insulation and equipment-level energy monitoring to reduce power demand.

The factory has also introduced water-reuse systems that allow treated effluent and reverse osmosis reject water to be used in fire hydrant and sanitary systems rather than being discharged.

Its waste reduction programme includes using recyclable PET bottles, reducing shrink-wrap film thickness and recovering cardboard, plastics and other materials through licensed waste management partners.

Steve Nyamori, deputy director at KNCPC, said the factory had implemented 23 resource efficiency and cleaner production interventions.

He said an investment of about $23,000 (Sh2.97 million) in cleaner production measures was reported to generate annual economic benefits and savings exceeding $50,000 (Sh6.45 million).

“Environmental performance and business competitiveness are not competing objectives. When companies use energy, water and materials more wisely, they can reduce costs, manage risk, strengthen resilience and create long-term value,” Nyamori said.

The assessment was conducted under the Sustainable Manufacturing and Environmental Pollution programme, funded by the UK government to support industries in developing economies to reduce pollution.

Of 225 industries mapped under the programme, 26 underwent comprehensive in-plant assessments covering water and wastewater management, energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, raw materials, solid waste, environmental compliance and other sustainability measures.

Tobias Alando, chief executive of the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, said resource efficiency was becoming an essential component of industrial competitiveness as businesses faced pressure to reduce costs and comply with environmental standards.

“The ability to produce more efficiently, minimise waste, reduce environmental impacts, and maximise value is increasingly essential to business success,” Alando said.

He urged manufacturers to embed sustainability into their operational decisions, arguing that the future of the sector would depend not only on the products made but also on how they were produced.

The company also received a Gold Award from the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents for workplace health and safety for the second consecutive year.

L’Oréal East Africa’s Nairobi plant is the group’s only manufacturing facility in East Africa. It produces local brands Nice & Lovely, Versman and Gold Touch, alongside international brands including Garnier and Mixa, serving markets across the region.

Its recognition offers an example of how investment in cleaner production can support Kenya’s wider industrialisation ambitions by improving resource productivity, strengthening environmental compliance and building more resilient manufacturing operations.

text:
New York-based Pathos AI has secured $237 million in Series E financing at a post-money valuation of approximately $3 billion. The round was led by Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS), with participation from existing investors.

The company develops its own therapeutic pipeline rather than simply licensing technology to others. It has built its strategy around Foundry, an AI platform that deploys thousands of specialized AI agents to continuously aggregate and synthesize information relevant to a given drug program. Pathos claims that Foundry draws on clinical data, genomics, biological specimen data, and shifting competitive intelligence in real time to help determine the optimal next step for a program. That could mean narrowing in on a precise biological subpopulation, pivoting a clinical trial design, or cutting a high-risk pathway early before it consumes further resources.

That approach has translated into rapid portfolio growth over the past several months, with Pathos using Foundry to execute a series of strategic transactions that expanded its clinical-stage oncology pipeline to four active assets. The new capital is earmarked to scale Foundry further while pushing those programs toward key milestones.

Top of the list is JSKN-016, a TROP2/HER3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that Pathos intends to advance into a registrational study. Funding will also support pocenbrodib in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, AZD4241, an ER PROTAC developed in partnership with AstraZeneca, and DO-2, a next-generation MET kinase inhibitor.

Pathos's broader pipeline already spans metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, multiple myeloma, MET-altered non-small-cell lung cancer, ER+/HER2-negative breast cancer, and TROP2/HER3-expressing solid tumors.

There is a general view that Series E funding could be the final preparatory stage to fuel a company’s next stage of growth – for example, going public. However, this has not been disclosed by Pathos.

Power in partnerships

Pathos has also disclosed a partnership with BMS and Tempus AI to build a specialized, curated dataset and agentic AI capabilities for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurological conditions. BMS also gains access to Pathos Foundry across its wider R&D portfolio.

“As an entrepreneur, seeing the engine your team built validated at this scale by a partner like BMS is the ultimate proof of concept. But we aren't stopping at oncology,” Pathos CEO Iker Huerga said on LinkedIn. “Together with Bristol Myers Squibb, we are expanding Foundry into Alzheimer’s and other neurological conditions. And to fuel that intelligence, we are partnering with Tempus AI to build the massive, longitudinal clinical dataset required to interrogate this biology at scale. Why neuroscience? Look at the numbers. 99% of clinical trials in neurodegenerative diseases fail.”

“You don't fix a 99% failure rate with incremental changes or by just working harder. You fix it by completely rewiring the foundation: how trials are designed, how patients are selected, and how human biology is understood. This is where AI is desperately needed, and where it will have the biggest impact,” he continued.

title: Reshoring prompts crucial decisions for medical device manufacturers | MedTech Dive
description:
For medical device manufacturers, reshoring plans have been part of the discussion for years.
That leaves them with crucial decisions to make, often with a high degree of risk and reward.
Reshoring is one part of a larger strategy Reshoring is far more than putting a new facility on domestic land.
“The ROI calculation can also include benefits that aren’t captured by simply comparing domestic and overseas production costs,” said Trompen.
Having production in your own backyard can provide greater control over all these factors.” Reshoring is also part of a broader leap in capacity in medical device manufacturing today.
text:
For medical device manufacturers, reshoring plans have been part of the discussion for years. Now, many are putting them into action and hitting familiar capacity challenges along the way.

New research from MedTech Dive and JR Automation shows why scaling is easier said than done. While 90% of manufacturers say increasing capacity is critically or very important to their competitive position, four in 10 have already paused or delayed investment due to uncertainty around which solution or approach to choose.

Most manufacturers don’t want to build new operations on outdated systems and processes. That leaves them with crucial decisions to make, often with a high degree of risk and reward.

Mick Trompen, Chief Engineer of Life Sciences at JR Automation, recently explained what’s behind this shift.

“The COVID pandemic was a big trigger. We were dependent on products made overseas, and then suddenly we needed to build machines in days to scale up domestic production. It was very… [reactive], and no one wants to be in that position again,” said Trompen. “The push to reshore is also regulatory and quality-driven. As devices become more advanced, and part of the competitive advantage, manufacturers want to be more protective of that technology and their IP.”

These factors may explain why manufacturers want production closer to home. But once they make that decision, an entirely different set of questions begins.

What should the new manufacturing environment look like?

Reshoring doesn’t mean taking an established overseas model and reproducing it domestically. According to Trompen, “It’s not going to be the same machines, computers, people, MES, or enterprise systems. Instead, it’s building from ground zero.”

This rebuilding process starts with the physical facility, deciding whether new construction or retrofitting makes the most sense, and extends to equipment and infrastructure.

Integration will likely be a core concern. The research shows the number one barrier to optimizing manufacturing operations is integration, cited by 47%. A reshoring initiative provides the opportunity to proactively address this leading barrier by focusing on how equipment, software, and data infrastructure work together from the start.

Leaders also need to consider what those systems will eventually support. AI is a major part of that equation: 84% say AI will be critically or very important to how they adapt and scale manufacturing over the next three to five years.

As AI and advanced analytics become increasingly important to operations, it makes sense to ensure the systems established during reshoring can support that vision long term.

How can we rethink manufacturability?

Even if a process is proven overseas, reshoring presents the opportunity to take a fresh look at design for manufacturing, including areas like automation, standardization, and modularity.

“When advanced devices first entered the market, the long-term potential wasn’t always considered. For example, can this device deliver more than one drug? Can we design it in a way that standardizes something simple like a spring? Can we use the same mechanics to avoid bottlenecks in our supply chain? Reshoring provides a perfect opportunity to explore those efficiencies and improve overall capacity,” said Trompen.

That means smart decisions made during the reshoring process can improve manufacturability now while supporting greater capacity for future products as well.

How will we staff the new operation?

Reshoring initiatives may compound existing staffing challenges: 42% say inadequate staffing is a barrier to optimization, the second-most-cited barrier.

One way to address staffing is to think beyond the number of hires, focusing instead on improving the roles people play alongside automation.

“Often, the answer becomes reallocating people into more technical positions. The person who might have been snapping two parts together or applying adhesive can now transition to quality inspection of the device, teaching robots, or maybe become part of the maintenance team,” said Trompen. Automation and workforce strategy should go hand in hand, especially during reshoring. Manufacturers can make informed decisions by evaluating what technical capabilities the new environment will require, which processes still need manual intervention, and where automation fits into the full picture.

Reshoring is one part of a larger strategy

Reshoring is far more than putting a new facility on domestic land. Every decision — from infrastructure and technology to automation and people — shapes what the new operation can deliver and at what cost.

“The ROI calculation can also include benefits that aren’t captured by simply comparing domestic and overseas production costs,” said Trompen. “For example, if poor quality was coming in from overseas, does bringing production closer offset that cost? Does greater automation improve consistency and therefore patient safety, which is always the number one priority? Having production in your own backyard can provide greater control over all these factors.”

Reshoring is also part of a broader leap in capacity in medical device manufacturing today. The findings shared in this article are one piece of that picture, with the broader story detailed in a new report from MedTech Dive and JR Automation. Based on a survey of 125 manufacturing decision-makers, the research reveals what’s challenging manufacturers most, where they’re headed, and what it will take to get there.

description:
Nvidia's sales and marketing organizations are seeing a changing of the guard as the AI boom reshapes demands on leadership.
Nvidia's sales pitch has evolved.
These customers care less about hardware specifications than how Nvidia's AI can be put to work.
Another Huang is gaining influence One insider bringing an unconventional background to Nvidia's marketing ranks is Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang.

text:
Nvidia's sales and marketing organizations are seeing a changing of the guard as the AI boom reshapes demands on leadership.

Veterans at Nvidia are retiring, opening the door for longtime employees. And CEO Jensen Huang is tapping talent from outside the company — and outside the chip industry — to meet new challenges.

Nvidia's sales pitch has evolved. It has already convinced companies to choose its chips. To keep growing, it has to convince more businesses to adopt AI. These customers care less about hardware specifications than how Nvidia's AI can be put to work.

Leadership changes are most visible in sales and marketing, said former vice president of corporate marketing Greg Estes, while other areas of the company, such as finance, legal, operations, and software and hardware engineering, have remained relatively stable.

In marketing, Nvidia tapped Google Cloud executive Alison Wagonfeld to become its first chief marketing officer earlier this year, while Microsoft veteran Nick Parker became its new sales chief in August. Neither comes from the chip industry, though both bring years of experience helping businesses adopt software and cloud services.

At the same time, Huang's daughter Madison has gained influence beyond her formal marketing role, two former employees said.

Huang regularly reshapes Nvidia as the business evolves, said Scott Baker, a sales VP who retired in July after 26 years.

"It's truly a battleship spinning on a dime, and everyone gets aligned," he said.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.

A 'deep bench' of younger Nvidia talent

Retirees this year include former sales EVP Jay Puri, VP of enterprise marketing Laura Fay, SVP of enterprise business Shanker Trivedi, and sales VP Kevin Connors.

Fay said Huang doesn't want to lose longtime executives, many of whom he personally recruited. But as they move on, the next generation is getting a chance.

Before leaving in April after 17 years, Trivedi made mentorship part of his mission. He was ready to pass the baton after years of grueling travel and seven-day workweeks.

"Time stops for nobody," the 69-year-old said.

Trivedi said Nvidia has a "deep bench" of younger sales and marketing talent who know its culture, market, and partners inside out, including Raj Mirpuri in AI cloud infrastructure, Kimberly Powell in healthcare, and Kari Briski in AI software.

When he retired, the company divided Trivedi's responsibilities among multiple leaders. As Nvidia's revenue soared during the AI boom, his job had ultimately become too big for one person.

"Better to flatten the structure and gain velocity," he said.

Another Huang is gaining influence

One insider bringing an unconventional background to Nvidia's marketing ranks is Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang.

Madison formerly worked at French luxury conglomerate LVMH in hospitality marketing before joining Nvidia as an MBA intern in 2020. She has quickly ascended to senior director of product marketing for physical AI.

One former employee said Madison's experience working on luxury brands brought a fresh perspective to a marketing team traditionally staffed by semiconductor veterans.

Job titles can be fluid at Nvidia, and a second former employee said Madison's remit extends beyond physical AI marketing. They said she exerts authority across multiple parts of the company and directs teams at all levels on strategy and business decisions.

Madison is also among a small circle of executives known to travel with her father. And their close relationship gives her the ability to anticipate his needs during high-level meetings and appearances, the first former employee said.

"She 'speaks Jensen' very well," the former employee said, "so he doesn't have to explain himself to her."

title: HP Inc (NYSE:HPQ) Rides an AI PC Refresh While Memory Costs Press on Margins
description:

For HP, among the leading makers of personal computers, this refresh supports demand across consumer and commercial lines.

text:
Highlights

HP has pointed to rising Personal Systems demand tied to an AI-capable personal-computer refresh.

Memory and storage costs have added pressure on margins across the hardware maker's lineup.

The company moves toward a fiscal-year quarterly report during the busiest reporting stretch of the autumn.

HP Inc (NYSE:HPQ) Technology HP Inc (NYSE:HPQ) 33.64 USD -0.120 ↓ 0.356% enters the final days of October as one of the more closely watched hardware makers on the American market, with market participants weighing a refresh cycle for AI-capable personal computers against persistent cost pressure in the memory market. The company's recent quarterly figures pointed to rising demand across its Personal Systems segment, keeping the maker of computers and printers near the center of conversation during the busiest reporting stretch of the autumn. The pairing of a demand recovery with a cost squeeze gives the name a clear tension that stands out amid a crowded wave of quarterly releases. The name continues to stand out among Value Stocks tracked by the market this month.

The timing matters because HP operates on a fiscal calendar that closes near the end of October, setting up a full-year report in the weeks that follow. As the broader market moves through its heaviest earnings window, the hardware maker has handed market observers a clear set of threads to track, from the pace of the AI PC refresh to the squeeze that higher component costs place on margins. The gap between the broader market's reporting peak and HP's own fiscal-year close keeps the name in focus well into the season.

What is driving attention to the hardware maker now

Attention has gathered around HP for a mix of reasons. A broad refresh of personal computers, spurred by AI-capable designs and the end of support for older operating-system versions, has supported demand in a category that had been soft for a stretch. At the same time, rising prices for memory and storage components have pressed on the cost side of the business, creating a tension that market participants are watching closely as it plays out across the hardware arena.

That tension, strong demand set against climbing component costs, sits at the heart of how the hardware maker is being described heading into its fiscal-year report. Market observers tracking the name weigh how far the demand recovery can offset the margin pressure, and how HP manages pricing to protect earnings across its lineup. The balance is a delicate one, since passing higher costs along can soften demand while absorbing them can compress margins, and the market will read the coming figures for signs of how the company is steering through it.

Inside the AI PC refresh cycle

The refresh of personal computers has been shaped by two forces working together. A wave of AI-capable machines, built with processors designed to handle on-device artificial-intelligence tasks, has given buyers a reason to upgrade. Alongside that, the retirement of support for older operating-system versions has pushed many households and organizations to replace aging hardware. The combination has lifted a category that had endured a prolonged soft stretch, giving makers a reason to describe the period ahead with more confidence.

For HP, among the leading makers of personal computers, this refresh supports demand across consumer and commercial lines. The company has pointed to rising Personal Systems revenue tied to the upgrade wave, and the pace of that refresh is among the most watched elements of its story as the fiscal-year report approaches. Commercial buyers, in particular, tend to upgrade in waves tied to operating-system transitions, which can give the refresh a longer runway across organizations than a consumer cycle alone.

Memory-cost pressure across the lineup

Rising prices for memory and storage components have emerged as a defining headwind for personal-computer makers. Demand for memory chips across data centers and artificial-intelligence systems has tightened supply, lifting costs for the makers that build finished computers. HP has flagged this dynamic as a pressure on margins, a theme market observers are tracking across the hardware sector as component prices climb.

How a maker manages this pressure, through pricing, component sourcing, and product mix, shapes how earnings bear up during a period of climbing costs. The balance between passing costs along and protecting demand is a delicate one, and HP's handling of it will be among the central threads in its fiscal-year report. Makers with scale can sometimes secure components on steadier terms, so the market will watch how the company's purchasing reach helps it navigate the squeeze relative to smaller rivals.

Inside the company's operations

HP operates across two broad segments, Personal Systems, which covers computers and related devices, and Printing, which spans hardware, supplies, and services. The combination gives the company a diversified base, with the steadier supplies business within Printing complementing the more cyclical personal-computer market. That mix has long shaped how market participants describe the firm, since the recurring demand for printing supplies can cushion the swings of the computer cycle.

The company has emphasized steady cash generation, disciplined cost management, and a dividend alongside a share-buyback program. Earlier in the fiscal year the firm reported revenue growth tied to Personal Systems demand, framing the approaching full-year report as another checkpoint on how the two segments are performing. The balance between the two segments is central to the company's story, and each report is read partly for how the cyclical and recurring pieces of the business are trending together.

The personal-computer and printing backdrop

The wider personal-computer arena has moved through a cycle of soft demand followed by a refresh wave, with AI-capable designs and operating-system transitions supporting a recovery. The printing arena, meanwhile, has been shaped by gradual shifts in office printing habits and steady demand for supplies, giving makers with strong supplies businesses a measure of stability through the swings of the hardware cycle.

HP sits within this backdrop as one of the largest makers of both personal computers and printers, with a brand familiar to households and organizations across the United States. The combination of a cyclical computer business and a steadier printing franchise places the company at an intersection that shapes how market participants describe its standing within the hardware sector. The recurring nature of supplies demand is part of why the printing business is often described as an anchor for the broader enterprise.

Where a value-oriented framing fits the story

HP frequently appears in discussions that group it among Value Stocks, a framing tied to its steady cash generation, its established market position in personal computers and printing, and its dividend alongside a buyback program. Names in this grouping tend to draw market participants who favor businesses with durable cash flows and tangible operations over faster-moving growth stories. Mature hardware makers, with their recognizable brands and steady supplies demand, often anchor such conversations during periods when market participants weigh defensive names against more cyclical areas.

As a member of the S&P 500, HP carries the visibility that comes with inclusion in a widely tracked benchmark, and that membership keeps the name in front of a broad audience whenever the technology-hardware sector comes into view. As a constituent of the NYSE Composite and the Russell 1000, the company sees its share-price moves feed directly into broad market readings. The pairing of benchmark membership with a clear demand-and-cost storyline has sharpened the spotlight on the maker heading into its fiscal-year report.

Partnerships and new technology directions

HP has pursued partnerships and technology directions that extend its reach beyond traditional hardware. The company has signed licensing arrangements covering wireless patents, pursued collaborations tied to artificial-intelligence platforms, and explored ventures in adjacent areas. Steps of this kind aim to broaden the business and keep the brand relevant as computing shifts toward AI-centric designs, giving the maker footholds in areas beyond the familiar computer and printer lines.

Moves such as these matter for a mature hardware maker because they open doors beyond the core businesses and can season the brand with newer technology associations. description:

text:
OpenAI has resumed training its most advanced artificial intelligence models after tightening security controls and restricting internet access, the company said on Friday. It also disclosed a vulnerability in widely used software that it discovered while testing its defences.

The announcement comes amid growing concern about the ability of increasingly capable AI agents to identify and exploit software vulnerabilities, including weaknesses in the safeguards designed to contain them.

OpenAI had paused training of its most capable models after one of its research models gained limited internet access in September because of a configuration error. The company said it contained the incident and used the pause to strengthen its security systems.

As part of the review, OpenAI deployed teams of AI agents to test whether they could escape their restricted environments. The agents uncovered previously unknown vulnerabilities, which the company said it had fixed. Model training resumed on 1 October.

During the testing, OpenAI discovered a flaw in Brotli, a widely used data compression tool.

The vulnerability could allow attackers to send malicious data that enables them to execute their own code on affected systems, according to OpenAI. Potentially exposed software includes widely used technologies such as Node.js, Bun and Envoy.

OpenAI said the underlying cause had been corrected in Brotli’s source code in February, before it was recognized as a security vulnerability. However, no updated software version was released at the time. Brotli has since issued updated versions and published a public record of the flaw following OpenAI’s disclosure.

The announcement followed a separate report on Thursday by AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research, which identified several vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal monitoring system during a pilot assessment earlier this year.

The researchers said one exploit could have allowed AI agents to conceal hundreds of actions from monitoring systems. OpenAI told the organizations that it had since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although the evaluators said they had not independently verified the fixes.

OpenAI has been conducting a broader review of its models’ activity since an incident involving an AI agent at the software development platform Hugging Face in July. The company has informed more than 100 organizations about incidents involving unauthorized activity linked to its AI agents.

description:

The deal addresses three key barriers to industrial AI adoption at scale – data sovereignty, cybersecurity and AI consumption costs.

text:
Schneider Electric announced a strategic collaboration with NVIDIA and HPE to accelerate the adoption of Physical AI across process and heavy industries. Built on HPE Private Cloud AI, autonomous AI agents operate directly within industrial environments, continuously monitoring, reasoning, and optimizing operations in real time. The deal addresses three key barriers to industrial AI adoption at scale – data sovereignty, cybersecurity and AI consumption costs.

While much of today’s Physical AI conversation is focused on robotics, humanoids and autonomous machines, process industries face a distinctly different challenge. Operators must manage complex, continuous operations where reliability, safety, cybersecurity and energy efficiency are critical to performance. Yet until now, there has been no clear blueprint for how Physical AI can be practically applied across these complex environments.

Schneider Electric, NVIDIA & HPE share a vision to bring AI closer to industrial operations, embedding intelligence directly within the environments where decisions are made and value is created. As an initial demonstration of this vision, the companies are today introducing Industrial AI Agents at the Edge.

The solution combines HPE Private Cloud AI, co-engineered with NVIDIA within the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA portfolio Schneider Electric’s deep operational technology expertise to enable organizations to securely deploy and scale AI applications at the industrial edge, bringing real-time intelligence closer to critical operations while maintaining control over sensitive data, security and costs.

Many industrial organizations continue to face challenges when scaling AI across operational environments. Requirements around data governance, cybersecurity, operational performance and AI deployment can create barriers to broader adoption.By operating at the edge, the solution helps address three challenges that continue to limit industrial AI at scale. Critical operational data is often too valuable, sensitive or regulated to move beyond operational boundaries. HPE Private Cloud AI provides the secure foundation for Industrial AI Agents at the Edge, enabling organizations to deploy AI close to operations while maintaining control, security and compliance.

Increased connectivity can also introduce additional risk across industrial and critical infrastructure environments. HPE Private Cloud AI reduces the attack surface by keeping and processing the data close to its source.

Cost is the third challenge. As AI usage grows, cloud inference, data transfer and token costs can climb, creating problems for organizations looking to scale AI across sites, assets and operations. Deploying AI at the edge with HPE Private Cloud AI can help reduce some of these costs while providing greater control over where and how AI workloads are executed.

Through Schneider Electric’s EcoStruxure Industrial Insights apps, customers can deploy, manage and govern multiple Industrial AI Agents through a single environment, simplifying lifecycle management, security oversight and maintaining full control of critical operations and infrastructure.

The first Industrial AI Agents focus on operational technology monitoring, cybersecurity and energy optimization. Their practical application can already be seen in industrial environments with companies such as CMPC Chile.

The foundation for this next step is already proven at CMPC Chile, part of Empresas CMPC S.A., one of Latin America’s largest pulp, paper and packaging producers. For the past three years, CMPC Chile has used Schneider Electric’s OTMS in production to monitor the health and availability of control systems across its continuous pulp and paper operations.

OTMS provides CMPC’s teams with a unified view of control systems, servers, workstations and switches, helping specialists identify emerging issues earlier, diagnose problems faster and establish clearer maintenance priorities. This proven deployment demonstrates the value of OTMS as a control-system monitoring solution and provides a strong operational foundation for the future introduction of Industrial AI Agents, with the potential to accelerate investigation and decision-making while keeping people in control of critical action.

The first three Industrial AI Agents at the edge cover OT monitoring, cybersecurity and energy optimization.

OT Monitoring Agents combine real-time operational data, equipment configurations, process topology, alarms, maintenance history and engineering context to understand the physical state of industrial operations. The agents identify emerging issues, reason about likely operational impacts, recommend or initiate corrective actions, and verify that the intervention delivers the expected physical outcome.

Cybersecurity Agents correlate network activity, control system behaviour, asset configurations, operational events and process context to detect abnormal conditions. The agents assess potential impacts on industrial operations, recommend or execute response measures, and validate that systems have returned to a secure and stable state.

Energy Optimization Agents integrate process data, energy consumption patterns, equipment performance, operating conditions and production requirements to understand how energy is used across industrial operations. The agents identify optimization opportunities, recommend or implement adjustments, and verify the resulting impact on energy efficiency, operational performance and sustainability outcomes.

“The next generation of industrial innovation will be driven by intelligence embedded directly into industrial operations,” said Gwenaelle Huet, Executive Vice President, Industrial Automation, Schneider Electric. “While much of today’s focus is on autonomous machines, we see a significant opportunity to apply Physical AI to the industrial systems that power the world’s critical industries. Together with NVIDIA and HPE, we are bringing together expertise in automation, AI and edge computing to help customers transform operational data into action, improving resilience, efficiency, cybersecurity and sustainability while laying the foundation for more autonomous industrial operations.”

“Industrial operations generate vast amounts of data, but turning that data into action remains one of industry’s biggest challenges. By combining NVIDIA Nemotron™ open AI models and HPE Private Cloud AI, a turnkey AI factory solution, with Schneider Electric’s industrial expertise and OTMS platform, Industrial AI Agents can monitor, reason and optimize operations in real time, accelerating the path to Physical AI for process industries,” commented Sri Kodali, Global Head of Developer Relations – Energy and Utilities at NVIDIA.

“Industrial organizations see real opportunities to use AI, and they want to be sure their sensitive data and critical systems will remain protected. Through our collaboration with NVIDIA and Schneider Electric, we’re helping customers use HPE Private Cloud AI to bring AI closer to where their data is generated and decisions are made. This gives customers a way to expand AI use across their facilities while maintaining the security, privacy and control their businesses require,” said Alexia Clements, SVP, Hybrid Cloud Solution Sales at HPE.

“For the past three years, OTMS has helped us improve visibility into the health and availability of our control systems. In continuous industrial operations, identifying issues early is critical to protecting production and avoiding costly disruption. Looking ahead, we see significant potential for AI Agents to build on this proven foundation, helping our specialists investigate issues faster and move more effectively from insight to action, while keeping people in control of critical decisions,” said Matías Jory, Digital & Process Manager, Industrial Operations Vice-Presidency, CMP.

Together, Schneider Electric, NVIDIA and HPE are creating the foundation for the next generation of industrial operations, where intelligent systems can continuously monitor, reason and optimize performance. Over time, these capabilities will help automate the automation, enabling safer, more efficient and increasingly autonomous operations across process industries.

title: Barclays plans 5,000 job cuts. Are Indian banks facing a similar shake-up? - India Today
description:
The British bank plans to eliminate around 5% of its global workforce, with approximately 1,000 positions already cut and another 4,000 expected to go by the end of the year.
Barclays has linked the move to wider cost-saving and technology-modernisation efforts, with AI expected to contribute to productivity gains.
ARE GLOBAL BANKS PLANNING WORKFORCE REDUCTIONS?
In May, Standard Chartered said it planned to eliminate more than 7,000 jobs globally by 2030, mainly from corporate and support functions.
In July, payments company Visa announced plans to cut around 2,600 jobs, or 7% of its global workforce.
text:
Barclays' plan to cut around 5,000 jobs by the end of 2026 has put the spotlight on how artificial intelligence (AI), automation and cost-cutting are changing the banking workforce. For India, the announcement comes amid a series of developments involving global financial companies and domestic lenders, although not all workforce reductions are layoffs or directly attributable to AI.

The British bank plans to eliminate around 5% of its global workforce, with approximately 1,000 positions already cut and another 4,000 expected to go by the end of the year. Around 60% of the planned reductions will affect support functions, including developers.

Barclays has linked the move to wider cost-saving and technology-modernisation efforts, with AI expected to contribute to productivity gains.

ARE GLOBAL BANKS PLANNING WORKFORCE REDUCTIONS?

Barclays is not the only international lender announcing cuts. In May, Standard Chartered said it planned to eliminate more than 7,000 jobs globally by 2030, mainly from corporate and support functions. The bank explicitly linked the reductions to automation and the growing use of AI, while saying some employees would be reskilled.

In March, HSBC was reported to be considering cutting as many as 20,000 roles, potentially affecting middle- and back-office functions. However, the proposal was still under discussion at the time and had not been finalised. It should therefore be treated as a potential workforce reduction, not a confirmed round of layoffs.

In July, payments company Visa announced plans to cut around 2,600 jobs, or 7% of its global workforce. Employees in India received layoff emails, although the company did not disclose how many Indian workers were affected.

Visa's move is relevant to the wider financial-services sector, but it is not a bank layoff. Nor can the entire reduction be attributed to AI, given the broader business and efficiency considerations behind restructuring.

THE INDIAN STORY

Domestic lenders present a different picture. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank and Axis Bank ended the 2025-26 financial year with more than 13,000 fewer employees combined, according to India Today Business.

ICICI Bank's workforce declined by 6,633 employees, HDFC Bank's by 3,343, and Axis Bank's by around 3,400. However, executives attributed the changes to factors including attrition, selective hiring, redeployment and technology-led productivity, rather than broad-based layoffs.

The distinction matters. Banks can reduce employee numbers by not replacing workers who leave or by moving staff into other functions, without dismissing thousands of employees.

BANKING JOBS ARE CHANGING, NOT DISAPPEARING UNIFORMLY

These developments point to a financial-services sector trying to improve productivity while investing in technology. Routine processing and administrative work may face greater pressure from automation, while demand can shift towards technology, cybersecurity, data analysis and customer-facing roles.

However, the available figures do not establish that AI caused every job reduction. Barclays and Standard Chartered have announced cuts linked partly to technology-led change; HSBC's reported plan remained under consideration; Visa announced layoffs; and India's largest private banks reduced headcount through different workforce measures.

For India, the central concern is how employees adapt as banks reorganise operations and change hiring priorities. The sector may continue to grow, but its workforce requirements could look increasingly different from those of the past.

text:
Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase graphics processing units, or GPUs, used to power artificial intelligence systems.

In a post on X on Sunday, Musk said SpaceX had closed the financing, adding that the company was investment grade and generated revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses.

In a follow-up post, he added that the financing, primarily consisted of callable debt for graphics processing units, is expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027.

Bloomberg reported earlier, citing people familiar with the matter, that SpaceX was in talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to purchase Nvidia chips.

The proposed financing would use a special purpose vehicle to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit ratings, according to Bloomberg.

Goldman Sachs was leading talks with investors, including Apollo Global Management, over the financing structure, according to Bloomberg.

The financing underscores the enormous capital requirements of the AI boom, as technology companies pour billions of dollars into advanced chips and data centers to support increasingly powerful AI models.

SpaceX has expanded aggressively into artificial intelligence this year, referring to the business as “Super Intelligence,” or SI.

The segment has become the company’s largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue surging ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million a year earlier, according to its latest earnings release.

Musk also said that debt markets have largely shut off access to financing for companies without substantial revenue outside AI data centers.

Nadella Bets on Agents, Model Choice and Cost

Nadella said the company has organized its business into "two new reporting segments: Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer." He described the change as a shift in how people use computers. title: Lilly advances amylin-based obesity combo to phase 3, tests tolerability amid Korea race
description:
Eli Lilly and Company will begin phase 3 trials of the obesity treatment combo "EloraTZP."
Lilly is focusing on the possibility that this drug could deliver greater weight loss than its own next-generation obesity candidate retatrutide.
◇ Amylin add-on boosts weight loss; treatment persistence is key EloraTZP is an obesity drug candidate that combines tirzepatide and eloralintide.
Lilly said adverse events occurred mainly during dose escalation and plans to refine the titration schedule in phase 3.
◇ Amylin emerges as a next-gen obesity drug keyword; Novo leads, Celltrion in pursuit Development of next-generation obesity treatments that leverage amylin's mechanism of action, like eloralintide, is active.
text:
Eli Lilly and Company will begin phase 3 trials of the obesity treatment combo "EloraTZP."

Lilly is focusing on the possibility that this drug could deliver greater weight loss than its own next-generation obesity candidate retatrutide. Retatrutide is a triple agonist that simultaneously targets GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors, and has been viewed as a strong contender after showing superior weight-loss effects to existing obesity drugs in late-stage trials.

The issue is tolerability—that is, "how well patients can endure side effects when taking the drug." For obesity drugs, the ability to continue long-term dosing is as critical a competitive edge as the amount of weight loss. In a prior phase 2 trial, EloraTZP's highest-dose group achieved an average weight-loss rate of 23.3%, but 27% of patients discontinued treatment due to adverse events.

◇ Amylin add-on boosts weight loss; treatment persistence is key

EloraTZP is an obesity drug candidate that combines tirzepatide and eloralintide.

Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Lilly's "zepbound" (sold in Korea as Mounjaro) and simultaneously activates the GIP and GLP-1 receptors, which are gut hormones. It promotes insulin secretion and blood sugar control while suppressing appetite to induce weight loss.

Eloralintide is a drug that mimics the action of amylin, a hormone secreted after meals. Amylin signals satiety to the brain and delays gastric emptying, helping reduce food intake.

In a phase 2 trial that followed 367 adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes for 48 weeks, the highest-dose group receiving tirzepatide 15 mg plus eloralintide 9 mg achieved an average weight-loss rate of 23.3%. By contrast, the rate was 14.8% in the group receiving tirzepatide 15 mg alone.

Blood sugar control also improved. Glycated hemoglobin, which reflects long-term glucose levels, fell by up to 2.9 percentage points in the combination group. The decrease in the tirzepatide 15 mg monotherapy group was 2.4 percentage points.

Of course, it is too early to interpret these figures as a definitive advantage. The phase 2 trial was designed primarily to assess efficacy versus placebo, and comparisons with tirzepatide monotherapy were secondary endpoints. Each dosing arm also had only about 37 patients, a small number.

The weight-loss rates likewise reflect an analysis that assumes patients continued treatment without discontinuation. In the EloraTZP combination arms, the treatment discontinuation rate due to adverse events ranged from 10.8% to 27.0%, depending on the dose combination. In the tirzepatide 15 mg monotherapy group, the discontinuation rate was 2.9%. Most events were gastrointestinal symptoms such as generally mild to moderate nausea and vomiting.

Lilly said adverse events occurred mainly during dose escalation and plans to refine the titration schedule in phase 3.

According to the U.S. clinical information site ClinicalTrials, Lilly recently registered two global phase 3 trials of EloraTZP (AMPLIFY-1, AMPLIFY-2). The large studies will enroll a total of 3,115 patients, stratified by the presence of type 2 diabetes, and both aim to complete in Nov. 2029.

◇ Amylin emerges as a next-gen obesity drug keyword; Novo leads, Celltrion in pursuit

Development of next-generation obesity treatments that leverage amylin's mechanism of action, like eloralintide, is active.

In terms of speed, Novo Nordisk's "cagrisema" is ahead. The drug combines the amylin analog cagrilintide with the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide and is under regulatory review in the United States.

However, for the phase 3 trial (REIMAGINE 5) comparing cagrisema with tirzepatide in patients with type 2 diabetes, rates of adverse events and treatment discontinuation have not yet been disclosed.

Barclays plans to cut around 5,000 jobs this year as it expands the use of artificial intelligence and simplifies its operations, while returning more cash to shareholders.The reductions amount to about 5% of its workforce, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. Chief Executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan described AI as enhancing the bank’s existing investment in technology.

Chief Financial Officer Anna Cross said 1,000 roles had already been eliminated, with the remainder due by year-end. Around 60% of the reductions affect support functions, including developers, according to Reuters’ results report.

The bank reported third-quarter pretax profit of approximately £2.3 billion, up 12%, and announced a further £500 million share buyback, according to The Guardian’s October 22 coverage. Group income increased 3% to £7.4 billion.

The investment bank delivered mixed results. Fixed-income trading income fell 19% to £1 billion, while equities revenue rose 47%, Reuters reported. That left the division’s income below analysts’ expectations.

The latest capital return follows the bank’s July 28 half-year announcement, which outlined a buyback of up to £1 billion and a dividend of 5.9 pence per ordinary share. Barclays then reported a common equity tier-one capital ratio of 14.3%.

For the six months ended June 30, pretax profit was £6.066 billion, compared with £5.203 billion a year earlier. Basic earnings per ordinary share rose to 30.7 pence from 24.7 pence, according to that regulatory report. The half-year dividend compared with 3.0 pence per ordinary share in the previous year.

Barclays’ workforce plans add to the debate over automation in professional services. Routine financial processing, customer service and administrative work are among the areas exposed to AI tools, reported by The FINANCIAL in September.

That report cautioned that exposure to automation does not automatically translate into job losses: corporate restructuring, changing demand and earlier hiring decisions also influence employment.

title: Delta Air Lines Won't Get Its Boeing 787-10s Until 2031, So The Airbus A350-1000 Has To ...
description:
Delta Air Lines is constructing a premium-heavy flagship operation centered around Seoul Incheon International Airport(ICN) and its foundational joint venture with Korean Air.
The newly ordered Boeing 787-10 fleet will not arrive until 2031, and so, the Airbus A350-1000 must carry that complex commercial strategy entirely on its own for years until the orders begin to arrive.
To support these high-frequency transpacific rotations, Delta is banking on sophisticated interior engineering capable of sustaining passenger comfort across ultra-long-haul durations.
To capture maximum revenue on transpacific routes, Delta designed its A350-1000 cabin around an unprecedented premium density.
Delta Air Lines' strategic reliance on the A350-1000 to spearhead its transpacific expansion highlights the high-stakes reality of modern fleet planning.
text:
Delta Air Lines is constructing a premium-heavy flagship operation centered around Seoul Incheon International Airport(ICN) and its foundational joint venture with Korean Air. The newly ordered Boeing 787-10 fleet will not arrive until 2031, and so, the Airbus A350-1000 must carry that complex commercial strategy entirely on its own for years until the orders begin to arrive.

How does placing the immediate transpacific burden on 20 A350-1000 airframes, scheduled to debut in early 2027, shape Delta's long-term competitive posture against rival US legacies? What forces compelled the airline to commit to a massive widebody modernization wave while accepting a multi-year delivery gap for its Dreamliner order? This article will cover exactly that.

Delta's New Asian Base

Delta is confirmed to debut its flagship Airbus A350-1000 aircraft in early 2027, deploying the widebody airframes on high-demand routes connecting Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to ICN, along with Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) to ICN, as detailed in reports from View Times. The deployment formalizes a major shift for the airline, leveraging Delta's joint venture with Korean Air to cement ICN as its main Asian transit hub. By funneling connecting traffic through ICN rather than traditional Tokyo gateways, Delta gains more efficient access to secondary markets across East Asia and Southeast Asia than it had before.

The Korean Air joint venture functions as an integrated commercial engine, aligning schedules, pricing, and frequent flyer benefits to capture high-yield corporate traffic moving between North America and Asian financial centers. According to Delta operational filings, passengers arriving at ICN on Delta flights can seamlessly connect to Korean Air's extensive regional network, bypassing the friction of multi-carrier itineraries. This partnership is incredibly important to Delta's transpacific profitability, because with it, every widebody flight departing US mega-hubs is backed by robust feed from both sides of the Pacific.

To support these high-frequency transpacific rotations, Delta is banking on sophisticated interior engineering capable of sustaining passenger comfort across ultra-long-haul durations. As Delta introduces the A350-1000, the layout of the cabin directly influences passenger acquisition and retention among high-paying business travelers who regularly compare legacy carriers with joint venture alternatives.

A Truly Premium Cabin Offering?

To capture maximum revenue on transpacific routes, Delta designed its A350-1000 cabin around an unprecedented premium density. As outlined in industry reports from Aviation Outlook, the aircraft features 53 Delta One Suites and 48 Premium Select seats, dedicating over 40% of total floor space to premium passengers. This heavy premium concentration reflects management's bet that corporate travel demand across the Pacific will continue to prioritize upgraded space and privacy over sheer economy volume.

Inside the cabin, the A350-1000 introduces Delta's next-generation Delta One Suite, which features fully flat beds measuring 6.5 feet (1.98 meters) long and personal entertainment screens using 24-inch 4K QLED technology. Furthermore, Airbus announcements confirm that Delta's 20 A350-1000s will be equipped with a first-of-its-kind multi-orbit inflight connectivity solution. With Hughes low-earth-orbit and geosynchronous-earth-orbit technology integrated through Airbus HBCplus, passengers will experience uninterrupted high-speed internet connectivity throughout transoceanic flights.

Integrating these advanced hardware amenities aligns directly with Delta's broader widebody modernization strategy. By outfitting its flagship fleet with next-generation suites and high-speed multi-orbit connectivity, the carrier can offer a standardized luxury product that reinforces its competitive edge in both corporate and premium leisure markets.

The Start Of The Modernization

Delta kicked off a massive widebody modernization campaign in the first half of 2026, placing firm orders for 95 new aircraft to replace aging twinjets across its international network. As detailed by Airways Magazine, this record order spree follows a phenomenal financial year in 2025, during which the carrier generated $5 billion in pre-tax profit on $63.4 billion in operating revenue. The order book includes 30 firm 787-10s alongside 30 options: 16 A330-900neos, 15 A350-900s, and 34 A321neos.

The multi-type acquisition drives a clear fleet segmentation strategy across Delta's global network. Network planners intend to deploy the newly ordered A350-1000s and A350-900s on ultra-long-haul transpacific sectors and high-demand Middle Eastern corridors, such as routes to Riyadh Airport(RUH), though the debut of this specific route has been delayed amid regional safety concerns. The incoming A330-900neos will primarily serve transatlantic markets and South American routes. This division ensures that each aircraft variant operates within its optimal range and payload envelope, maximizing fuel efficiency and reducing unit operating costs across distinct geographical regions.

The A350-900s and A330neos ultimately handle core international growth in the near term, but the delayed arrival of the 787-10 fleet shifts the real heavy lifting onto the A350-1000 program, turning it into the central pillar of Delta's long-haul evolution, a role that was not necessarily envisaged when the -1000 variant entered Delta's fleet plans.

Is The A350-1000 Enough In The Meantime?

The scheduled arrival of Delta's 30 firm 787-10s beginning in 2031 has created a significant operational timeline gap. Industry reports from Simple Flying show that manufacturing backlogs and production slot allocations pushed the first Dreamliner deliveries five years out from the initial order announcement. Consequently, Delta will need to rely entirely on its Airbus widebody deliveries to bridge the gap between retiring older 767s and 777s and the eventual arrival of the 787-10 fleet.

From an operating economics standpoint, the A350-1000 brings immediate relief through advanced propulsion technology. Powered by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines, the A350-1000 delivers up to 20% lower fuel burn per seat-mile compared to the older aircraft it replaces, supported by Airbus data indicating a 15% to 25% lower overall seat-mile cost than legacy widebody competitors. However, concentrating all ultra-long-haul growth onto a single Airbus flagship type exposes Delta to supply chain vulnerabilities, spare-engine availability constraints, and intensive maintenance scheduling pressures across its Atlanta maintenance bases.

Keeping these manufacturing delays under control is a great challenge for Delta and demands rigorous maintenance planning and careful route allocation. Network managers have to extract maximum utilization from initial A350-1000 deliveries, and at the same time, safeguard spare parts inventory and pilot training pipelines to prevent any potential disruptions from becoming more problematic across the broader transpacific network.

Still A Wait To Be At Full Strength

Relying on a constrained initial batch of airframes isn't ideal from a network scheduling standpoint. Although Delta holds 20 firm A350-1000 orders, contractually committed delivery schedules allocate only the first eight aircraft to arrive through 2027, following earlier projections that anticipated 2026 handovers, as per Engine Cowl. The limited initial inventory means network planners will need to concentrate the new flagships strictly on core profit generators like the ATL and DTW routes to ICN, leaving little spare capacity for speculative route launches.

Expanding into emerging long-haul markets, such as launching service to RUH or evaluating a potential return to Indian airspace, depends entirely on subsequent A350-1000 deliveries arriving in 2028 and beyond and how fast those actually come in. If delivery slots slip or global supply chain snags delay airframe handovers, Delta will have little choice but to defer secondary route expansion plans to protect frequencies on its crucial Korean Air joint-venture corridors. Balancing high-yielding joint venture commitments with adventurous new city pairs will really show the elasticity of Delta's rather narrow widebody inventory.

Balancing these competing operational pressures dictates the pace of Delta's international network evolution. Because the initial wave of A350-1000 deliveries will have to cover essential joint-venture routes to ICN, any unexpected supply chain friction or maintenance issue directly impacts the airline's capacity to test new long-haul markets and, therefore, compete more fiercely with its Transpacific rivals.

Is Help Needed?

Delta Air Lines' strategic reliance on the A350-1000 to spearhead its transpacific expansion highlights the high-stakes reality of modern fleet planning. Delta has set its operational focus around Seoul Incheon and the Korean Air joint venture while accepting a five-year wait for its Boeing 787-10 deliveries. As a result, the carrier is placing an immense operational bet on a single Airbus flagship arriving in stages. What this shows is that network success depends as much on delivery schedule timing as on onboard product innovation.

Sustaining this ambitious strategy through 2031 will be hard, requiring flawless execution from both Airbus and engine manufacturer Rolls-Royce, along with consistent corporate yields across transpacific corridors. The first A350-1000s are set to enter service in early 2027, and at that point, maintenance metrics, cabin reliability, and connection volumes at ICN will be what determines if Delta's interim flagship can successfully carry its Asian ambitions alone, or whether it desperately needs some assistance.

name: Walmart
title: Can Walmart's New Bundled Subscription Beat Amazon? - The Globe and Mail
description:
Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) is offering a bundled subscription deal that could knock Amazon's (NASDAQ: AMZN) Prime membership off its pedestal.
Memberships have proven to be lucrative revenue channels for companies like Walmart and Amazon.
So can Walmart's new subscription bundle dethrone Amazon Prime?
Amazon Prime is so deeply entrenched at this point that the mix of streaming, fast shipping, and ubiquity among consumers is almost immovable.
Walmart's membership growth was also impressive at 17%.
text:
Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) is offering a bundled subscription deal that could knock Amazon's (NASDAQ: AMZN) Prime membership off its pedestal. Earlier this week, the company announced a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for just $120 per year. That's $100 less than the two programs priced separately, and $19 less than Amazon Prime's $139 cost.

The bundle includes free delivery, 2% Sam's Cash on select purchases, $0.10 off per gallon of gas, and a choice between Peacock and Paramount+ streaming, among other perks. The catch is that it is only available as an annual subscription, and there's no free trial or monthly option available at this time.

Memberships have proven to be lucrative revenue channels for companies like Walmart and Amazon. Shoppers tend to spend significantly more with the merchant when they have a membership, roughly four times as much as non-members in Walmart's case.

So can Walmart's new subscription bundle dethrone Amazon Prime? Probably not. Amazon Prime is so deeply entrenched at this point that the mix of streaming, fast shipping, and ubiquity among consumers is almost immovable. However, Walmart doesn't have to beat Amazon to succeed. This is what investors should focus on.

This particular offering strengthens Walmart's flywheel and advertising business. Walmart stock trades at a hefty premium, leaving little room for stumbles this holiday season. Some investors may want to wait for a better entry point. Still, overall, Walmart is an incredibly strong business that just created a new product that will help solidify and deepen customer engagement.

Shares of Walmart have risen nearly 6% year to date as of this writing. The stock is trading at roughly 40 times both forward and trailing earnings. The company's e-commerce segment continues to grow substantially, increasing 23% in the fiscal 2027 second quarter. Walmart's membership growth was also impressive at 17%.

Whether it overtakes Amazon or not, Walmart is a worthy investment.
